# Lie groups and Lie algebras {#sec-lie-theory}

Lie groups are groups that are also manifolds, so that their elements depend smoothly on continuous parameters; their Lie algebras are the infinitesimal generators, and the exponential map turns generators into group elements. The chapter has two parts: the structure of Lie groups and Lie algebras (matrix groups, brackets, the exponential map, Maurer-Cartan forms), and their representations (weights of $su(2)$, roots of $su(3)$, and the branching of a representation under a subalgebra).

## Lie groups and Lie algebras {#sec-lie-groups-algebras}

Lie groups are groups that are also manifolds, so that their elements can be multiplied and also differentiated: the
rotations of space, the unitary matrices of quantum mechanics and the phases of electromagnetism are the standard
examples. This chapter has four sections. Lie groups defines the objects, the matrix groups that realise all the
examples used in these lectures, their subgroups, their smooth actions on manifolds and the coverings between them,
with $U(1)$, $SO(3)$ and $SU(2)$ as running examples. Lie algebras linearises a group at its identity: a vector space
with a bracket, described by structure constants, acted on by the group through the adjoint representation and
equipped with the Killing form. The exponential map goes back from the algebra to the group through one-parameter
subgroups, and Maurer-Cartan forms carry the bracket over the whole group as left-invariant vector fields and one-forms
obeying the Maurer-Cartan equation. Every statement is followed by three examples and three exercises with hidden
solutions, and many exercises have Sage solutions.

### Lie groups {#sec-lie-groups}

Symmetries of a space form a group, and when the symmetries depend smoothly on parameters, as rotations depend on
angles, the group is itself a manifold: a Lie group. Isometry groups of metrics, and quotients of one Lie group by
another, are the two ways in which Lie groups enter geometry later in the book. This section defines Lie groups,
matrix groups, subgroups, actions and covers, and works them out for $U(1)$, $SO(3)$ and $SU(2)$.

#### Lie groups

The definition combines two structures met earlier, a group and a smooth manifold, and asks only that they be
compatible. Compatibility means that the two group operations, multiplication and inversion, are smooth maps in the
charts of the manifold.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-lie-group}
#### Lie group

A **Lie group** is a group $G$ (@def-group) that is also a smooth manifold (@def-manifold), such that
multiplication $G \times G \to G$ and inversion $G \to G$ are smooth maps. Its **dimension** is its dimension as a
manifold.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest non-trivial Lie group is one-dimensional and abelian. It is the group of phases, which is at the same time
the circle and the rotation group of the plane.

::: {#exm-lie-group-u1}
#### The circle group

$U(1) = \{e^{i\alpha}\}$ is the circle $S^1$ with the multiplication $e^{i\alpha}e^{i\beta} = e^{i(\alpha + \beta)}$,
smooth in the angle chart: a Lie group of dimension $1$, abelian. The rotations $SO(2)$ of the plane are the
same Lie group (@exm-iso-so2-u1).
:::

Matrices give non-abelian examples in which smoothness is automatic, because products and inverses are polynomial or
rational functions of the entries. The group of unit quaternions, written as $2 \times 2$ unitary matrices, is the
three-sphere.

::: {#exm-lie-group-su2}
#### $SU(2)$ is the three-sphere

$SU(2)$ is the manifold $S^3$ of @exm-su2-chart, and matrix multiplication and inversion ($g^{-1} = g^\dagger$)
are polynomial in the entries, hence smooth: a Lie group of dimension $3$. The torus $T^2 = U(1) \times U(1)$ is
an abelian Lie group of dimension $2$, and $\mathbb{R}^n$ under addition a Lie group of dimension $n$.
:::

The rotations of three-dimensional space are the most familiar non-abelian Lie group. Their manifold is not a sphere
but the quotient of $S^3$ by the antipodal map, and finite groups appear as the zero-dimensional extreme.

::: {#exm-lie-group-so3}
#### The rotation group

$SO(3)$ is a Lie group of dimension three (a rotation is specified by an axis, two parameters, and an angle); it
is the quotient $SU(2)/\{\pm 1\}$ (@exm-iso-double-cover, @fig-double-cover), hence the manifold $S^3$ with
antipodal points identified, the real projective space $\mathbb{RP}^3$. Finite groups such as $S_3$ are Lie groups
of dimension $0$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise examines a group of upper triangular matrices that is non-abelian but still very close to the
vector space $\mathbb{R}^3$. It checks the smoothness of the group operations by computing them explicitly.

::: {#exr-lg-heisenberg-group}
#### The Heisenberg group

Let $h(x, y, z) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x & z \\ 0 & 1 & y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Compute $h(x_1, y_1, z_1)
h(x_2, y_2, z_2)$ and $h(x, y, z)^{-1}$, conclude that these matrices form a Lie group of dimension $3$ diffeomorphic
to $\mathbb{R}^3$, and show that it is not abelian.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The product is $h(x_1 + x_2, y_1 + y_2, z_1 + z_2 + x_1y_2)$ and the inverse is $h(-x, -y, xy - z)$: both are
polynomial in the coordinates $(x, y, z)$, which form a single global chart identifying the group with
$\mathbb{R}^3$. The commutator $g_1g_2 - g_2g_1$ has the single entry $x_1y_2 - x_2y_1$ in the corner, which is
non-zero in general, so the group is not abelian; only the third coordinate feels the non-commutativity.

{{< sage exr-lg-heisenberg-group >}}
:::

New Lie groups can be made from old ones by taking products. The second exercise shows that the product of two Lie
groups is again one, and identifies the tori as products of circles.

::: {#exr-lg-product-group}
#### Products of Lie groups

Show that if $G$ and $H$ are Lie groups then $G \times H$, with the componentwise product $(g, h)(g', h') = (gg',
hh')$, is a Lie group of dimension $\dim G + \dim H$. Deduce that the torus $T^n = U(1)^n$ is an abelian Lie group of
dimension $n$, and that $SU(2) \times U(1)$ has dimension $4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The product manifold $G \times H$ has charts $\phi \times \psi$ built from charts of the factors, and its dimension is
the sum. In such charts the multiplication $((g, h), (g', h')) \mapsto (gg', hh')$ has components that are the
multiplications of $G$ and of $H$ in their own charts, which are smooth; the same holds for the inversion $(g, h)
\mapsto (g^{-1}, h^{-1})$. Applied $n$ times to $U(1)$ this gives the torus $T^n$, abelian because each factor is, of
dimension $n \cdot 1$. $SU(2) \times U(1)$ has dimension $3 + 1 = 4$, the same as $U(2)$, to which it is related by
the two-to-one map $(g, e^{i\alpha}) \mapsto e^{i\alpha}g$.
:::

A Lie group structure is not attached to a set but to the operations put on it, and the same manifold can carry an
unexpected product. The third exercise transports the multiplication of the positive reals to a half-line by a change
of coordinates.

::: {#exr-lg-twisted-line}
#### A twisted product on a half-line

On $M = (-1, \infty)$ define $x * y = x + y + xy$. Show that $(M, *)$ is a Lie group: find the identity and the
inverse, prove associativity, and exhibit an isomorphism with the multiplicative group $(0, \infty)$ and then with
$(\mathbb{R}, +)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The map $\phi(x) = 1 + x$ sends $M$ to $(0, \infty)$ and $\phi(x * y) = 1 + x + y + xy = (1 + x)(1 + y) =
\phi(x)\phi(y)$, so $*$ is the ordinary product transported by $\phi$. Associativity, the identity $0 = \phi^{-1}(1)$
and the inverse $x^{-1} = \phi^{-1}(1/(1 + x)) = -x/(1 + x)$ follow from those of the multiplicative group; all three
operations are smooth on $M$. Composing with the logarithm gives $\log(1 + x)$, a diffeomorphism $M \to \mathbb{R}$
turning $*$ into addition, so $(M, *)$ is the one-dimensional Lie group $\mathbb{R}$ in disguise.
:::
::::

All the examples above are groups of matrices or are isomorphic to such groups. The next definition singles out this
class, which is large enough for every group used in these lectures and comes with a ready-made manifold structure.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-matrix-lie-group}
#### Matrix Lie group

A **matrix Lie group** is a subgroup of $GL(n, \mathbb{R})$ or $GL(n, \mathbb{C})$ that is a closed subset
(@def-open-set); every closed subgroup of $GL(n)$ is a Lie group, with the manifold structure inherited from the
matrix entries. All Lie groups in these lectures are matrix Lie groups.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The largest matrix group is the group of all invertible matrices. Because its defining condition is an inequality,
it is an open subset of the space of matrices and its dimension is the full number of entries.

::: {#exm-matrix-gl}
#### The general linear group

$GL(n, \mathbb{R})$, the invertible $n \times n$ real matrices, is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ (the
complement of the closed set $\det = 0$), so it is a Lie group of dimension $n^2$ with the identity chart;
$GL(n, \mathbb{C})$ has real dimension $2n^2$.
:::

Imposing that a matrix preserve the Euclidean inner product cuts the general linear group down to a closed subgroup.
The dimension count, entries minus independent equations, is the method used throughout this section.

::: {#exm-matrix-orthogonal}
#### Orthogonal and special orthogonal groups

$O(n) = \{R : R^{\mathsf{T}}R = 1\}$, the isometries of $\mathbb{R}^n$ fixing the origin, is closed in $GL(n,
\mathbb{R})$ and has dimension $n(n-1)/2$ (the $n(n+1)/2$ equations $R^{\mathsf{T}}R = 1$ cut $n^2$ dimensions
down); $SO(n)$ is its component of determinant one (@exm-connected-groups), the rotations. $SO(2)$ has dimension
$1$ and $SO(3)$ dimension $3$.
:::

The complex analogue preserves the Hermitian inner product of $\mathbb{C}^n$. Adding the condition of unit
determinant removes one real dimension, and the special unitary groups include the gauge groups of particle physics.

::: {#exm-matrix-unitary}
#### Unitary and special unitary groups

$U(n) = \{U : U^\dagger U = 1\}$ is closed in $GL(n, \mathbb{C})$ with dimension $n^2$, and $SU(n)$, its
subgroup of determinant one, has dimension $n^2 - 1$: $SU(2)$ has dimension $3$ and $SU(3)$, the gauge group of
the strong interaction, dimension $8$. $U(1)$ is the case $n = 1$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The figure below shows the relation between the two three-dimensional groups $SU(2)$ and $SO(3)$ along one
one-parameter subgroup. The interactive version then follows rotations about several axes acting on a vector.

$SU(2)$, which returns to the identity only at $t = 4\pi$ ($e^{2\pi T_3} = -1$). Right: the circle of rotations
$R(t)$ about the $Z$-axis in $SO(3)$, of period $2\pi$. The dotted lines show the two-to-one map: $t$ and $t +
2\pi$ give the same rotation. Computed with Sage's matrix exponential. Generated by
`figures/double_cover.sage`.](figures/double_cover.svg){#fig-double-cover width=85%}

{{< interactive double_cover 460 >}}

The interactive version draws the orbits of the vector $v = (0.8, 0, 0.6)$ of the unit sphere under the rotations
$e^{t\,n \cdot L}$ about three axes $n$. Hovering a marker shows $t$, the rotated vector and one of the two elements

The first exercise on matrix groups counts dimensions by subtracting the number of independent equations from the
number of real entries. It confirms the values quoted in the examples for small $n$.

::: {#exr-dimension-count}
#### Dimensions of matrix groups

Count the dimensions of $O(n)$, $U(n)$ and $SU(n)$ from the number of independent equations defining them, and
check the values for $n = 2, 3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$R^{\mathsf{T}}R = 1$ is a symmetric matrix equation, $n(n+1)/2$ real conditions on $n^2$ entries: $\dim O(n) =
n(n-1)/2$, giving $1$ and $3$. $U^\dagger U = 1$ is Hermitian, $n^2$ real conditions on $2n^2$ real entries:
$\dim U(n) = n^2$, giving $4$ and $9$; $\det U = 1$ removes one more (the phase), $\dim SU(n) = n^2 - 1$, giving
$3$ and $8$. The equal dimensions $3$ of $SO(3)$ and $SU(2)$ are explained by the double cover.
:::

The dimension count can be made rigorous with the regular value theorem: a level set of a function whose gradient
never vanishes on it is a submanifold. The second exercise applies this to the determinant.

::: {#exr-lg-sl2-dimension}
#### $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ is three-dimensional

Show that $SL(2, \mathbb{R}) = \{\det = 1\}$ is a closed subgroup of $GL(2, \mathbb{R})$, compute the gradient of
$\det$ on $\mathbb{R}^4$, and deduce that it is a submanifold of dimension $3$ whose tangent space at $1$ is the space
of traceless matrices.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ is a subgroup because $\det$ is multiplicative, and closed because $\det$ is continuous. For
$M = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ the gradient of $\det = ad - bc$ is $(d, -c, -b, a)$, which vanishes
only at $M = 0$, where $\det = 0$; so $1$ is a regular value and $\{\det = 1\}$ is a submanifold of dimension $4 - 1 =
3$. At the identity the gradient is $(1, 0, 0, 1)$, and a tangent vector $X$ must satisfy $X_{11} + X_{22} = 0$: the
tangent space is $\{\operatorname{tr} X = 0\}$, the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R})$ of
@exm-u1-algebra. The curve in the Sage output has determinant one and a traceless velocity at $t = 0$.

{{< sage exr-lg-sl2-dimension >}}
:::

Groups preserving a bilinear form other than the inner product are matrix groups in the same way. The third exercise
treats the antisymmetric form of classical mechanics, whose group is the symplectic group.

::: {#exr-lg-symplectic}
#### The symplectic group

Let $J = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1_n \\ -1_n & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $Sp(2n, \mathbb{R}) = \{M : M^{\mathsf{T}}JM = J\}$.
Show that it is a matrix Lie group, that $Sp(2, \mathbb{R}) = SL(2, \mathbb{R})$, and that its dimension is $n(2n +
1)$; check the dimension with Sage for $n = 1, 2, 3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $M$ and $N$ preserve $J$ then $(MN)^{\mathsf{T}}J(MN) = N^{\mathsf{T}}(M^{\mathsf{T}}JM)N = J$, and taking
determinants of $M^{\mathsf{T}}JM = J$ gives $(\det M)^2 = 1$, so $M$ is invertible with inverse $J^{-1}M^{\mathsf{T}}J$
in the group; the condition is polynomial, so the subgroup is closed. For $n = 1$ a direct computation gives
$M^{\mathsf{T}}JM = (\det M)\,J$, so the condition is $\det M = 1$. In general $M^{\mathsf{T}}JM$ is antisymmetric,
so the equation imposes $2n(2n - 1)/2 = n(2n - 1)$ conditions on $4n^2$ entries, leaving $4n^2 - n(2n - 1) = n(2n +
1)$; Sage confirms this by computing the dimension of the tangent space $\{X^{\mathsf{T}}J + JX = 0\}$:

{{< sage exr-lg-symplectic >}}
:::
::::

Inside a Lie group, the subsets that are groups and submanifolds at the same time inherit the structure. The next
definition names them and includes the most important case, the image of a homomorphism from the real line.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-lie-subgroup}
#### Lie subgroup

A **Lie subgroup** of $G$ is a subgroup that is also a submanifold; closed subgroups of a Lie group are Lie
subgroups. A **one-parameter subgroup** is a smooth homomorphism $\mathbb{R} \to G$, $t \mapsto g(t)$ with $g(s)g(t)
= g(s + t)$ (@sec-exponential).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The rotations about one fixed axis are the basic example of a closed subgroup. In $SU(2)$ the corresponding subgroup
is the circle of diagonal matrices, and the double cover maps the second onto the first.

::: {#exm-lie-subgroup-so2}
#### $SO(2) \subset SO(3)$ and $U(1) \subset SU(2)$

The rotations about the $Z$-axis form a closed subgroup $SO(2)$ of $SO(3)$, a circle inside $\mathbb{RP}^3$; the
diagonal matrices $e^{tT_3}$ form a closed subgroup $U(1)$ of $SU(2)$, a great circle of $S^3$
(@fig-double-cover). Both are one-parameter subgroups, $R(s)R(t) = R(s + t)$ (@prp-so2-group).
:::

A one-parameter subgroup is always a Lie subgroup, but it need not be closed. On the torus the slope of the line decides
between a closed circle and a dense winding.

::: {#exm-lie-subgroup-torus}
#### Subgroups of the torus

In $T^2 = U(1) \times U(1)$ the subgroup $\{(e^{it}, e^{it})\}$ is a closed circle, while $\{(e^{it}, e^{i\alpha
t})\}$ with $\alpha$ irrational is a one-parameter subgroup that winds densely around the torus
(@exm-torus-curve) and is not closed: a Lie subgroup need not be closed.
:::

Discrete subgroups are the zero-dimensional Lie subgroups. Dividing by them does not change the dimension but can
change the global shape, as the passage from $SU(2)$ to $SO(3)$ shows.

::: {#exm-lie-subgroup-finite}
#### Discrete subgroups

$\{\pm 1\} \subset SU(2)$, $\mathbb{Z}_n \subset U(1)$ (the $n$-th roots of unity) and $2\pi\mathbb{Z} \subset
\mathbb{R}$ are closed subgroups of dimension $0$; quotients by them, $SU(2)/\{\pm 1\} = SO(3)$, $U(1)/\mathbb{Z}_n
\cong U(1)$ and $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z} = U(1)$, are again Lie groups of the same dimension.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Closedness is the property that guarantees a subgroup is a Lie subgroup with the induced topology. The first exercise
sorts four subgroups by this criterion.

::: {#exr-closed-subgroup}
#### Closed or not

Decide which of the following subgroups of a Lie group are closed: $SO(2) \subset SO(3)$; the diagonal matrices
in $GL(n, \mathbb{R})$; the irrational line $\{(e^{it}, e^{i\sqrt2 t})\} \subset T^2$; $\mathbb{Q} \subset
\mathbb{R}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$SO(2)$ is closed (defined by the equations $R e_3 = e_3$). The diagonal invertible matrices are closed (the
off-diagonal entries vanish), a Lie group of dimension $n$. The irrational line is not closed: it is dense in
the torus, and its closure is all of $T^2$. $\mathbb{Q}$ is not closed in $\mathbb{R}$ (its closure is
$\mathbb{R}$) and is not a Lie subgroup at all, being countable but not discrete.
:::

The elements commuting with the whole group form a closed subgroup, the centre. The second exercise computes it for
$SU(2)$ and relates it to the kernel of the double cover.

::: {#exr-lg-centre-su2}
#### The centre of $SU(2)$

Show that $g \in SU(2)$ commutes with all of $SU(2)$ if and only if it commutes with the three generators $T_a$, and
deduce that the centre is $\{\pm 1\}$. Is it a closed subgroup?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $g$ commutes with every element it commutes with $e^{tT_a}$ for all $t$, and differentiating at $t = 0$ gives
$gT_a = T_ag$; conversely, every element of $SU(2)$ is a product of exponentials of the $T_a$ (@eq-euler-angles), so
commuting with the $T_a$ suffices. A $2 \times 2$ matrix commuting with $\sigma_3$ is diagonal, and a diagonal matrix
commuting with $\sigma_1$ has equal diagonal entries: $g = \lambda 1$. Unitarity and $\det g = \lambda^2 = 1$ give
$\lambda = \pm 1$. The centre $\{\pm 1\}$ is finite, hence closed, and it is the kernel of $g \mapsto
\operatorname{Ad}_g$, since $\operatorname{Ad}_g = 1$ means precisely that $g$ commutes with the Lie algebra.
:::

Closed abelian subgroups that are as large as possible play the role of coordinate axes in a compact group. The third
exercise finds them for the special unitary groups.

::: {#exr-lg-maximal-torus}
#### The diagonal torus of $SU(n)$

Show that the diagonal matrices in $SU(n)$ form a closed subgroup isomorphic to the torus $T^{n - 1}$, and that for
$n = 2$ it is the subgroup $U(1)$ of @exm-lie-subgroup-so2.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A diagonal unitary matrix has entries of modulus one, $\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\alpha_1}, \dots, e^{i\alpha_n})$,
and the determinant condition is $\alpha_1 + \dots + \alpha_n \in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$. The vanishing of the off-diagonal
entries is a closed condition and products of diagonal matrices are diagonal, so this is a closed subgroup. The map
$(e^{i\alpha_1}, \dots, e^{i\alpha_{n-1}}) \mapsto \operatorname{diag}(e^{i\alpha_1}, \dots, e^{i\alpha_{n-1}},
e^{-i(\alpha_1 + \dots + \alpha_{n-1})})$ is an isomorphism from $T^{n-1}$ onto it, smooth with smooth inverse. For $n =
2$ the subgroup is $\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\alpha}, e^{-i\alpha}) = e^{-2\alpha T_3}$, the circle of
@exm-lie-subgroup-so2.
:::
::::

#### Actions and covers

A Lie group is usually met through what it does to another manifold. The definition of a smooth action adds to the
group action of an abstract group the requirement that it depend smoothly on both the group element and the point.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-smooth-action}
#### Smooth action

A **smooth action** of a Lie group $G$ on a manifold $M$ is a group action (@def-group-action) $(g, p) \mapsto
g \cdot p$ that is a smooth map $G \times M \to M$. The **orbit map** $g \mapsto g \cdot p$ is then smooth, and the
stabiliser $G_p$ (@def-stabiliser) is a closed subgroup, called the **isotropy group** of $p$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Rotations acting on the sphere are the model of a transitive action with a non-trivial isotropy group. The sphere is
then recovered as a quotient of the group by that isotropy group.

::: {#exm-action-so3-sphere}
#### Rotations of the sphere

$SO(3)$ acts smoothly and transitively on $S^2$ by matrix multiplication; the isotropy group of the north pole is
$SO(2)$, and the orbit-stabiliser bijection $SO(3)/SO(2) \to S^2$ is a diffeomorphism (@sec-coset-spaces). The
orbits of the subgroup $SO(2)$ are the parallels and the two poles.
:::

An action can also be free, with every isotropy group trivial. The circle acting on the three-sphere by right
multiplication is free, and its orbit space is the two-sphere.

::: {#exm-action-u1-s3}
#### $U(1)$ on the three-sphere

$U(1)$ acts on $SU(2) = S^3$ by right multiplication $g \mapsto g\,e^{tT_3}$, smoothly and freely (no fixed
points); the orbits are circles, the fibres of the Hopf fibration (@sec-hopf), and the quotient is $S^2$.
:::

The isometries of a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian metric form a Lie group acting on the manifold. This is the source
of most actions in physics, with spacetime symmetries as the leading case.

::: {#exm-action-isometries}
#### Isometry groups

The isometries of a metric (@def-isometry) form a Lie group acting smoothly on the manifold: $SO(3)$ for the round
sphere, $U(1)$ for the circle, the Euclidean group $E(2)$ for the plane, the Poincaré group for Minkowski space,
with the Killing fields of @sec-killing as generators (@sec-exponential).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The isotropy group of a point can be found infinitesimally, by asking which generators leave the point fixed. The
first exercise does this for the north pole of the sphere and then describes the orbits of the isotropy group.

::: {#exr-lg-orbit-stabiliser}
#### The isotropy group of the north pole

Find all $X = x_aL_a \in \mathfrak{so}(3)$ with $Xe_3 = 0$, check that the rotations $e^{tL_3}$ fix $e_3$, and compute
the orbit of the point $(\sin\theta, 0, \cos\theta)$ under them.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$Xe_3 = (x_2, -x_1, 0)$, which vanishes exactly when $x_1 = x_2 = 0$: the generators of the isotropy group are the
multiples of $L_3$, and the isotropy group of $e_3$ is the $SO(2)$ of rotations about the $Z$-axis. Its orbit through
$(\sin\theta, 0, \cos\theta)$ is $(\cos t\sin\theta, \sin t\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$, the parallel at height
$\cos\theta$ and radius $\sin\theta$, which shrinks to a point at the poles:

{{< sage exr-lg-orbit-stabiliser >}}
:::

Freeness of an action is a statement about isotropy groups and can be checked by solving a single equation. The
second exercise checks it for the right action of $U(1)$ on $SU(2)$.

::: {#exr-lg-free-action-hopf}
#### The Hopf action is free

Show that $g\,e^{tT_3} = g$ for some $g \in SU(2)$ implies $e^{tT_3} = 1$, so that the right action of the circle
$\{e^{tT_3} : t \in [0, 4\pi)\}$ on $SU(2)$ is free. Contrast it with the left action of the same circle on the sphere
$S^2$ through $SO(3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Multiplying $g\,e^{tT_3} = g$ on the left by $g^{-1}$ gives $e^{tT_3} = 1$, so $t \in 4\pi\mathbb{Z}$ by @eq-exp-t3-t1:
only the identity of the circle fixes a point, at every point. This argument works for right (or left) multiplication
in any group. Acting on $S^2$ through the double cover, the same circle maps to the rotations about the $Z$-axis, which
fix both poles: there the isotropy group is the whole circle, while at every other point it is $\{\pm 1\}$, the
elements $t = 0, 2\pi$ that act as the identity rotation. That action is neither free nor effective.
:::

The upper half-plane carries an action of the group $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ by fractional linear maps. The third exercise
checks that it is an action and finds the isotropy group of the point $i$.

::: {#exr-lg-mobius-action}
#### Möbius transformations of the half-plane

For $M = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} \in SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ and $\operatorname{Im} z > 0$ let $M \cdot z
= (az + b)/(cz + d)$. Show that $A \cdot (B \cdot z) = (AB) \cdot z$, that $\operatorname{Im}(M \cdot z) > 0$, and that
the isotropy group of $i$ is $SO(2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Composing two fractional linear maps multiplies their matrices, as Sage confirms symbolically. With $z = x + iy$,
$\operatorname{Im}(M \cdot z) = y\det M/|cz + d|^2 = y/|cz + d|^2 > 0$. The condition $M \cdot i = i$ reads $ai + b =
i(ci + d)$, whose real and imaginary parts give $c = -b$ and $d = a$; then $\det M = a^2 + b^2 = 1$ and $M$ is a
rotation matrix. So the half-plane is the orbit $SL(2, \mathbb{R})/SO(2)$, just as the sphere is $SO(3)/SO(2)$
(@exm-action-so3-sphere). Since $-1$ acts trivially, the action is not effective; the effective group is $PSL(2,
\mathbb{R})$.

{{< sage exr-lg-mobius-action >}}
:::
::::

Two different Lie groups can have the same local structure, one being a quotient of the other by a discrete subgroup.
The definition of a covering homomorphism makes this relation precise.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-covering-homomorphism}
#### Covering homomorphism

A surjective homomorphism of Lie groups $\pi : \tilde G \to G$ with finite kernel is a **covering**; it is
locally a diffeomorphism, and $\tilde G$ and $G$ have the same Lie algebra (@sec-lie-algebras). When the kernel
has two elements it is a **double cover**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The double cover of the rotation group by $SU(2)$ is the most important covering in physics. It is realised by the
adjoint action of $SU(2)$ on its own Lie algebra.

::: {#exm-cover-su2}
#### $SU(2) \to SO(3)$

The adjoint homomorphism $g \mapsto \operatorname{Ad}_g$ of @exm-iso-double-cover is a double cover: each
rotation has the two preimages $\pm g$ (@fig-double-cover, @exr-lie-double-cover). A $2\pi$ rotation lifts to $-1$,
which is why spinors (@sec-spinors) change sign under a full turn.
:::

The real line covers the circle with infinitely many sheets. This covering is the exponential map of the circle group
and explains the angle coordinate defined up to multiples of $2\pi$.

::: {#exm-cover-r-u1}
#### $\mathbb{R} \to U(1)$

$t \mapsto e^{it}$ is a surjective homomorphism with infinite kernel $2\pi\mathbb{Z}$: a covering with infinitely
many sheets, the universal cover of the circle, which is why the circle is $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$
(@exm-first-iso-exp).
:::

The double cover of $SO(3)$ is the first member of a family. The spin groups cover all rotation groups of dimension at
least three, and the Lorentz group has an analogous cover.

::: {#exm-cover-spin}
#### Spin groups

$Spin(n)$ is the double cover of $SO(n)$ for $n \geq 3$: $Spin(3) = SU(2)$ and $Spin(4) = SU(2) \times SU(2)$
(@sec-branching); the Lorentz group $SO(3, 1)$ has the double cover $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$, on which the spinors of
Part II live.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise constructs the double cover explicitly on a one-parameter subgroup. It shows that the rotation
angle is twice the angle in $SU(2)$, which is the source of the factor two between their periods.

::: {#exr-lie-double-cover}
#### The double cover $SU(2) \to SO(3)$

Show that $\operatorname{Ad}_g$ for $g = e^{tT_3}$ acts on the basis $T_a$ as the rotation by $t$ about the third
axis, and that $g = e^{2\pi T_3} = -1$ acts trivially: the map $g \mapsto \operatorname{Ad}_g$ is a two-to-one
homomorphism $SU(2) \to SO(3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g T_3 g^{-1} = T_3$ since $g$ is a function of $T_3$; and with @eq-pauli,
$g T_1 g^{-1} = \cos t\, T_1 + \sin t\, T_2$, $g T_2 g^{-1} = -\sin t\, T_1 + \cos t\, T_2$ (expand
$g = \cos\frac{t}{2} - i\sin\frac{t}{2}\sigma_3$ and use $\sigma_3\sigma_1\sigma_3 = -\sigma_1$,
$\sigma_3\sigma_1 = i\sigma_2$). The matrix $R_{ab}$ defined by $g T_b g^{-1} = R_{ab} T_a$ is the rotation by
$t$, and at $t = 2\pi$ it is the identity while $g = -1$. Since $\operatorname{Ad}_{-g} = \operatorname{Ad}_g$,
the homomorphism is two-to-one, and every rotation arises (any rotation is a product of rotations about axes,
each of which is $\operatorname{Ad}$ of some $e^{tT_a}$). In Sage:

{{< sage exr-double-cover >}}
:::

A covering of the circle by itself has a finite kernel of any size. The second exercise identifies the kernel and the
number of sheets of the power maps.

::: {#exr-lg-kernel-cover}
#### Power maps of the circle

Show that $p_n : U(1) \to U(1)$, $z \mapsto z^n$ for $n \geq 1$, is a surjective homomorphism, find its kernel, and
show that it is an $n$-sheeted covering in the sense of @def-covering-homomorphism. Which $p_n$ factor through the
double cover $p_2$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(zw)^n = z^nw^n$ because the group is abelian, and $e^{i\alpha}$ has the preimage $e^{i\alpha/n}$, so $p_n$ is a
surjective homomorphism. Its kernel is the set of $n$-th roots of unity $\mathbb{Z}_n$, a finite group, so $p_n$ is a
covering with $n$ preimages over every point; in the angle chart it is $\alpha \mapsto n\alpha$, whose derivative $n$
never vanishes, so it is a local diffeomorphism. $p_n = q \circ p_2$ for a homomorphism $q$ exactly when the kernel
$\{\pm 1\}$ of $p_2$ lies in $\mathbb{Z}_n$, that is, when $n$ is even, and then $q = p_{n/2}$.
:::

The double cover can be inverted explicitly: given a rotation one can solve for the two elements of $SU(2)$ above it.
The third exercise does this for a quarter turn about the $X$-axis.

::: {#exr-lg-su2-preimage}
#### Lifting a rotation to $SU(2)$

Write $g = a_0 1 + 2(a_1T_1 + a_2T_2 + a_3T_3)$ with $a_0^2 + \dots + a_3^2 = 1$ and solve $\operatorname{Ad}_g =
R_X(\pi/2)$, the rotation by $\pi/2$ about the $X$-axis. Compare the solutions with $\pm e^{(\pi/2)T_1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The general element of $SU(2)$ is $a_0 1 - i a_k\sigma_k$ with $(a_0, a)$ a unit vector, which is the given form since
$2T_k = -i\sigma_k$. The equations $\operatorname{Ad}_g = R$ have exactly two solutions, $(a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3) = \pm
(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, 0, 0)$; by @eq-exp-su2 the plus sign is $e^{(\pi/2)T_1} = \cos\frac{\pi}{4} -
i\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\sigma_1$, and the minus sign is $-e^{(\pi/2)T_1} = e^{(\pi/2 + 2\pi)T_1}$. In general $g$ covers the
rotation by $2\arccos a_0$ about the unit vector $a/|a|$, and $-g$ gives the angle $2\pi - 2\arccos a_0$ about
$-a/|a|$, which is the same rotation:

{{< sage exr-lg-su2-preimage >}}
:::
::::

The rotations about the $Z$-axis have been used throughout the section as the basic one-parameter subgroup. The
proposition below records their three defining properties: the identity at zero, the composition law and orthogonality.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-so2-group}
#### $SO(2)$ is a one-parameter group of orthogonal matrices

$R(0) = 1$, $R(s)R(t) = R(s + t)$ and $R(t)R(t)^{\mathsf{T}} = 1$ for the rotation matrices about the $Z$-axis.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.rotation_zero`, `KaluzaKlein.rotation_mul` and `KaluzaKlein.rotation_orthogonal`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.rotation_mul >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The composition law of the proposition is a pair of trigonometric identities in disguise. Writing out one entry of the
product makes the connection explicit.

::: {#exm-lg-so2-addition}
#### The addition formulas

The upper left entry of $R(s)R(t)$, with $R(t) = \begin{pmatrix} \cos t & -\sin t & 0 \\ \sin t & \cos t & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}$, is $\cos s\cos t - \sin s\sin t$, and the lower left entry of the upper block is $\sin s\cos t + \cos
s\sin t$; the identity $R(s)R(t) = R(s + t)$ is the addition formulas for cosine and sine. In complex form, $R(t)$ acts
on $x + iy$ as multiplication by $e^{it}$, and the law becomes $e^{is}e^{it} = e^{i(s + t)}$.
:::

Orthogonality says that the inverse of a rotation is its transpose. Combined with the composition law it identifies
this inverse as the rotation by the opposite angle.

::: {#exm-lg-so2-inverse}
#### Inverse equals transpose

From $R(s)R(t) = R(s + t)$ and $R(0) = 1$, $R(t)R(-t) = 1$, so $R(t)^{-1} = R(-t)$; and $R(-t) = R(t)^{\mathsf{T}}$
because cosine is even and sine odd. This is $R(t)R(t)^{\mathsf{T}} = 1$ again, so the three statements of the
proposition are consistent: $t \mapsto R(t)$ is a homomorphism into $O(3)$, and since $\det R(t) = \cos^2t + \sin^2t =
1$ its image lies in $SO(3)$.
:::

The composition law says that $t \mapsto R(t)$ is a homomorphism from the real line. Its kernel identifies the image
with a circle.

::: {#exm-lg-so2-period}
#### $SO(2) \cong \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z} \cong U(1)$

$R(t) = 1$ exactly when $\cos t = 1$, that is, $t \in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$: the homomorphism $\mathbb{R} \to SO(3)$ has
kernel $2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ and its image, the subgroup $SO(2)$ of rotations about the $Z$-axis, is isomorphic to
$\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$. The map $R(t) \mapsto e^{it}$ is then a well-defined isomorphism $SO(2) \cong U(1)$, the
identification of @exm-lie-group-u1.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the three statements in a computer algebra system and adds the determinant and the period.
It is a quick consistency check of the matrix used throughout the chapter.

::: {#exr-lg-so2-group-law}
#### Checking the group law symbolically

With Sage, verify $R(0) = 1$, $R(s)R(t) = R(s + t)$, $R(t)R(t)^{\mathsf{T}} = 1$, $\det R(t) = 1$, $R(t)^{-1} = R(-t)$
and $R(2\pi) = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
All six statements hold symbolically after `trig_expand`, which applies the addition formulas of
@exm-lg-so2-addition:

{{< sage exr-lg-so2-group-law >}}
:::

The proposition shows that every $R(t)$ lies in $SO(2)$, the group of rotations of the plane spanned by $e_1$ and
$e_2$. The second exercise proves the converse, that every rotation of the plane is some $R(t)$.

::: {#exr-lg-so2-abelian}
#### Every plane rotation is an $R(t)$

Show that every $2 \times 2$ real matrix $M$ with $M^{\mathsf{T}}M = 1$ and $\det M = 1$ is $\begin{pmatrix} \cos t & -
\sin t \\ \sin t & \cos t \end{pmatrix}$ for some $t$, unique modulo $2\pi$. Conclude that $SO(2)$ is abelian.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The first column $(a, b)$ of $M$ is a unit vector, so $(a, b) = (\cos t, \sin t)$ for a unique $t$ modulo $2\pi$. The
second column is a unit vector orthogonal to it, hence $\pm(-b, a)$, and $\det M = 1$ selects the plus sign. So $M =
R(t)$, and $SO(2) = \{R(t)\}$. Two rotations commute because $R(s)R(t) = R(s + t) = R(t + s) = R(t)R(s)$; this fails
for $SO(3)$, where rotations about different axes do not commute.
:::

Replacing the Euclidean form by the Minkowski form of the plane turns rotations into boosts. The third exercise checks
which properties of the proposition survive.

::: {#exr-lg-so11-boosts}
#### Boosts of the Minkowski plane

Let $B(w) = \begin{pmatrix} \cosh w & \sinh w \\ \sinh w & \cosh w \end{pmatrix}$ and $\eta = \operatorname{diag}(1, -
1)$. Show that $B(0) = 1$, $B(v)B(w) = B(v + w)$ and $B(w)^{\mathsf{T}}\eta B(w) = \eta$, but that $B(w)$ is not
orthogonal and that $w \mapsto B(w)$ is injective.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The composition law is the addition formulas for $\cosh$ and $\sinh$, and $B^{\mathsf{T}}\eta B = \eta$ is
$\cosh^2w - \sinh^2w = 1$; so the boosts form a one-parameter subgroup of $SO(1, 1)$, the group preserving $\eta$.
$BB^{\mathsf{T}} = B(2w) \neq 1$ for $w \neq 0$, so they are not orthogonal. The trace $2\cosh w$ equals $2$ only at
$w = 0$, so $B(w) = 1$ only for $w = 0$: the kernel is trivial and the subgroup is a line, not a circle. The rapidity
$w$ is additive, as the rotation angle is.

{{< sage exr-lg-so11-boosts >}}
:::
::::

### Lie algebras {#sec-lie-algebras}

The structure of a Lie group near the identity is captured by a vector space with a bracket, its Lie algebra, and most
computations with Lie groups are done there: gauge fields take values in a Lie algebra, and symmetry conditions on
fields become linear equations in one. This section defines Lie algebras abstractly and as tangent spaces of matrix
groups, introduces structure constants, the adjoint representation and the Killing form, and works out
$\mathfrak{so}(3)$ and $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ in detail.

#### Lie algebras

The abstract definition keeps only the algebraic properties of the commutator of matrices. A bracket that is bilinear,
antisymmetric and obeys the Jacobi identity is all that is needed for the theory that follows.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-lie-algebra}
#### Lie algebra

A **Lie algebra** is a vector space $\mathfrak{g}$ with a bilinear **bracket** $[X, Y]$ that is antisymmetric,
$[X, Y] = -[Y, X]$, and satisfies the **Jacobi identity** $[X, [Y, Z]] + [Y, [Z, X]] + [Z, [X, Y]] = 0$. It is
**abelian** if all brackets vanish.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The commutator of matrices is the bracket from which the definition was abstracted. Every associative algebra gives a
Lie algebra in the same way, and the matrix Lie algebras of this chapter are subspaces closed under it.

::: {#exm-lie-algebra-matrices}
#### Matrices with the commutator

Any associative algebra, in particular the $n \times n$ matrices, is a Lie algebra with the **commutator** $[X, Y]
= XY - YX$: antisymmetry is clear and the Jacobi identity follows by expanding the twelve products, which
cancel in pairs. The antisymmetric $3 \times 3$ matrices are closed under the commutator (@exm-so3-algebra), and
so are the traceless anti-Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrices (@exm-su2-algebra).
:::

Vector fields on a manifold have no product that is a vector field, but they do have a bracket. The Lie bracket makes
them an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra, and the Killing fields form a finite-dimensional subalgebra.

::: {#exm-lie-algebra-vector-fields}
#### Vector fields with the Lie bracket

The vector fields on a manifold form a Lie algebra under the Lie bracket @eq-lie-bracket (@exr-jacobi-identity),
infinite-dimensional; the Killing fields of a metric form a finite-dimensional subalgebra, the isometry algebra
(@def-isometry-algebra), which for the sphere is $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ with the structure constants of
@eq-killing-brackets.
:::

The trivial bracket is allowed and gives the abelian Lie algebras. They are the Lie algebras of the abelian groups, the
torus and the vector spaces.

::: {#exm-lie-algebra-abelian}
#### Abelian Lie algebras

$\mathbb{R}^n$ with the zero bracket is an abelian Lie algebra; it is the Lie algebra of the torus $T^n$ and of
$\mathbb{R}^n$. The one-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{u}(1) = i\mathbb{R}$ of the circle group is abelian,
with $[iX, iY] = 0$, which is why $U(1)$ gauge theory has no self-interaction of the gauge field.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The cross product of vectors in space is the oldest example of a non-associative bracket. The first exercise shows
that it satisfies the axioms of a Lie algebra and identifies its structure constants.

::: {#exr-lg-cross-product}
#### The cross product

Show that $(\mathbb{R}^3, \times)$ is a Lie algebra: the cross product is bilinear and antisymmetric, and the Jacobi
identity follows from $a \times (b \times c) = b(a \cdot c) - c(a \cdot b)$. Show that $e_a \times e_b = \epsilon_{abc}
e_c$ and that the cross product is not associative.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Bilinearity and antisymmetry are visible in the component formula $(a \times b)_c = \epsilon_{cde}a_db_e$. Summing
the identity $a \times (b \times c) = b(a \cdot c) - c(a \cdot b)$ over the three cyclic permutations, the six terms
cancel in pairs, which is the Jacobi identity. The basis vectors give $e_1 \times e_2 = e_3$ and cyclically, the
structure constants $\epsilon_{abc}$ of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ (@eq-so3-brackets). Associativity fails: $(e_1 \times e_1)
\times e_2 = 0$ while $e_1 \times (e_1 \times e_2) = -e_2$.

{{< sage exr-lg-cross-product >}}
:::

A subspace of matrices closed under the commutator is a Lie algebra by restriction. The second exercise finds such a
subspace that is not one of the classical Lie algebras of compact groups.

::: {#exr-lg-upper-triangular}
#### Upper triangular matrices

Show that the upper triangular $n \times n$ matrices $\mathfrak{b}_n$ form a Lie algebra under the commutator, that the
commutator of two of them is strictly upper triangular, and that the strictly upper triangular matrices
$\mathfrak{n}_n$ form a Lie algebra too. Describe $\mathfrak{b}_2$ and $\mathfrak{n}_3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The product of two upper triangular matrices is upper triangular, with diagonal entries $(XY)_{ii} = X_{ii}Y_{ii}$. So
$XY - YX$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $X_{ii}Y_{ii} - Y_{ii}X_{ii} = 0$: strictly upper triangular.
In particular both $\mathfrak{b}_n$ and $\mathfrak{n}_n$ are closed under the commutator; Jacobi is inherited from
all matrices. $\mathfrak{b}_2$ has the basis $E_{11}, E_{22}, E_{12}$ with $[E_{11}, E_{12}] = E_{12}$, $[E_{22},
E_{12}] = -E_{12}$, $[E_{11}, E_{22}] = 0$: the affine algebra $[X, Y] = Y$ (@exm-structure-affine) plus the
identity matrix $E_{11} + E_{22}$, which commutes with everything. $\mathfrak{n}_3$ has the basis $E_{12}, E_{23},
E_{13}$ with the single bracket $[E_{12}, E_{23}] = E_{13}$: the Lie algebra of the Heisenberg group of
@exr-lg-heisenberg-group.
:::

In dimension two there is only one non-abelian Lie algebra up to isomorphism. The third exercise proves this,
showing that the affine algebra is the general case.

::: {#exr-lg-two-dim-algebras}
#### Two-dimensional Lie algebras

Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a two-dimensional Lie algebra with basis $X, Y$ and $[X, Y] = aX + bY \neq 0$. Show that there is
a basis $X', Y'$ with $[X', Y'] = Y'$, so that every two-dimensional Lie algebra is abelian or isomorphic to the affine
algebra of @exm-structure-affine.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every bracket is a multiple of $[X, Y]$, by bilinearity and antisymmetry, so the derived space $[\mathfrak{g},
\mathfrak{g}]$ is the line spanned by $Y' = aX + bY$. For any $Z$, $[Z, Y']$ lies on this line, $[Z, Y'] =
\lambda(Z)Y'$ with $\lambda$ linear; from $[X, Y'] = b[X, Y] = bY'$ and $[Y, Y'] = -a[X, Y] = -aY'$, $\lambda(X) = b$
and $\lambda(Y) = -a$, not both zero. Since $\lambda(Y') = ab - ba = 0$, any $X'$ with $\lambda(X') = 1$ is
independent of $Y'$, and $[X', Y'] = Y'$.
:::
::::

A Lie algebra of finite dimension is described completely by the brackets of the elements of one basis. The numbers
appearing in these brackets are its structure constants.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-structure-constants}
#### Structure constants

A basis $T_A$ of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra is a set of **generators**, and the numbers $f_{AB}{}^C$ defined
by $[T_A, T_B] = f_{AB}{}^C T_C$ are the **structure constants** in that basis. They are antisymmetric in $A, B$,
and the Jacobi identity reads $f_{AB}{}^D f_{DC}{}^E + f_{BC}{}^D f_{DA}{}^E + f_{CA}{}^D f_{DB}{}^E = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the rotation algebra the structure constants are the components of the Levi-Civita symbol. This is the
algebraic content of the cross product of the previous exercise.

::: {#exm-structure-so3}
#### $\mathfrak{so}(3)$: the Levi-Civita symbol

In the basis $L_a$ of @eq-so3-basis, $f_{ab}{}^c = \epsilon_{abc}$ (@prp-so3-structure, @fig-structure-constants):
$[L_1, L_2] = L_3$, $[L_2, L_3] = L_1$, $[L_3, L_1] = L_2$. The Jacobi identity reduces to the identity
$\epsilon_{bcd}\epsilon_{ade} + \epsilon_{cad}\epsilon_{bde} + \epsilon_{abd}\epsilon_{cde} = 0$ (@exr-jacobi).
:::

The anti-Hermitian generators of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ are normalised so that their structure constants are the same as
those of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$. The two Lie algebras are therefore isomorphic, although the groups are not.

::: {#exm-structure-su2}
#### $\mathfrak{su}(2)$: the same constants

In the basis $T_a = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ of @exm-su2-algebra, $[T_a, T_b] = \epsilon_{abc}T_c$
(@prp-su2-structure): the same structure constants as $\mathfrak{so}(3)$, so the two Lie algebras are
isomorphic, $\mathfrak{su}(2) \cong \mathfrak{so}(3)$, although the groups differ by the double cover.
:::

The affine group of the line gives the smallest non-abelian structure constants. A single non-zero number describes the
whole algebra, which serves as a test case in the rest of the chapter.

::: {#exm-structure-affine}
#### The affine group of the line

The maps $x \mapsto ax + b$ with $a > 0$ form a two-dimensional Lie group whose Lie algebra has generators $X$
(dilations) and $Y$ (translations) with $[X, Y] = Y$: a single non-zero structure constant $f_{XY}{}^Y = 1$, the
smallest non-abelian Lie algebra (@fig-affine-group-fields, @exr-affine-left-invariant).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The figure shows the structure constants of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ as three slices, one for each value of the upper index.
Each slice is an antisymmetric matrix, which reflects the antisymmetry of the bracket.

![The structure constants of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ as three $3 \times 3$ slices $f_{ab}{}^c$, one per value of $c$:
each slice is the antisymmetric pattern of the Levi-Civita symbol, with the single entry $+1$ at $(a, b) =
(c + 1, c + 2)$ and $-1$ at the transposed position. Checked against Sage's `LieAlgebra` module. Generated by
`figures/structure_constants.sage`.](figures/structure_constants.svg){#fig-structure-constants width=90%}

In terms of structure constants the Jacobi identity becomes a quadratic identity. The first exercise checks it for the
Levi-Civita symbol with the contraction identity of two epsilons.

::: {#exr-jacobi}
#### The Jacobi identity for $\epsilon$

Show that the Jacobi identity for $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ is equivalent to $\epsilon_{bcd}\epsilon_{ade} +
\epsilon_{cad}\epsilon_{bde} + \epsilon_{abd}\epsilon_{cde} = 0$, and verify it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[L_a, [L_b, L_c]] = \epsilon_{bcd}[L_a, L_d] = \epsilon_{bcd}\epsilon_{ade} L_e$, and summing the three cyclic
permutations of $(a, b, c)$ gives the stated coefficient of $L_e$. Using $\epsilon_{bcd}\epsilon_{ade} =
\delta_{ba}\delta_{ce} - \delta_{be}\delta_{ca}$ (contracting one index of two $\epsilon$'s), the three terms are
$\delta_{ba}\delta_{ce} - \delta_{be}\delta_{ca} + \delta_{cb}\delta_{ae} - \delta_{ce}\delta_{ab} +
\delta_{ac}\delta_{be} - \delta_{ae}\delta_{bc} = 0$. For the matrices $L_a$ the Jacobi identity also holds
automatically, since the bracket is the commutator of matrices.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The Jacobi identity holds automatically for the matrices $L_a$, since the bracket is the commutator, and the
structure constants are `KaluzaKlein.so3_structure` (@prp-so3-structure).

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The structure constants of a nilpotent algebra have a particularly simple pattern. The second exercise reads them off
for the Lie algebra of the Heisenberg group.

::: {#exr-lg-heisenberg-structure}
#### Structure constants of the Heisenberg algebra

In the basis $X = E_{12}$, $Y = E_{23}$, $Z = E_{13}$ of $\mathfrak{n}_3$ (@exr-lg-upper-triangular) compute all the
structure constants, check the Jacobi identity in the form of @def-structure-constants, and compare with the canonical
commutation relation $[q, p] = i\hbar$ of quantum mechanics.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$E_{12}E_{23} = E_{13}$ and $E_{23}E_{12} = 0$, so $[X, Y] = Z$; $Z$ commutes with $X$ and $Y$ because $E_{12}E_{13} =
E_{13}E_{12} = 0$ and likewise for $E_{23}$. The only non-zero structure constants are $f_{XY}{}^Z = -f_{YX}{}^Z = 1$.
In the Jacobi identity every term $f_{AB}{}^Df_{DC}{}^E$ needs $D = Z$ for the first factor to be non-zero, and then
$f_{ZC}{}^E = 0$: all terms vanish. The operators $q$, $p$ and $i\hbar 1$ satisfy the same relations, $[q, p] = i\hbar
1$ with $1$ central, which is why this algebra and its group are named after Heisenberg.
:::

Structure constants depend on the choice of basis, but in a controlled way. The third exercise derives their
transformation law and applies it to rescalings of the rotation generators.

::: {#exr-lg-change-of-basis}
#### Changing the basis

If $T'_A = M_A{}^BT_B$ with $M$ invertible, show that $f'_{AB}{}^C = M_A{}^DM_B{}^Ef_{DE}{}^F(M^{-1})_F{}^C$. Apply this
to $L'_a = \lambda L_a$ for $\lambda > 0$ and to the complex basis $J_a = iL_a$ of the complexified algebra, and explain
why the sign of $\lambda$ cannot be absorbed in $\mathfrak{so}(3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[T'_A, T'_B] = M_A{}^DM_B{}^E[T_D, T_E] = M_A{}^DM_B{}^Ef_{DE}{}^FT_F$, and $T_F = (M^{-1})_F{}^CT'_C$, which gives the
formula: the structure constants transform as a tensor with two lower and one upper index. For $L'_a = \lambda L_a$,
$[L'_a, L'_b] = \lambda^2\epsilon_{abc}L_c = \lambda\epsilon_{abc}L'_c$, so $f' = \lambda\epsilon$. For $J_a = iL_a$,
$[J_a, J_b] = -\epsilon_{abc}L_c = i\epsilon_{abc}J_c$, the physicists' angular momentum algebra. Replacing $L_a$ by
$-L_a$ gives $f' = -\epsilon$, which is again of the form $\epsilon$ after the orientation-reversing relabelling $L_1
\leftrightarrow L_2$; so the sign is a matter of orientation, while the scale $\lambda$ is fixed by a normalisation
such as $\operatorname{tr}(L_aL_b) = -2\delta_{ab}$.
:::
::::

#### The Lie algebra of a matrix group

For a matrix group the Lie algebra is a concrete space of matrices. It consists of the generators of the one-parameter
subgroups of the group, equivalently of the tangent vectors at the identity.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-lie-algebra-of-group}
#### Lie algebra of a matrix Lie group

The **Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{g}$ of a matrix Lie group $G$ is the set of matrices $X$ such that $e^{tX} \in G$
for all real $t$, where $e^X = \sum_{k \geq 0} X^k/k!$ is the matrix exponential (@sec-exponential). It is a vector
space closed under the commutator, hence a Lie algebra, and it is the tangent space $T_eG$ of $G$ at the identity:
$X$ is the velocity $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tX}|_{t = 0}$ of the curve $e^{tX}$ through $e$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Differentiating the orthogonality condition along a curve gives the Lie algebra of the rotation group. Its standard
basis is fixed by the conventions of the book.

::: {#exm-so3-algebra}
#### $\mathfrak{so}(3)$: antisymmetric matrices

Differentiating $R(t)^{\mathsf{T}} R(t) = 1$ at $t = 0$ for a curve $R(t)$ in $SO(3)$ through $1$ gives $X^{\mathsf{T}} +
X = 0$: $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ consists of the antisymmetric $3 \times 3$ matrices, a three-dimensional space with
the basis $(L_a)_{bc} = -\epsilon_{abc}$ of @sec-conventions-lie,
$$
L_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
L_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
L_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-so3-basis}
Multiplying out, $L_1 L_2$ has a single non-zero entry, $(L_1 L_2)_{21} = (L_1)_{23}(L_2)_{31} = (-1)(-1) = 1$,
while $(L_2 L_1)_{12} = (L_2)_{13}(L_1)_{32} = 1$, so $[L_1, L_2]$ has entries $+1$ at $(2, 1)$ and $-1$ at $(1,
2)$: it is $L_3$. Cyclically,
$$
[L_1, L_2] = L_3, \qquad [L_2, L_3] = L_1, \qquad [L_3, L_1] = L_2, \qquad \text{i.e.}\quad [L_a, L_b] = \epsilon_{abc} L_c .
$$ {#eq-so3-brackets}
:::

The same procedure for $SU(2)$ gives the traceless anti-Hermitian matrices. The Pauli matrices provide a basis whose
products are known in closed form.

::: {#exm-su2-algebra}
#### $\mathfrak{su}(2)$: the Pauli matrices

Differentiating $U^\dagger U = 1$ and $\det U = 1$ gives $X^\dagger = -X$ and $\operatorname{tr} X = 0$:
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$ is the three-dimensional space of traceless anti-Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrices, with the
basis $T_a = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ built from the **Pauli matrices**
$$
\sigma_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\sigma_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\sigma_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
\sigma_a \sigma_b = \delta_{ab} 1 + i\epsilon_{abc}\sigma_c .
$$ {#eq-pauli}
From the product rule, $[\sigma_a, \sigma_b] = 2i\epsilon_{abc}\sigma_c$, hence
$$
[T_a, T_b] = \left(-\tfrac{i}{2}\right)^2 [\sigma_a, \sigma_b] = -\tfrac14 \cdot 2i\epsilon_{abc}\sigma_c
  = -\tfrac{i}{2}\epsilon_{abc}\sigma_c = \epsilon_{abc} T_c .
$$ {#eq-su2-brackets}
The normalisation is $\operatorname{tr}(T_a T_b) = -\tfrac14 \operatorname{tr}(\sigma_a\sigma_b) = -
\tfrac12\delta_{ab}$, as fixed in @sec-conventions-lie (@prp-su2-structure).
:::

The remaining classical cases follow the same pattern. Each defining condition of the group becomes a linear condition
on its Lie algebra, and the determinant condition becomes the vanishing of the trace.

::: {#exm-u1-algebra}
#### $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ and $\mathfrak{gl}(n)$

$\mathfrak{u}(1) = \{ix : x \in \mathbb{R}\}$, since $e^{tix}$ has modulus one (@fig-exp-circle of
@sec-exponential); $\mathfrak{gl}(n, \mathbb{R})$ is all $n \times n$ matrices, since $e^{tX}$ is always invertible;
$\mathfrak{sl}(n)$ is the traceless matrices, since $\det e^{tX} = e^{t\operatorname{tr}X}$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The group $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ has a non-compact Lie algebra with a convenient basis of a diagonal and two nilpotent
matrices. The first exercise computes its brackets and the corresponding one-parameter subgroups.

::: {#exr-lg-sl2-algebra}
#### The Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R})$

With $H = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $E = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $F =
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, compute $[H, E]$, $[H, F]$, $[E, F]$ and the exponentials $e^{tH}$,
$e^{tE}$, $e^{tF}$, and check that they lie in $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[H, E] = 2E$, $[H, F] = -2F$ and $[E, F] = H$. The exponentials are $e^{tH} = \operatorname{diag}(e^t, e^{-t})$, a
squeeze, and $e^{tE} = 1 + tE$, $e^{tF} = 1 + tF$, two shears; all have determinant $e^{t\operatorname{tr}X} = 1$.
Unlike $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, the eigenvalues of $\operatorname{ad}_H$ are the real numbers $0, \pm 2$ and the subgroup
$e^{tH}$ is not periodic:

{{< sage exr-lg-sl2-algebra >}}
:::

The symplectic group of @exr-lg-symplectic has a Lie algebra described by one linear condition. The second exercise
finds this condition and counts its solutions.

::: {#exr-lg-sp2-algebra}
#### The symplectic Lie algebra

Show that the Lie algebra of $Sp(2n, \mathbb{R})$ is $\mathfrak{sp}(2n) = \{X : X^{\mathsf{T}}J + JX = 0\}$, that
$X \in \mathfrak{sp}(2n)$ exactly when $JX$ is symmetric, and deduce $\dim \mathfrak{sp}(2n) = n(2n + 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Differentiating $e^{tX^{\mathsf{T}}}Je^{tX} = J$ at $t = 0$ gives $X^{\mathsf{T}}J + JX = 0$; conversely, if this
holds then $\frac{d}{dt}(e^{tX^{\mathsf{T}}}Je^{tX}) = e^{tX^{\mathsf{T}}}(X^{\mathsf{T}}J + JX)e^{tX} = 0$, so
$e^{tX}$ stays in the group. Since $J^{\mathsf{T}} = -J$, $(JX)^{\mathsf{T}} = X^{\mathsf{T}}J^{\mathsf{T}} = -
X^{\mathsf{T}}J$, so the condition says $(JX)^{\mathsf{T}} = JX$. As $J$ is invertible, $X \mapsto JX$ is a linear
bijection onto the symmetric $2n \times 2n$ matrices, of dimension $2n(2n + 1)/2 = n(2n + 1)$, in agreement with the
group dimension of @exr-lg-symplectic.
:::

The rotation groups in higher dimension have Lie algebras with a basis labelled by pairs of indices. The third exercise
computes their brackets, which reduce to @eq-so3-brackets for $n = 3$.

::: {#exr-lg-so-n-dim}
#### The Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(n)$

Show that $\mathfrak{so}(n)$ consists of the antisymmetric $n \times n$ matrices, with basis $M_{jk} = E_{jk} - E_{kj}$
for $j < k$ and dimension $n(n - 1)/2$, and that $[M_{ij}, M_{kl}] = \delta_{jk}M_{il} - \delta_{ik}M_{jl} -
\delta_{jl}M_{ik} + \delta_{il}M_{jk}$. Identify the $L_a$ of @eq-so3-basis among the $M_{jk}$ for $n = 3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
As in @exm-so3-algebra, differentiating $R^{\mathsf{T}}R = 1$ gives $X^{\mathsf{T}} = -X$, and the $M_{jk}$ with $j < k$
form a basis of these matrices, $n(n - 1)/2$ of them, the dimension of $O(n)$ of @exm-matrix-orthogonal. With
$E_{ij}E_{kl} = \delta_{jk}E_{il}$, $M_{ij}M_{kl} = \delta_{jk}E_{il} - \delta_{jl}E_{ik} - \delta_{ik}E_{jl} +
\delta_{il}E_{jk}$; subtracting the same expression with $(ij) \leftrightarrow (kl)$ and collecting the $E$'s into
$M$'s gives the stated bracket. For $n = 3$, $L_1 = -M_{23}$, $L_2 = M_{13}$, $L_3 = -M_{12}$ by @eq-so3-basis, i.e.
$L_a = -\tfrac12\epsilon_{ajk}M_{jk}$, and the bracket then reproduces $[L_1, L_2] = L_3$.
:::
::::

#### The adjoint representation and the Killing form

Every Lie algebra acts on itself through its own bracket, and every Lie group acts on its Lie algebra by conjugation.
These two actions are the adjoint representations of the algebra and of the group.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-adjoint}
#### Adjoint representation

For $X \in \mathfrak{g}$ the linear map $\operatorname{ad}_X : Y \mapsto [X, Y]$ is the **adjoint
representation** of the Lie algebra on itself, a representation (@def-representation) by the Jacobi identity;
in a basis, $(\operatorname{ad}_{T_A})^C{}_B = f_{AB}{}^C$. For $g \in G$, $\operatorname{Ad}_g : Y \mapsto g Y g^{-1}$
is the adjoint representation of the group on $\mathfrak{g}$, and $\operatorname{ad}$ is its derivative at the
identity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the rotation algebra the matrices of the adjoint representation are the generators themselves. The adjoint
representation is therefore the defining representation on vectors of $\mathbb{R}^3$.

::: {#exm-adjoint-so3}
#### $\mathfrak{so}(3)$: the adjoint is the vector representation

$(\operatorname{ad}_{L_a})^c{}_b = \epsilon_{abc} = (L_a)_{cb}$, so $\operatorname{ad}_{L_a}$ is the matrix $L_a$
itself: the adjoint representation of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ is its defining representation on $\mathbb{R}^3$
(@exm-equivalent-adjoint). The gauge field of Part IV takes values in the adjoint representation.
:::

For $SU(2)$ the adjoint action on the three-dimensional Lie algebra is by rotations. This is the double cover of the
previous section seen from the Lie algebra.

::: {#exm-adjoint-su2}
#### $\operatorname{Ad}$ of $SU(2)$ is the double cover

$\operatorname{Ad}_g$ for $g \in SU(2)$ acts on $\mathfrak{su}(2) \cong \mathbb{R}^3$ by the rotation of
@exr-lie-double-cover; this is the homomorphism $SU(2) \to SO(3)$, and $\operatorname{ad}_{T_a}$ is again the matrix
$L_a$ in the basis $T_b$.
:::

For the affine algebra the adjoint matrices can be read off from the single bracket. They show that the adjoint
representation detects non-commutativity.

::: {#exm-adjoint-affine}
#### The affine algebra

For $[X, Y] = Y$, $\operatorname{ad}_X$ has matrix $\operatorname{diag}(0, 1)$ in the basis $(X, Y)$ and
$\operatorname{ad}_Y$ has the single entry $(\operatorname{ad}_Y)^Y{}_X = -1$: the adjoint representation of a
non-abelian Lie algebra is never trivial, while for an abelian one it is zero.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
For a nilpotent algebra the adjoint matrices are themselves nilpotent, and their products vanish quickly. The first
exercise computes them for the Heisenberg algebra.

::: {#exr-lg-ad-heisenberg}
#### The adjoint representation of the Heisenberg algebra

For $[X, Y] = Z$ with $Z$ central (@exr-lg-heisenberg-structure), write the matrices of $\operatorname{ad}_X$,
$\operatorname{ad}_Y$, $\operatorname{ad}_Z$ in the basis $(X, Y, Z)$, and show that every product of two of them
vanishes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{ad}_X$ sends $X \mapsto 0$, $Y \mapsto Z$, $Z \mapsto 0$, so its only non-zero entry is $1$ in row $Z$,
column $Y$; $\operatorname{ad}_Y$ sends $X \mapsto -Z$, so its only entry is $-1$ in row $Z$, column $X$; and
$\operatorname{ad}_Z = 0$. Each $\operatorname{ad}_A$ maps into the line of $Z$, which every $\operatorname{ad}_B$
kills, so $\operatorname{ad}_A\operatorname{ad}_B = 0$. In particular each $\operatorname{ad}_A$ is nilpotent, and the
Killing form of @def-killing-form vanishes identically.
:::

The definition calls $\operatorname{ad}$ a representation, which means it turns brackets into commutators. The second
exercise derives this from the Jacobi identity and checks it on $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R})$.

::: {#exr-lg-ad-homomorphism}
#### $\operatorname{ad}$ is a representation

Show that $\operatorname{ad}_{[X, Y]} = [\operatorname{ad}_X, \operatorname{ad}_Y]$ is equivalent to the Jacobi
identity. Compute the matrices of $\operatorname{ad}_H$, $\operatorname{ad}_E$, $\operatorname{ad}_F$ for
$\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R})$ (@exr-lg-sl2-algebra) in the basis $(H, E, F)$ and check the identity with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Applied to $Z$, the identity reads $[[X, Y], Z] = [X, [Y, Z]] - [Y, [X, Z]]$; by antisymmetry this is $[X, [Y, Z]] +
[Y, [Z, X]] + [Z, [X, Y]] = 0$, the Jacobi identity. For $\mathfrak{sl}(2)$, $\operatorname{ad}_H =
\operatorname{diag}(0, 2, -2)$, while $\operatorname{ad}_E$ sends $H \mapsto -2E$, $F \mapsto H$ and $\operatorname{ad}_F$
sends $H \mapsto 2F$, $E \mapsto -H$:

{{< sage exr-lg-ad-homomorphism >}}
:::

The kernel of the adjoint representation consists of the elements that commute with everything. The third exercise
identifies it and decides when the adjoint representation is faithful.

::: {#exr-lg-ad-kernel}
#### The kernel of $\operatorname{ad}$

Show that the kernel of $X \mapsto \operatorname{ad}_X$ is the centre $\mathfrak{z} = \{X : [X, Y] = 0 \text{ for all
} Y\}$. Find it for $\mathfrak{so}(3)$, for the affine algebra, for the Heisenberg algebra and for $\mathfrak{u}(2) =
\mathfrak{u}(1) \oplus \mathfrak{su}(2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{ad}_X = 0$ means $[X, Y] = 0$ for every $Y$, the definition of the centre. For $\mathfrak{so}(3)$,
$[x_aL_a, L_b] = x_a\epsilon_{abc}L_c$ vanishes for all $b$ only if $x = 0$: the centre is zero and $\operatorname{ad}$
is faithful, as @exm-adjoint-so3 shows. For the affine algebra $[xX + yY, X] = -yY$ and $[xX + yY, Y] = xY$, so the
centre is zero again. For the Heisenberg algebra the centre is the line of $Z$. For $\mathfrak{u}(2)$, the anti-Hermitian
$2 \times 2$ matrices, the multiples $i\lambda 1$ of the identity commute with everything, and the centre is this
$\mathfrak{u}(1)$; the adjoint representation of $\mathfrak{u}(2)$ only sees its $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ part.
:::
::::

Traces of products of adjoint matrices give a bilinear form on any Lie algebra, canonically attached to it. Its
signature distinguishes compact from non-compact groups.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-killing-form}
#### Killing form

The **Killing form** of a Lie algebra is the symmetric bilinear form (@def-symmetric-form) $\kappa(X, Y) =
\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}_X \operatorname{ad}_Y)$, with components $\kappa_{AB} = f_{AC}{}^D f_{BD}{}^C$.
It is invariant, $\kappa([Z, X], Y) + \kappa(X, [Z, Y]) = 0$, and it is negative definite exactly for the compact
semisimple Lie algebras such as $\mathfrak{su}(2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Because the adjoint matrices of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ are the generators, its Killing form is a trace of products of
generators. It is negative definite, which reflects the compactness of the rotation group.

::: {#exm-killing-so3}
#### The Killing form of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$

Since $\operatorname{ad}_{L_a} = L_a$, $\kappa(L_a, L_b) = \operatorname{tr}(L_a L_b) = -2\delta_{ab}$
(@prp-so3-killing-form, @exr-killing-form): negative definite. The form $-\kappa/2 = \delta_{ab}$ is the invariant
inner product on the Lie algebra from which the bi-invariant metric of $SU(2)$ is built (@sec-maurer-cartan).
:::

At the other extreme, the Killing form can vanish or be degenerate. This happens for abelian algebras and for the affine
algebra, which are not semisimple.

::: {#exm-killing-abelian}
#### Degenerate Killing forms

For an abelian Lie algebra $\operatorname{ad} = 0$ and $\kappa = 0$; for the affine algebra $[X, Y] = Y$,
$\kappa(X, X) = 1$ and all other components vanish, a degenerate form. Non-degeneracy of $\kappa$ characterises
the **semisimple** Lie algebras (Cartan's criterion).
:::

Sage computes Killing forms directly from structure constants. The example points to an exercise that builds
$\mathfrak{so}(3)$ in Sage's Lie algebra module.

::: {#exm-killing-sage}
#### Sage's Lie algebra module

`lie_algebras.so(QQ, 3)` and `LieAlgebra(QQ, {...})` build $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ from its structure constants, check
the Jacobi identity, and compute the Killing form with `killing_form_matrix` (@exr-so3-lie-algebra):
$-2\delta_{ab}$, negative definite, and the algebra is simple of type $A_1$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A simple Lie algebra of a non-compact group has a non-degenerate but indefinite Killing form. The first exercise
computes it for $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R})$.

::: {#exr-lg-killing-sl2}
#### The Killing form of $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R})$

Compute $\kappa$ in the basis $(H, E, F)$ from the adjoint matrices of @exr-lg-ad-homomorphism, show that $\kappa(X, Y)
= 4\operatorname{tr}(XY)$, and find its signature.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\kappa(H, H) = \operatorname{tr}\operatorname{diag}(0, 4, 4) = 8$, $\kappa(E, F) = \kappa(F, E) = 4$, and all other
components vanish, while $\operatorname{tr}(H^2) = 2$, $\operatorname{tr}(EF) = 1$: $\kappa = 4\operatorname{tr}$. The
matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $8, 4, -4$, so $\kappa$ is
non-degenerate of signature $(2, 1)$: $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R})$ is semisimple but its group is not compact. The
negative direction is $E - F$, the generator of the rotations $SO(2) \subset SL(2, \mathbb{R})$.

{{< sage exr-lg-killing-sl2 >}}
:::

The definition asserts that the Killing form is invariant under the adjoint action. The second exercise proves this
from the representation property of $\operatorname{ad}$ and the cyclicity of the trace.

::: {#exr-lg-killing-invariance}
#### Invariance of the Killing form

Prove $\kappa([Z, X], Y) + \kappa(X, [Z, Y]) = 0$, and deduce the group version $\kappa(\operatorname{Ad}_gX,
\operatorname{Ad}_gY) = \kappa(X, Y)$ for $g = e^{tZ}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @exr-lg-ad-homomorphism, $\operatorname{ad}_{[Z, X]} = [\operatorname{ad}_Z, \operatorname{ad}_X]$, so with $A =
\operatorname{ad}_Z$, $B = \operatorname{ad}_X$, $C = \operatorname{ad}_Y$ the sum is $\operatorname{tr}((AB - BA)C) +
\operatorname{tr}(B(AC - CA)) = \operatorname{tr}(ABC) - \operatorname{tr}(BAC) + \operatorname{tr}(BAC) -
\operatorname{tr}(BCA) = 0$ by cyclicity. For $g = e^{tZ}$, $\frac{d}{dt}\kappa(\operatorname{Ad}_gX,
\operatorname{Ad}_gY) = \kappa([Z, \operatorname{Ad}_gX], \operatorname{Ad}_gY) + \kappa(\operatorname{Ad}_gX, [Z,
\operatorname{Ad}_gY]) = 0$, since $\frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{tZ}}W = [Z, \operatorname{Ad}_{e^{tZ}}W]$; at
$t = 0$ the value is $\kappa(X, Y)$.
:::

For the matrix algebras of compact groups the Killing form is a multiple of the trace form of the defining
representation. The third exercise finds the multiple for $\mathfrak{su}(n)$.

::: {#exr-lg-killing-su-n}
#### The Killing form of $\mathfrak{su}(n)$

Compute the Killing form of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ from the adjoint matrices in a real basis of
traceless anti-Hermitian matrices, and verify $\kappa(X, Y) = 2n\operatorname{tr}(XY)$. What is $\kappa(T_a, T_b)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Sage computes $\operatorname{ad}$ in a real basis by solving for coordinates, and finds $\kappa = 4\operatorname{tr}$ for
$n = 2$ and $\kappa = 6\operatorname{tr}$ for $n = 3$, both negative definite. For $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, $\kappa(T_a,
T_b) = 4\operatorname{tr}(T_aT_b) = -2\delta_{ab}$, the same as for $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ (@exm-killing-so3), as it must be
for isomorphic Lie algebras. The general formula follows from the decomposition of $\mathfrak{gl}(n)$ under the
adjoint action.

{{< sage exr-lg-killing-su-n >}}
:::
::::

The examples so far quoted the brackets of the generators $L_a$. The proposition states them for all pairs of indices,
with the Levi-Civita symbol as structure constants.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-so3-structure}
#### Structure constants of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$

The matrices @eq-so3-basis satisfy $[L_a, L_b] = \sum_c \epsilon_{abc} L_c$ for all $a, b$.
:::

for the nine pairs.

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The generators $L_a$ act on vectors by a cross product. This makes the proposition the statement that the commutator of
$\mathfrak{so}(3)$ is the cross product of $\mathbb{R}^3$.

::: {#exm-lg-so3-cross}
#### Generators as cross products

$(L_av)_b = (L_a)_{bc}v_c = -\epsilon_{abc}v_c = \epsilon_{bac}v_c = (e_a \times v)_b$, so $L_av = e_a \times v$ and,
for $n \in \mathbb{R}^3$, $(n \cdot L)v = n \times v$: the infinitesimal rotation about $n$. The bracket $[n \cdot L, m
\cdot L] = (n \times m) \cdot L$ is then the proposition written without indices, and its Jacobi identity is that of
the cross product (@exr-lg-cross-product, @exr-lg-so3-cross-product).
:::

The bracket of two generators has a direct geometric meaning in the group. It is the leading term of the commutator of
two small rotations.

::: {#exm-lg-so3-small-rotations}
#### Small rotations do not commute

Rotating by a small angle $\varepsilon$ about $X$, then about $Y$, then back about $X$ and back about $Y$ does not
return every vector to itself: to second order the result is the rotation $1 + \varepsilon^2[L_1, L_2] = 1 +
\varepsilon^2L_3$ about $Z$ (@exr-lg-so3-commutator). The structure constant $\epsilon_{123} = 1$ measures this
failure, and its sign fixes the orientation of the resulting rotation.
:::

Quantum mechanics uses Hermitian generators instead of anti-Hermitian ones. The proposition then takes the familiar
form of the angular momentum commutation relations.

::: {#exm-lg-so3-angular-momentum}
#### Angular momentum operators

With $J_a = iL_a$, Hermitian matrices, the proposition becomes $[J_a, J_b] = i^2\epsilon_{abc}L_c = i\epsilon_{abc}J_c$,
the commutation relations of angular momentum in units $\hbar = 1$ (@exr-lg-change-of-basis). The matrices $J_a$ are the
spin-one representation: $J_3 = iL_3$ has eigenvalues $-1, 0, 1$, and $\sum_aJ_a^2 = -\sum_aL_a^2 = 2 \cdot 1 = j(j +
1)1$ with $j = 1$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise builds $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ from its structure constants in Sage's Lie algebra module. It then
compares the abstract brackets with those of the matrices of the proposition.

::: {#exr-so3-lie-algebra}
#### $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ in Sage's Lie algebra module

Build $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ from its structure constants with `LieAlgebra`, check its brackets against the matrices
$L_a$, and compute its Killing form.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-so3-lie-algebra >}}
:::

The cross product description of the generators can be checked symbolically for arbitrary vectors. The second exercise
does this and recovers the proposition from it.

::: {#exr-lg-so3-cross-product}
#### The commutator is the cross product

For $n, m, v \in \mathbb{R}^3$ show that $(n \cdot L)v = n \times v$ and $[n \cdot L, m \cdot L] = (n \times m) \cdot L$,
and recover $[L_a, L_b] = \epsilon_{abc}L_c$ by choosing $n = e_a$, $m = e_b$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The first identity is @exm-lg-so3-cross. For the second, apply both sides to $v$: $[n \cdot L, m \cdot L]v = n \times (m
\times v) - m \times (n \times v) = (n \times m) \times v$ by the Jacobi identity of the cross product, which is $((n
\times m) \cdot L)v$. With $n = e_a$, $m = e_b$, $e_a \times e_b = \epsilon_{abc}e_c$ gives the proposition:

{{< sage exr-lg-so3-cross-product >}}
:::

The geometric meaning of the bracket can be tested by multiplying rotation matrices and expanding in the angle. The
third exercise carries out the expansion of @exm-lg-so3-small-rotations.

::: {#exr-lg-so3-commutator}
#### The group commutator of two rotations

Expand $R_X(\varepsilon)R_Y(\varepsilon)R_X(-\varepsilon)R_Y(-\varepsilon)$ to second order in $\varepsilon$, where
$R_X(t) = e^{tL_1}$ and $R_Y(t) = e^{tL_2}$, and compare with $1 + \varepsilon^2[L_1, L_2]$. What happens if the two
axes are exchanged?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $e^{\pm\varepsilon L} = 1 \pm \varepsilon L + \frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}L^2 + O(\varepsilon^3)$, the terms of first
order cancel, the squares cancel against the cross terms $-\varepsilon^2L_1^2$ and $-\varepsilon^2L_2^2$, and what
remains at second order is $\varepsilon^2(L_1L_2 - L_2L_1) = \varepsilon^2L_3$. Exchanging the axes gives $1 -
\varepsilon^2L_3$, the rotation about $Z$ in the opposite sense:

{{< sage exr-lg-so3-commutator >}}
:::
::::

The same structure constants appear for $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, together with a trace normalisation that fixes the scale
of the generators. Both are identities between complex $2 \times 2$ matrices.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-su2-structure}
#### Structure constants and normalisation of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$

The matrices $T_a = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ satisfy $[T_1, T_2] = T_3$, $[T_2, T_3] = T_1$, $[T_3, T_1] = T_2$ and
$\operatorname{tr}(T_a T_b) = -\tfrac12\delta_{ab}$.
:::

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.su2_brackets` and `KaluzaKlein.trace_T_mul`, proved entry by entry over $\mathbb{C}$.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.su2_brackets >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
