:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In quantum mechanics the generators of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ are written as Hermitian spin matrices. The proposition
then becomes the spin commutation relations of a spin one-half particle.

::: {#exm-lg-su2-spin}
#### Spin one-half

The Hermitian matrices $S_a = iT_a = \tfrac12\sigma_a$ satisfy $[S_a, S_b] = i\epsilon_{abc}S_c$ by the proposition,
the same relations as the $J_a$ of @exm-lg-so3-angular-momentum. Here $S_3 = \operatorname{diag}(\tfrac12, -
\tfrac12)$ and $\sum_aS_a^2 = \tfrac34 1 = j(j + 1)1$ with $j = \tfrac12$: the defining representation of
$SU(2)$ is the spin one-half representation, which has no counterpart for $SO(3)$.
:::

Twice the generators satisfy the multiplication rules of the quaternion units. This identifies $SU(2)$ with the unit
quaternions of @exm-lie-group-su2.

::: {#exm-lg-su2-quaternions}
#### Quaternions

Let $\mathbf{i} = 2T_1 = -i\sigma_1$, $\mathbf{j} = 2T_2$, $\mathbf{k} = 2T_3$. Then $\mathbf{i}^2 = -\sigma_1^2 = -1$,
and likewise for $\mathbf{j}$, $\mathbf{k}$, while $\mathbf{i}\mathbf{j} = -\sigma_1\sigma_2 = -i\sigma_3 = \mathbf{k}$
by @eq-pauli: Hamilton's relations. The bracket $[2T_1, 2T_2] = 2\mathbf{k}$ is the proposition multiplied by four, and
the element $a_0 + a_1\mathbf{i} + a_2\mathbf{j} + a_3\mathbf{k}$ with $\sum a_\mu^2 = 1$ is a general element of
$SU(2)$ (@exr-lg-su2-preimage).
:::

The trace normalisation turns the trace into an inner product on the Lie algebra. It gives a formula for the
components of any element in the basis $T_a$.

::: {#exm-lg-su2-components}
#### Components from traces

For $X = x_aT_a$, $\operatorname{tr}(T_bX) = x_a\operatorname{tr}(T_bT_a) = -\tfrac12x_b$, so $x_b = -
2\operatorname{tr}(T_bX)$, the formula used for the Maurer-Cartan forms in @def-maurer-cartan-form. Explicitly $X =
\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix} -ix_3 & -ix_1 - x_2 \\ -ix_1 + x_2 & ix_3 \end{pmatrix}$, with $\det X = \tfrac14|x|^2$
(@exr-lg-su2-components).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The trace formula for components and the determinant of a Lie algebra element can be checked symbolically. The first
exercise also computes the square of a general element.

::: {#exr-lg-su2-components}
#### The trace form of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$

For $X = x_aT_a$ and $Y = y_aT_a$ verify $x_a = -2\operatorname{tr}(T_aX)$, $X^2 = -\tfrac14|x|^2 1$, $\det X =
\tfrac14|x|^2$ and $-2\operatorname{tr}(XY) = x \cdot y$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
From @eq-pauli, $(x_a\sigma_a)^2 = x_ax_b(\delta_{ab} + i\epsilon_{abc}\sigma_c) = |x|^2 1$, so $X^2 =
(-\tfrac{i}{2})^2|x|^2 1 = -\tfrac14|x|^2 1$; taking the trace of $XY$ in the same way gives $-\tfrac12x \cdot y$.
For a traceless $2 \times 2$ matrix $X^2 = -\det X \cdot 1$ (Cayley-Hamilton), so $\det X = \tfrac14|x|^2$:

{{< sage exr-lg-su2-components >}}
:::

The brackets and the trace both follow from the product rule of the Pauli matrices. The second exercise derives this
rule from the matrices and then derives the proposition from it.

::: {#exr-lg-su2-product-rule}
#### The product rule of the Pauli matrices

Check $\sigma_a\sigma_b = \delta_{ab}1 + i\epsilon_{abc}\sigma_c$ on the explicit matrices, deduce $T_aT_b = -
\tfrac14\delta_{ab}1 + \tfrac12\epsilon_{abc}T_c$, and obtain both statements of the proposition from this single
formula.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each $\sigma_a^2 = 1$ by direct multiplication, and $\sigma_1\sigma_2 = \begin{pmatrix} i & 0 \\ 0 & -i \end{pmatrix} =
i\sigma_3$, with the cyclic permutations similar and $\sigma_b\sigma_a = -\sigma_a\sigma_b$ for $a \neq b$. Then
$T_aT_b = -\tfrac14\sigma_a\sigma_b = -\tfrac14\delta_{ab}1 - \tfrac{i}{4}\epsilon_{abc}\sigma_c = -
\tfrac14\delta_{ab}1 + \tfrac12\epsilon_{abc}T_c$, since $-\tfrac{i}{4}\sigma_c = \tfrac12T_c$. Antisymmetrising in $a,
b$ removes the $\delta$ term and doubles the $\epsilon$ term, $[T_a, T_b] = \epsilon_{abc}T_c$; taking the trace
removes the $T_c$ term, $\operatorname{tr}(T_aT_b) = -\tfrac14\delta_{ab} \cdot 2 = -\tfrac12\delta_{ab}$.
:::

Equal structure constants mean that $T_a \mapsto L_a$ extends to an isomorphism of Lie algebras. The third exercise
proves this and identifies the isomorphism with the adjoint representation.

::: {#exr-lg-su2-so3-isomorphism}
#### $\mathfrak{su}(2) \cong \mathfrak{so}(3)$

Show that the linear map $\phi(x_aT_a) = x_aL_a$ satisfies $\phi([X, Y]) = [\phi(X), \phi(Y)]$, and that $\phi(X)$ is
the matrix of $\operatorname{ad}_X$ in the basis $T_b$. Is there a group isomorphism $SU(2) \to SO(3)$ with derivative
$\phi$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both sides are bilinear, so it suffices to check basis elements: $\phi([T_a, T_b]) = \epsilon_{abc}L_c = [L_a, L_b]$ by
the two propositions. The matrix of $\operatorname{ad}_{T_a}$ has entries $(\operatorname{ad}_{T_a})_{cb} =
\epsilon_{abc} = (L_a)_{cb}$, exactly as for $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ in @exm-adjoint-so3, so $\phi = \operatorname{ad}$. No
group isomorphism exists, since $SU(2)$ has centre $\{\pm 1\}$ (@exr-lg-centre-su2) while the centre of $SO(3)$ is
trivial; the group homomorphism with derivative $\phi$ is $\operatorname{Ad} : SU(2) \to SO(3)$, the double cover.
:::
::::

The Killing form of the rotation algebra was computed in the examples. The proposition records the result in the basis
of the generators $L_a$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-so3-killing-form}
#### The Killing form of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$

$\kappa(L_a, L_b) = \operatorname{tr}(L_a L_b) = -2\delta_{ab}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.so3_killing_form`.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Expanding the proposition for general elements gives the Killing form in terms of vectors. Up to a factor it is the
Euclidean dot product.

::: {#exm-lg-killing-so3-dot}
#### The Killing form as a dot product

For $X = x \cdot L$ and $Y = y \cdot L$, bilinearity gives $\kappa(X, Y) = x_ay_b\kappa(L_a, L_b) = -2x \cdot y$. So
$-\tfrac12\kappa$ is the Euclidean inner product of $\mathbb{R}^3 \cong \mathfrak{so}(3)$, and the invariance of
$\kappa$ is the invariance of the dot product under rotations (@exr-lg-killing-so3-invariance).
:::

For $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ the Killing form coincides with the trace form of the defining representation. In higher
dimensions a factor depending on $n$ appears.

::: {#exm-lg-killing-trace-so-n}
#### Killing form and trace

Because $\operatorname{ad}_{L_a} = L_a$, $\kappa(X, Y) = \operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{so}(3)$. For
$\mathfrak{so}(n)$ the general formula is $\kappa(X, Y) = (n - 2)\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ (@exr-lg-killing-so4), which
gives $1$ for $n = 3$; for $n = 2$ the factor vanishes, as it must for the abelian algebra $\mathfrak{so}(2)$.
:::

A non-degenerate invariant form can be inverted and contracted with two generators. The result is the quadratic Casimir
element, which commutes with every generator.

::: {#exm-lg-killing-casimir}
#### The Casimir element

With $\kappa_{ab} = -2\delta_{ab}$ the inverse is $\kappa^{ab} = -\tfrac12\delta_{ab}$, and the Casimir element in the
defining representation is $C = \kappa^{ab}L_aL_b = -\tfrac12\sum_aL_a^2$. Since $L_a^2 = -(1 - e_ae_a^{\mathsf{T}})$,
$\sum_aL_a^2 = -2 \cdot 1$ and $C = 1$: a multiple of the identity, as Schur's lemma requires for an irreducible
representation, and $C$ commutes with every $L_b$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the Killing form from the adjoint matrices by hand. It is the computation behind the
proposition.

::: {#exr-killing-form}
#### The Killing form

Compute the matrices $\operatorname{ad}_{L_a}$ in the basis $L_b$ and the Killing form of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{ad}_{L_a} L_b = \epsilon_{abc} L_c$, so the matrix of $\operatorname{ad}_{L_a}$ in the basis
$L_b$ has entries $(\operatorname{ad}_{L_a})_{cb} = \epsilon_{abc} = -\epsilon_{acb} = (L_a)_{cb}$ by
@eq-so3-basis: $\operatorname{ad}_{L_a}$ is the matrix $L_a$ itself, and $\kappa(L_a, L_b) =
\operatorname{tr}(L_a L_b)$. For $a = b = 3$, $L_3^2 = \operatorname{diag}(-1, -1, 0)$ has trace $-2$; for $a \neq
b$ the product has zero diagonal. So $\kappa = -2\delta_{ab}$. In Sage:

{{< sage exr-killing-form >}}
:::

The proportionality between the Killing form and the trace form holds for all rotation algebras. The second exercise
checks it for $n = 3, 4, 5$.

::: {#exr-lg-killing-so4}
#### The Killing form of $\mathfrak{so}(n)$

With the basis $M_{jk}$ of @exr-lg-so-n-dim compute the Killing form of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ and verify $\kappa(X, Y) =
2\operatorname{tr}(XY)$; check $\kappa = (n - 2)\operatorname{tr}$ also for $n = 3, 5$ and conclude that these
algebras are semisimple with negative definite Killing form.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{tr}(M_{jk}M_{lm}) = -2\delta_{jl}\delta_{km}$ for $j < k$, $l < m$, so the trace form is $-2$ times the
identity in this basis, and $\kappa = (n - 2)\operatorname{tr}$ is $-2(n - 2)$ times the identity: $-2$, $-4$, $-6$ for
$n = 3, 4, 5$. All are negative definite, so the algebras are semisimple and the groups compact:

{{< sage exr-lg-killing-so4 >}}
:::

The dot product description of the Killing form makes its invariance a familiar fact. The third exercise derives it
from the transformation of generators under rotations.

::: {#exr-lg-killing-so3-invariance}
#### Invariance under rotations

Show that $RL_aR^{-1} = R_{ba}L_b$ for $R \in SO(3)$, i.e. $\operatorname{Ad}_R(x \cdot L) = (Rx) \cdot L$, and deduce
$\kappa(\operatorname{Ad}_RX, \operatorname{Ad}_RY) = \kappa(X, Y)$ from the proposition.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @exm-lg-so3-cross, $(x \cdot L)v = x \times v$, and for a rotation $R(x \times R^{-1}v) = (Rx) \times v$, since
rotations preserve the cross product (they have determinant one). Hence $R(x \cdot L)R^{-1} = (Rx) \cdot L$. With
$\kappa(x \cdot L, y \cdot L) = -2x \cdot y$ (@exm-lg-killing-so3-dot), $\kappa(\operatorname{Ad}_RX,
\operatorname{Ad}_RY) = -2(Rx) \cdot (Ry) = -2x \cdot y = \kappa(X, Y)$, since $R$ is orthogonal.
:::
::::

### The exponential map {#sec-exponential}

The exponential of a matrix turns a Lie algebra element into a one-parameter subgroup of the Lie group, and this is how
the Lie algebra, a linear object, controls the group near the identity. The exponentials of the $\mathfrak{su}(2)$
generators give the Euler-angle parametrisation of $SU(2)$ used throughout, and the exponential of $L_3$ is the
rotation matrix, characterised as the solution of a differential equation. This section defines the matrix
exponential, one-parameter subgroups and the exponential map, works them out for $U(1)$, $SO(3)$ and $SU(2)$, and
composes two rotations by multiplying their exponentials in $SU(2)$.

#### The matrix exponential

The exponential series makes sense for square matrices because matrix powers are defined and the factorials make the
series converge. Its properties are those of the scalar exponential, except where non-commutativity intervenes.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-matrix-exponential}
#### Matrix exponential

The **matrix exponential** of a square matrix $X$ is $e^X = \sum_{k \geq 0} X^k/k!$, a convergent series for
every $X$. It satisfies $e^0 = 1$, $e^{sX}e^{tX} = e^{(s + t)X}$, $(e^X)^{-1} = e^{-X}$, $e^{gXg^{-1}} = ge^Xg^{-1}$
and $\det e^X = e^{\operatorname{tr}X}$; when $X$ and $Y$ commute, $e^{X + Y} = e^Xe^Y$, but not in general.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
When a matrix is diagonal the series acts entry by entry, and when it is nilpotent the series stops. These two cases
already produce the dilations and the translations of the affine group.

::: {#exm-exp-diagonal}
#### Diagonal and nilpotent matrices

For $X = \operatorname{diag}(x_1, \dots, x_n)$, $e^X = \operatorname{diag}(e^{x_1}, \dots, e^{x_n})$; for the
nilpotent $Y = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $Y^2 = 0$ and $e^{tY} = 1 + tY = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & t
\\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, the translations of the affine group (@exr-affine-left-invariant).
:::

For the $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ generators the square of each Pauli matrix is the identity. The series then splits into a
cosine and a sine, at half the angle.

::: {#exm-exp-su2}
#### Exponentials of the $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ generators

Because $\sigma_a^2 = 1$, the series for $e^{tT_a} = e^{-it\sigma_a/2}$ splits into even and odd powers:
$$
e^{tT_a} = \sum_k \frac{(-it/2)^k \sigma_a^k}{k!}
  = \cos\tfrac{t}{2}\, 1 - i\sin\tfrac{t}{2}\, \sigma_a ,
$$ {#eq-exp-su2}
so that
$$
e^{\varphi T_3} = \begin{pmatrix} e^{-i\varphi/2} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{i\varphi/2} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
e^{\theta T_1} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\frac{\theta}{2} & -i\sin\frac{\theta}{2} \\ -i\sin\frac{\theta}{2} & \cos\frac{\theta}{2} \end{pmatrix}
$$ {#eq-exp-t3-t1}
(@exr-exp-su2). The one-parameter subgroup $e^{tT_3}$ returns to the identity at $t = 4\pi$, not $2\pi$:
$e^{2\pi T_3} = -1$ (@fig-double-cover). This is the origin of the range $\psi \in (0, 4\pi)$ in @eq-euler-angles.
:::

For a rotation generator the powers repeat with period four up to sign, as for the imaginary unit. The series sums to
the rotation matrix, at the full angle.

::: {#exm-exp-so3}
#### The rotation subgroup of $SO(3)$

For $L_3$ the same splitting works with $L_3^2 = \operatorname{diag}(-1, -1, 0)$ and $L_3^3 = -L_3$
(@exr-exp-rotation): $e^{tL_3} = 1 + \sin t\, L_3 + (1 - \cos t)L_3^2 = R(t)$, the rotation by $t$ about the
third axis, with $R(2\pi) = 1$: $SO(3)$ closes after one turn where $SU(2)$ needs two. What characterises $R(t)$
as the one-parameter subgroup generated by $L_3$ is the pair of properties $R(0) = 1$ and $\dot R(t) = L_3 R(t)$,
which have a unique solution (@prp-rotation-subgroup).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The simplest exponential map is that of the circle group, where the exponential series is the ordinary complex
exponential. The figure shows how it wraps the Lie algebra around the group.

![The exponential map of the circle group: the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{u}(1) = i\mathbb{R}$ is the tangent line
at the identity $1$, and $\exp$ wraps it onto the circle, $it \mapsto e^{it}$; the segment $[0, 2\pi)$ covers the
circle once and $2\pi i$ lands on $1$ again, so the kernel of $\exp$ is $2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$. Generated by
`figures/exp_circle.sage`.](figures/exp_circle.svg){#fig-exp-circle width=40%}

The first exercise compares Sage's matrix exponential with the closed form of @eq-exp-su2. It also evaluates the
subgroup at the two special parameters $2\pi$ and $4\pi$.

::: {#exr-exp-su2}
#### Exponentials of the $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ generators

With Sage's matrix exponential, compute $e^{tT_a}$ for $a = 1, 2, 3$, compare with @eq-exp-su2, and evaluate
$e^{2\pi T_3}$ and $e^{4\pi T_3}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-exp-su2 >}}
:::

The determinant identity of the definition is the reason the exponential of a traceless matrix has unit determinant.
The second exercise proves it and checks it on an upper triangular matrix.

::: {#exr-lg-det-exp}
#### $\det e^X = e^{\operatorname{tr}X}$

Prove $\det e^{tX} = e^{t\operatorname{tr}X}$ by showing that $f(t) = \det e^{tX}$ satisfies $f' =
(\operatorname{tr}X)f$. Compute $e^X$ for $X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and check the identity.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f(t + s) = \det(e^{sX}e^{tX}) = \det e^{sX}\, f(t)$, and $\det e^{sX} = \det(1 + sX + O(s^2)) = 1 +
s\operatorname{tr}X + O(s^2)$, so $f'(t) = (\operatorname{tr}X)f(t)$ with $f(0) = 1$, whose solution is
$e^{t\operatorname{tr}X}$. For the given $X$, with eigenvalues $1$ and $3$, $e^X$ is upper triangular with diagonal
$(e, e^3)$ and corner entry $2(e^3 - e)/(3 - 1) = e^3 - e$, as one checks from $Xe^X = e^XX$. Its determinant is $e
\cdot e^3 = e^4 = e^{\operatorname{tr}X}$.
:::

For non-commuting matrices the exponential of a sum is not the product of the exponentials. The third exercise
measures the discrepancy and finds that its leading term is the commutator.

::: {#exr-lg-exp-noncommuting}
#### Exponentials of non-commuting matrices

For $X = E$ and $Y = F$ of @exr-lg-sl2-algebra compute $e^Xe^Y$ and $e^{X + Y}$ and show they differ. Then show that
$e^{sX}e^{sY} = e^{s(X + Y) + \frac{s^2}{2}[X, Y] + O(s^3)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^Xe^Y = (1 + X)(1 + Y) = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, while $(X + Y)^2 = 1$ gives $e^{X + Y} =
\cosh 1 \cdot 1 + \sinh 1\,(X + Y)$, a symmetric matrix with diagonal $\cosh 1 \neq 2$. Expanding both sides to second
order, $e^{sX}e^{sY} = 1 + s(X + Y) + \frac{s^2}{2}(X^2 + 2XY + Y^2)$, while $e^{s(X + Y)}$ has
$\frac{s^2}{2}(X^2 + XY + YX + Y^2)$: the difference is $\frac{s^2}{2}[X, Y]$, the first term of the
Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula.

{{< sage exr-lg-exp-noncommuting >}}
:::
::::

#### One-parameter subgroups and the exponential map

The curves $t \mapsto e^{tX}$ are homomorphisms from the real line into the group. The definition turns this property
into the definition of a one-parameter subgroup, for any Lie group.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-one-parameter-subgroup}
#### One-parameter subgroup

A **one-parameter subgroup** of a Lie group $G$ is a smooth homomorphism $\gamma : (\mathbb{R}, +) \to G$,
$\gamma(s)\gamma(t) = \gamma(s + t)$, $\gamma(0) = e$. Its **generator** is the velocity $X = \dot\gamma(0) \in
\mathfrak{g}$, and $\gamma$ is determined by $X$: for a matrix group, $\gamma(t) = e^{tX}$, the unique solution of
$\dot\gamma = X\gamma$ with $\gamma(0) = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Rotations about a fixed axis are the one-parameter subgroups of $SO(3)$. Acting on the sphere they are the flows of the
Killing fields.

::: {#exm-one-parameter-rotations}
#### Rotations about an axis

$t \mapsto R(t)$ is the one-parameter subgroup of $SO(3)$ generated by $L_3$ (@prp-rotation-subgroup); its orbits
on the sphere are the parallels, the integral curves of the Killing field $K_3 = \partial_\varphi$ (@sec-killing),
whose flow it is.
:::

In $SU(2)$ the one-parameter subgroups are great circles of the three-sphere through the identity. Each covers a
rotation subgroup of $SO(3)$ twice.

::: {#exm-one-parameter-su2}
#### Great circles of $SU(2)$

$t \mapsto e^{tT_a}$ are one-parameter subgroups of $SU(2)$, great circles of $S^3$ through the identity of
period $4\pi$ (@eq-exp-su2); every one-parameter subgroup of $SU(2)$ is $e^{t(n_aT_a)}$ for a unit vector $n$, a
rotation about the axis $n$ after the double cover.
:::

On the torus every one-parameter subgroup is a straight line in the angle coordinates. Its slope decides whether it
closes up.

::: {#exm-one-parameter-torus}
#### Lines on the torus

$t \mapsto (e^{it}, e^{i\alpha t})$ is a one-parameter subgroup of $T^2$ with generator $(i, i\alpha)$: closed
when $\alpha$ is rational, dense when it is irrational (@exm-lie-subgroup-torus); the exponential map of the torus
is $\mathbb{R}^2 \to T^2$, $(x, y) \mapsto (e^{ix}, e^{iy})$, with kernel $2\pi\mathbb{Z}^2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The one-parameter subgroups of the affine group can be computed in closed form. The first exercise does this for one
generator and checks both characterisations of the definition.

::: {#exr-lg-one-param-affine}
#### A one-parameter subgroup of the affine group

With $X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $Y = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ compute
$\gamma(t) = e^{t(X + Y)}$, check $\gamma(s)\gamma(t) = \gamma(s + t)$ and $\dot\gamma = (X + Y)\gamma$, describe the
curve in the coordinates $(a, b)$, and compute $e^{xX + yY}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(X + Y)^2 = X + Y$, so $e^{t(X + Y)} = 1 + (e^t - 1)(X + Y) = \begin{pmatrix} e^t & e^t - 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$:
in coordinates $(a, b) = (e^t, e^t - 1)$, the half-line $b = a - 1$ through the identity $(1, 0)$, i.e. the maps $x
\mapsto e^tx + e^t - 1$ fixing the point $x = -1$. The group law and the differential equation hold, and in general
$e^{xX + yY} = \begin{pmatrix} e^x & y(e^x - 1)/x \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ (with $y$ in the corner when $x = 0$):

{{< sage exr-lg-one-param-affine >}}
:::

The definition claims that a one-parameter subgroup is determined by its generator. The second exercise proves this
for matrix groups through a differential equation.

::: {#exr-lg-one-param-uniqueness}
#### A one-parameter subgroup is an exponential

Let $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to GL(n)$ be differentiable with $\gamma(s + t) = \gamma(s)\gamma(t)$ and let $X =
\dot\gamma(0)$. Show that $\dot\gamma(t) = X\gamma(t)$ and that $\gamma(t) = e^{tX}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Differentiating $\gamma(s + t) = \gamma(s)\gamma(t)$ in $s$ at $s = 0$ gives $\dot\gamma(t) = X\gamma(t)$; setting
$s = t = 0$ in the group law gives $\gamma(0) = \gamma(0)^2$, so $\gamma(0) = 1$ since $\gamma(0)$ is invertible. Then
$\frac{d}{dt}(e^{-tX}\gamma(t)) = e^{-tX}(-X\gamma + \dot\gamma) = 0$, so $e^{-tX}\gamma(t) = \gamma(0) = 1$ and
$\gamma(t) = e^{tX}$. The same argument, with $\dot\gamma = \gamma X$, follows from differentiating in $t$ instead.
:::

The closed form @eq-exp-su2 holds for the generators along the coordinate axes. The third exercise extends it to an
arbitrary axis.

::: {#exr-lg-one-param-su2-axis}
#### One-parameter subgroups of $SU(2)$ about any axis

For a unit vector $n$ show that $e^{t\,n \cdot T} = \cos\frac{t}{2}1 - i\sin\frac{t}{2}\,n \cdot \sigma$, that it has
period $4\pi$, and that its image in $SO(3)$ is the rotation by $t$ about $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @eq-pauli, $(n \cdot \sigma)^2 = n_an_b(\delta_{ab} + i\epsilon_{abc}\sigma_c) = |n|^2 1 = 1$, so the series for
$e^{-it\,n \cdot \sigma/2}$ splits into even and odd powers exactly as in @exm-exp-su2. The result equals $1$ when
$\cos\frac{t}{2} = 1$, i.e. $t \in 4\pi\mathbb{Z}$, and $-1$ at $t = 2\pi$. Its image under $\operatorname{Ad}$ is
$e^{t\,\operatorname{ad}_{n \cdot T}} = e^{t\,n \cdot L}$ (@exr-lg-su2-so3-isomorphism, @exr-lg-ad-exp), the rotation
by $t$ about $n$ (@exm-lg-rotation-rodrigues), which has period $2\pi$.
:::
::::

Following each one-parameter subgroup for unit time defines a map from the Lie algebra to the group. This is the
exponential map, and it identifies a neighbourhood of zero with a neighbourhood of the identity.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-exponential-map}
#### Exponential map of a Lie group

The **exponential map** $\exp : \mathfrak{g} \to G$ sends $X$ to $\gamma_X(1) = e^X$, the point reached after unit
time along its one-parameter subgroup. It is a diffeomorphism from a neighbourhood of $0$ in $\mathfrak{g}$ onto
a neighbourhood of $e$, and for compact connected groups it is surjective; the representations of $G$ and of
$\mathfrak{g}$ correspond through it, $\rho(e^X) = e^{\rho(X)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the circle group the exponential map is the complex exponential on the imaginary axis. It is the covering of the
circle by the line.

::: {#exm-exponential-u1}
#### $\mathfrak{u}(1) \to U(1)$

$\exp(it) = e^{it}$ wraps the tangent line onto the circle (@fig-exp-circle): surjective, locally bijective, with
kernel $2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$; it is the covering $\mathbb{R} \to U(1)$ of @exm-cover-r-u1. A representation of $U(1)$
of charge $q$, $e^{i\alpha} \mapsto e^{iq\alpha}$, corresponds to the Lie algebra representation $i \mapsto iq$.
:::

For $SU(2)$ the exponential map is surjective but collapses a whole sphere to a single point. The Euler angles give an
alternative description of every element as a product of exponentials.

::: {#exm-exponential-su2}
#### $\mathfrak{su}(2) \to SU(2)$

$\exp$ sends the ball $|X| < 2\pi$ (with $|n_aT_a| = 1$ for unit $n$) onto $SU(2)$ minus $-1$ and the whole sphere
$|X| = 2\pi$ to $-1$: surjective but not injective. Every element of $SU(2)$ is an exponential, and the Euler
angles @eq-euler-angles write it as a product of three.
:::

Multiplying the exponentials of the Euler angles gives the explicit element of $SU(2)$ used throughout the book. Its
entries are the coordinates of the three-sphere.

::: {#exm-exponential-euler}
#### The Euler-angle matrix

Multiplying @eq-exp-t3-t1 in the order of @eq-euler-angles, row by row: the first row of
$e^{\varphi T_3} e^{\theta T_1}$ is $e^{-i\varphi/2}(\cos\frac{\theta}{2}, -i\sin\frac{\theta}{2})$ and the second is
$e^{i\varphi/2}(-i\sin\frac{\theta}{2}, \cos\frac{\theta}{2})$; multiplying by $e^{\psi T_3}$ on the right scales
the first column by $e^{-i\psi/2}$ and the second by $e^{i\psi/2}$, giving
$$
g(\theta, \varphi, \psi) = \begin{pmatrix}
  \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\, e^{-i(\varphi+\psi)/2} & -i\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\, e^{-i(\varphi-\psi)/2} \\
  -i\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\, e^{i(\varphi-\psi)/2} & \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\, e^{i(\varphi+\psi)/2}
\end{pmatrix},
$$ {#eq-euler-matrix}
which has the form @eq-su2-matrix with $a = \cos\frac{\theta}{2} e^{-i(\varphi+\psi)/2}$ and
$b = -i\sin\frac{\theta}{2} e^{i(\varphi-\psi)/2}$, the entries @eq-su2-euler-entries used for the embedding of
$SU(2)$ in @sec-induced-metrics (@exr-euler-matrix). At $\theta = 0$ the matrix is $e^{(\varphi+\psi)T_3}$, which
depends only on $\varphi + \psi$: the chart degenerates there, as announced.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise multiplies the three exponentials of the Euler angles with Sage. It checks the result against
@eq-euler-matrix and confirms the degeneration of the chart at $\theta = 0$.

::: {#exr-euler-matrix}
#### The Euler-angle element

Multiply the three exponentials of @eq-euler-angles with Sage, read off $a$ and $b$, check $|a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$
and $\det g = 1$, and confirm the degeneration at $\theta = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-euler-matrix >}}
:::

For compact connected groups the exponential map is surjective, but for non-compact groups it can fail to be. The
second exercise finds an element of $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ that is not an exponential.

::: {#exr-lg-exp-not-surjective}
#### An element that is not an exponential

For $X \in \mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R})$ show that $X^2 = -(\det X)1$ and that $\operatorname{tr}e^X \geq -2$. Deduce
that $g = \operatorname{diag}(-2, -\tfrac12) \in SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ is not $e^X$ for any $X$, although it is a product
of two exponentials.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For a traceless $2 \times 2$ matrix the Cayley-Hamilton theorem gives $X^2 - (\operatorname{tr}X)X + (\det X)1 = X^2 +
(\det X)1 = 0$. If $\det X = -\lambda^2 < 0$, $X^2 = \lambda^21$ and $e^X = \cosh\lambda\,1 + \frac{\sinh\lambda}{\lambda}X$,
with trace $2\cosh\lambda \geq 2$; if $\det X = \mu^2 > 0$, $e^X = \cos\mu\,1 + \frac{\sin\mu}{\mu}X$ with trace $2\cos\mu
\geq -2$; if $\det X = 0$, $e^X = 1 + X$ with trace $2$. Since $\operatorname{tr}g = -\tfrac52 < -2$, $g$ is not an
exponential. But $g = (-1)\operatorname{diag}(2, \tfrac12) = e^{\pi(E - F)}e^{(\log 2)H}$, since $E - F$ generates the
rotations and the rotation by $\pi$ is $-1$.
:::

The correspondence $\rho(e^X) = e^{\rho(X)}$ of the definition applies in particular to the adjoint representation. The
third exercise checks $\operatorname{Ad}_{e^X} = e^{\operatorname{ad}_X}$ for $SU(2)$ and $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$.

::: {#exr-lg-ad-exp}
#### $\operatorname{Ad}_{e^X} = e^{\operatorname{ad}_X}$

Compute the matrix of $\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{tT_3}}$ in the basis $T_a$ and compare with $e^{tL_3}$; compute
$\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{tH}}$ on $(H, E, F)$ and compare with $e^{t\operatorname{ad}_H}$. Prove the identity in general
by a differential equation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both sides are one-parameter subgroups of $GL(\mathfrak{g})$ in $t$ (for $X$ replaced by $tX$), and their derivatives at
$t = 0$ are $Y \mapsto XY - YX = \operatorname{ad}_XY$; by @exr-lg-one-param-uniqueness they coincide. For $SU(2)$,
$\operatorname{ad}_{T_3} = L_3$ in the basis $T_a$, and the matrix of $\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{tT_3}}$ is the rotation
$e^{tL_3}$; for $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$, $e^{tH}Ee^{-tH} = e^{2t}E$ and $e^{tH}Fe^{-tH} = e^{-2t}F$, which is
$e^{t\operatorname{diag}(0, 2, -2)}$:

{{< sage exr-lg-ad-exp >}}
:::
::::

The rotation matrix about the $Z$-axis is the basic example of the section. The proposition collects its properties as
a one-parameter subgroup, from the powers of $L_3$ to the differential equation.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-rotation-subgroup}
#### The rotation matrix is the one-parameter subgroup of $L_3$

$L_3^2 = \operatorname{diag}(-1, -1, 0)$, $L_3^3 = -L_3$, and the matrix $R(t)$ satisfies $R(0) = 1$, $R(s)R(t) =
R(s+t)$, $R(t)R(t)^{\mathsf{T}} = 1$ and $\dot R(t) = L_3 R(t)$ entry by entry.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

of the exponential recipe, which covers nilpotent and rationally diagonalisable generators, whereas a rotation
generator has eigenvalues $\pm i$ (recorded as a building-block gap).

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.L2R_sq`, `KaluzaKlein.L2R_cube`, `KaluzaKlein.rotation_zero`, `KaluzaKlein.rotation_mul`,
`KaluzaKlein.rotation_orthogonal` and `KaluzaKlein.rotation_deriv`; the identification $R(t) = \exp(tL_3)$ is not
formalised.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.rotation_deriv >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The differential equation $\dot R = L_3R$ can be checked column by column. Each column moves on a circle with velocity
given by the cross product with the axis.

::: {#exm-lg-rotation-ode}
#### The rotation equation column by column

The first column of $R(t)$ is $(\cos t, \sin t, 0)$, with derivative $(-\sin t, \cos t, 0)$, and $L_3(\cos t, \sin t, 0)
= e_3 \times (\cos t, \sin t, 0) = (-\sin t, \cos t, 0)$ by @exm-lg-so3-cross; the second column works the same way, and
the third column $e_3$ is constant with $L_3e_3 = 0$. So $\dot R = L_3R$ says that every point moves with the velocity
$e_3 \times x$ of a rigid rotation with unit angular velocity about $Z$.
:::

The two algebraic identities of the proposition, $L_3^2 = \operatorname{diag}(-1, -1, 0)$ and $L_3^3 = -L_3$, hold for
any unit axis. They give a closed form for every rotation.

::: {#exm-lg-rotation-rodrigues}
#### Rodrigues' formula

For a unit vector $n$ and $N = n \cdot L$, $N^2 = nn^{\mathsf{T}} - 1$ and $N^3 = -N$ (@exr-lg-rodrigues), so the
exponential series sums as in @exm-exp-so3:
$$
e^{tN} = 1 + \sin t\,N + (1 - \cos t)N^2 ,
$$
the rotation by $t$ about $n$. Applied to $v$ it reads $v\cos t + (n \times v)\sin t + n(n \cdot v)(1 - \cos t)$, and
for $n = e_3$ it is the matrix $R(t)$ of the proposition.
:::

The period of the rotation subgroup is read off from the eigenvalues of its generator. Comparing with $SU(2)$ shows
where the factor two of the double cover comes from.

::: {#exm-lg-rotation-spectrum}
#### Eigenvalues and periods

$L_3$ has eigenvalues $0$ (eigenvector $e_3$) and $\pm i$ (eigenvectors $(1, \mp i, 0)/\sqrt2$), so $R(t) = e^{tL_3}$
has eigenvalues $1$ and $e^{\pm it}$ and returns to the identity first at $t = 2\pi$. The generator $T_3$ of $SU(2)$ has
eigenvalues $\mp\tfrac{i}{2}$, half as large, and $e^{tT_3}$ needs $t = 4\pi$. The adjoint representation doubles the
eigenvalues: those of $\operatorname{ad}_{T_3}$ are the differences of the eigenvalues of $T_3$, namely $0$ and $\pm i$,
the eigenvalues of $L_3$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise sums the exponential series of $L_3$ by hand. Sage then confirms that it equals the rotation matrix.

::: {#exr-exp-rotation}
#### Exponentiating a rotation generator

Compute $L_3^2$ and $L_3^3$, sum the exponential series for $e^{tL_3}$, and identify the result.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$L_3^2 = \operatorname{diag}(-1, -1, 0)$ and $L_3^3 = -L_3$, so the powers cycle with period four on the upper
$2 \times 2$ block, exactly like $i$: $e^{tL_3} = 1 + L_3 (t - t^3/3! + \dots) + L_3^2 (t^2/2! - t^4/4! + \dots)
= 1 + \sin t\, L_3 + (1 - \cos t) L_3^2$, which is the rotation by $t$ about the third axis,
$\begin{pmatrix} \cos t & -\sin t & 0 \\ \sin t & \cos t & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. In Sage:

{{< sage exr-exp-rotation >}}
:::

Rodrigues' formula follows from an algebraic identity for $n \cdot L$ that holds for every vector $n$. The second
exercise checks this identity symbolically and evaluates a rotation about a diagonal axis.

::: {#exr-lg-rodrigues}
#### Rotations about an arbitrary axis

Show that $(n \cdot L)^2 = nn^{\mathsf{T}} - |n|^21$ and $(n \cdot L)^3 = -|n|^2(n \cdot L)$ for all $n \in
\mathbb{R}^3$, derive Rodrigues' formula of @exm-lg-rotation-rodrigues for $|n| = 1$, and show that the rotation by
$2\pi/3$ about $(1, 1, 1)/\sqrt3$ permutes the coordinate axes cyclically.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(n \cdot L)^2v = n \times (n \times v) = n(n \cdot v) - |n|^2v$ gives the first identity, and multiplying by $n \cdot L$,
with $(n \cdot L)n = n \times n = 0$, gives the second. For $|n| = 1$ the odd powers of $N$ are $\pm N$ and the even
ones $\pm N^2$, and the series sums to $1 + \sin t\,N + (1 - \cos t)N^2$. At $t = 2\pi/3$ and $n = (1, 1, 1)/\sqrt3$ the
result is the permutation matrix sending $e_1 \to e_2 \to e_3 \to e_1$, a symmetry of the cube:

{{< sage exr-lg-rodrigues >}}
:::

The proposition shows that $R(t)$ satisfies the differential equation, and the definition says the solution is unique.
The third exercise proves the uniqueness directly, using only orthogonality and antisymmetry.

::: {#exr-lg-rotation-uniqueness}
#### Uniqueness of the rotation subgroup

Let $M(t)$ be a differentiable family of $3 \times 3$ matrices with $M(0) = 1$ and $\dot M = L_3M$. Show that
$\frac{d}{dt}(R(t)^{\mathsf{T}}M(t)) = 0$ and conclude that $M(t) = R(t) = e^{tL_3}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By the proposition $\dot R = L_3R$, so $\frac{d}{dt}(R^{\mathsf{T}}M) = (L_3R)^{\mathsf{T}}M + R^{\mathsf{T}}L_3M =
R^{\mathsf{T}}(L_3^{\mathsf{T}} + L_3)M = 0$, since $L_3$ is antisymmetric. Hence $R(t)^{\mathsf{T}}M(t) =
R(0)^{\mathsf{T}}M(0) = 1$, and with $RR^{\mathsf{T}} = 1$ from the proposition, $M(t) = R(t)$. The same argument with
$e^{tL_3}$ in place of $M$ identifies $R(t)$ with the exponential, the step that the proposition does not state.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The identification $R(t) = e^{tL_3}$ is the step of @prp-rotation-subgroup that is not formalised; this exercise
supplies it by hand.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The one-parameter subgroups give every rotation as an exponential, but they do not say which rotation the product of
two rotations about different axes is. Since $SU(2)$ covers $SO(3)$ and its elements are $2 \times 2$ matrices, the
product is computed most easily there, which is also how rotations are composed in numerical work
[@boudreau2018applied, Sec. 14.2.2]; the proposition gives the result in closed form.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-lg-rotation-composition}
#### Composition of rotations

For unit vectors $n_1, n_2 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and angles $t_1, t_2$, write $c_i = \cos\frac{t_i}{2}$ and $s_i =
\sin\frac{t_i}{2}$. The elements $e^{t_in_i \cdot T} = c_i1 - is_i\,n_i \cdot \sigma$ of $SU(2)$ multiply to
$e^{t_1n_1 \cdot T}e^{t_2n_2 \cdot T} = c1 - i\,v \cdot \sigma$ with
$$
c = c_1c_2 - s_1s_2\,n_1 \cdot n_2, \qquad v = s_1c_2\,n_1 + c_1s_2\,n_2 + s_1s_2\,n_1 \times n_2 ,
$$ {#eq-lg-rotation-composition}
and $c^2 + |v|^2 = 1$. Writing $c = \cos\frac t2$ and $v = \sin\frac t2\,n$ with a unit vector $n$, the rotation by
$t_2$ about $n_2$ followed by the rotation by $t_1$ about $n_1$, $e^{t_1n_1 \cdot L}e^{t_2n_2 \cdot L}$, is the rotation
$e^{tn \cdot L}$ by $t$ about $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The formula follows from the product rule $(n_1 \cdot \sigma)(n_2 \cdot \sigma) = n_1 \cdot n_2\,1 + i(n_1 \times n_2) \cdot
\sigma$ of @exr-lg-su2-product-rule, and the last sentence from $\operatorname{Ad}(e^{tn \cdot T}) = e^{tn \cdot L}$
(@exr-lg-ad-exp), since $\operatorname{Ad}$ is a homomorphism. Two quarter turns about perpendicular axes give the
simplest composite that is not about one of the two axes; it is the rotation of @exr-lg-rodrigues that permutes the
coordinate axes.

::: {#exm-lg-comp-quarter-turns}
#### Two quarter turns

For $t_1 = t_2 = \frac\pi2$, $n_1 = e_1$ and $n_2 = e_2$, $c_i = s_i = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so $c = \frac12$ and $v =
\frac12(e_1 + e_2 + e_3)$: the composite is the rotation by $t = \frac{2\pi}{3}$ about $n = (1, 1, 1)/\sqrt3$. Directly,
the quarter turn about $e_2$ followed by the quarter turn about $e_1$ sends $e_1 \to -e_3 \to e_2$, $e_2 \to e_2 \to e_3$
and $e_3 \to e_1 \to e_1$, the cyclic permutation of @exr-lg-rodrigues.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The cross product in @eq-lg-rotation-composition is the only term that changes sign when the two factors are
exchanged. The second example uses it to compare the two orders, and relates the composite axis to the classical
construction on the sphere [@sinha2023rigid, Sec. 1.1.4].

::: {#exm-lg-comp-order}
#### The order matters

Exchanging the factors keeps $c$, hence the angle, and replaces $n_1 \times n_2$ by $n_2 \times n_1$: the axis of
$e^{t_2n_2 \cdot L}e^{t_1n_1 \cdot L}$ is the mirror image of $n$ in the plane of $n_1$ and $n_2$. For the quarter turns
of @exm-lg-comp-quarter-turns the reversed composite is the rotation by $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ about $(1, 1, -1)/\sqrt3$. For
small angles the two vectors $v$ differ by $2s_1s_2\,n_1 \times n_2 \approx \frac12t_1t_2\,n_1 \times n_2$, of second
order: the bracket $[n_1 \cdot L, n_2 \cdot L] = (n_1 \times n_2) \cdot L$ of @exm-lg-so3-cross seen in the group, as in
@exm-lg-so3-small-rotations. On the unit sphere, with $0 < t_1, t_2 < 2\pi$, the axis is the third vertex $C$ of the
spherical triangle with vertices $A = n_1$ and $B = n_2$, angles $\frac{t_1}{2}$ at $A$ and $\frac{t_2}{2}$ at $B$, on the
side of $n_1 \times n_2$; the composite angle is $-2\gamma$, minus twice the angle at $C$ (@exr-lg-comp-hamilton).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Half-turns are the rotations with $c_i = 0$, and for them the formula collapses to a dot and a cross product. The
third example shows that two half-turns make a rotation about their common perpendicular.

::: {#exm-lg-comp-half-turns}
#### Two half-turns

For $t_1 = t_2 = \pi$, $c_i = 0$ and $s_i = 1$, so $c = -n_1 \cdot n_2$ and $v = n_1 \times n_2$. If the axes make an angle
$\alpha \in (0, \pi)$, then $\cos\frac t2 = -\cos\alpha$ and $\sin\frac t2 = \sin\alpha$: the composite is the rotation
by $2\pi - 2\alpha$ about $n_1 \times n_2/\sin\alpha$, that is, by $2\alpha$ about $n_2 \times n_1/\sin\alpha$. In the
plane perpendicular to that axis each half-turn acts as the reflection in a line, and two reflections in lines at an
angle $\alpha$ make a rotation by $2\alpha$. Conversely every rotation by $2\alpha$ is a product of two half-turns about
axes at the angle $\alpha$ perpendicular to its axis, which is the idea of @exr-lg-comp-hamilton.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
