:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A product computed in $SU(2)$ has to be converted back into an axis and an angle. The first exercise does this in two
ways, by traces and by an eigenvector, as a numerical library would [@boudreau2018applied, Sec. 14.2.2].

::: {#exr-lg-comp-axis-angle}
#### Axis and angle of a product

For $g = c1 - i\sin\frac t2\,n \cdot \sigma \in SU(2)$ show that $c = \frac12\operatorname{tr}g$ and $\sin\frac t2\,n_a =
\frac i2\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_ag)$, and that the eigenvalues of $g$ are $e^{\mp it/2}$, with unit eigenvectors
$\xi_\pm$ satisfying $(n \cdot \sigma)\xi_\pm = \pm\xi_\pm$ and $n = \xi_+^\dagger\sigma\xi_+$. Apply both methods with
Sage to the product of @exm-lg-comp-quarter-turns, and check that $\operatorname{Ad}$ of the product is
$e^{\frac\pi2L_1}e^{\frac\pi2L_2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Since $\operatorname{tr}\sigma_a = 0$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_a\sigma_b) = 2\delta_{ab}$, $\operatorname{tr}g = 2c$
and $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_ag) = -2i\sin\frac t2\,n_a$. The matrix $n \cdot \sigma$ is Hermitian and traceless with
square $1$, so its eigenvalues are $\pm1$, and on its eigenvectors $g$ acts as $\cos\frac t2 \mp i\sin\frac t2 =
e^{\mp it/2}$. The projector onto $\xi_+$ is $\xi_+\xi_+^\dagger = \frac12(1 + n \cdot \sigma)$, so $\xi_+^\dagger\sigma_a\xi_+ =
\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_a\xi_+\xi_+^\dagger) = n_a$. For the quarter turns both methods give $t = \frac{2\pi}{3}$ and $n =
(1, 1, 1)/\sqrt3$:

{{< sage exr-lg-comp-axis-angle >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Rotations about three concurrent axes through twice the angles of the spherical triangle they span compose to the
identity. This is Hamilton's theorem [@sinha2023rigid, Sec. 1.1.5], and the half-turns of @exm-lg-comp-half-turns prove
it in one line.

::: {#exr-lg-comp-hamilton}
#### Hamilton's theorem

Let $A, B, C$ be unit vectors with $\det(A, B, C) > 0$, the vertices of a spherical triangle with angles $\alpha, \beta,
\gamma$, let $p, q, r$ be unit normals of the planes of the sides $CA$, $AB$, $BC$, and let $H(u) = e^{\pi u \cdot L}$ be
the half-turn about $u$. Show that $e^{2\alpha A \cdot L} = H(p)H(q)$, $e^{2\beta B \cdot L} = H(q)H(r)$ and $e^{2\gamma C
\cdot L} = H(r)H(p)$, and deduce $e^{2\alpha A \cdot L}e^{2\beta B \cdot L}e^{2\gamma C \cdot L} = 1$. Check the result with
Sage for the octant triangle and for a generic triangle, and show that the reversed order fails.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The normals $p$ and $q$ are perpendicular to $A$, which lies on both sides $CA$ and $AB$, so by
@exm-lg-comp-half-turns $H(p)H(q)$ is a rotation about the line through $A$ by twice the angle between the planes $OCA$
and $OAB$, which is the angle $\alpha$ of the triangle. Whether it turns by $2\alpha$ about $A$ or about $-A$ depends on the
orientation, and for $\det(A, B, C) > 0$ it is $e^{2\alpha A \cdot L}$, as the Sage check confirms; the other two
identities are the same statement for $B$ and $C$. Since $H(u)^2 = 1$, the product is $H(p)H(q)H(q)H(r)H(r)H(p) = 1$. For
the octant triangle $A = e_1$, $B = e_2$, $C = e_3$ all angles are $\frac\pi2$ and the theorem reads
$\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1)\operatorname{diag}(-1, 1, -1)\operatorname{diag}(-1, -1, 1) = 1$:

{{< sage exr-lg-comp-hamilton >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Rotations about parallel axes have no common fixed point, so they compose outside $SO(3)$, in the group of rigid
motions of the plane. The third exercise composes them there and finds a translation where the angles cancel
[@sinha2023rigid, Sec. 1.1.6].

::: {#exr-lg-comp-parallel-axes}
#### Rotations about parallel axes

A rigid motion of the plane is $x \mapsto Rx + b$ with $R \in SO(2)$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}^2$, represented by the
matrix $\begin{pmatrix} R & b \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ acting on $(x, 1)$; these matrices form a matrix Lie group of
dimension $3$, like the affine group of the line in @exm-structure-affine. Write the rotation by $t$ about a point $p$ in
this form. Show that the rotation by $t$ about $p$ followed by the rotation by $-t$ about $q$ is the translation by
$(R(-t) - 1)(p - q)$, of length $2|\sin\frac t2|\,|p - q|$, and that for $t_1 + t_2 \notin 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ the rotation by
$t_1$ about $p$ followed by the rotation by $t_2$ about $q$ is the rotation by $t_1 + t_2$ about a third point.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The rotation by $t$ about $p$ is $x \mapsto R(t)(x - p) + p$, so $R = R(t)$ and $b = (1 - R(t))p$. The composite is $x
\mapsto R(-t)\bigl(R(t)(x - p) + p - q\bigr) + q = x + (R(-t) - 1)(p - q)$, a translation; since $R(-t)$ turns the vector
$p - q$ by $-t$, the chord has length $2|\sin\frac t2|\,|p - q|$. In general the composite is
$x \mapsto R(t_1 + t_2)x + b'$ for some $b'$. If $t_1 + t_2 \notin 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, $1 - R(t_1 + t_2)$ is invertible,
the point $x_0 = (1 - R(t_1 + t_2))^{-1}b'$ is fixed, and the motion is $x \mapsto R(t_1 + t_2)(x - x_0) + x_0$, the rotation by $t_1 + t_2$ about
$x_0$. A rotation about one axis followed by a translation perpendicular to it is therefore a rotation about a parallel
axis, and only the case $t_1 + t_2 \in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ leaves a pure translation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### Maurer-Cartan forms {#sec-maurer-cartan}

A Lie group carries a frame of vector fields and a dual frame of one-forms that are the same at every point as seen
from the group itself: the left-invariant fields and forms. They turn the Lie algebra into geometry on the group and
give the bi-invariant metric of $SU(2)$, and they reappear later in the book as frames on homogeneous spaces. This
section defines them, packages the forms into the Maurer-Cartan form, verifies the Maurer-Cartan equation on
$SU(2)$, and reads the forms of $SO(3)$ as the angular velocity of a rotating body.

#### Left-invariant fields and forms

Multiplication by a fixed element moves every point of the group, and it is a diffeomorphism. These maps are the
group acting on itself, and they allow a vector at the identity to be transported to every other point.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-left-translation}
#### Left translation

For $h \in G$ the **left translation** $L_h : G \to G$, $g \mapsto hg$, is a diffeomorphism of the group
(with inverse $L_{h^{-1}}$); **right translation** is $R_h : g \mapsto gh$. Left translations form a group of
diffeomorphisms isomorphic to $G$, acting freely and transitively on $G$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the circle a left translation is a rotation by a fixed angle. Since the group is abelian, left and right
translations coincide.

::: {#exm-translation-u1}
#### Rotations of the circle

On $U(1)$ the left translation by $e^{i\alpha}$ is the rotation $e^{i\beta} \mapsto e^{i(\alpha + \beta)}$,
$\varphi \mapsto \varphi + \alpha$ in the angle chart; left and right translations coincide because the group is
abelian.
:::

On the affine group left translations combine a dilation and a shift of the coordinates. They are not isometries of the
flat metric of the half-plane.

::: {#exm-translation-affine}
#### The affine group

For the group of maps $x \mapsto ax + b$ with $a > 0$, coordinates $(a, b)$ on the half-plane, left translation by
$(a_0, b_0)$ is $(a, b) \mapsto (a_0a, a_0b + b_0)$ (@fig-affine-group-fields, @exr-affine-left-invariant): a
dilation and a shift, not an isometry of the Euclidean half-plane.
:::

On $SU(2)$, translations by the diagonal subgroup act on the Euler angles in a simple way. Left translations shift
$\varphi$ and right translations shift $\psi$.

::: {#exm-translation-su2}
#### Left and right translations on $SU(2)$

Left and right translations by $e^{tT_3}$ on $SU(2)$ shift the Euler angles $\varphi$ and $\psi$ respectively, as
@eq-euler-angles shows: $e^{tT_3} g(\theta, \varphi, \psi) = g(\theta, \varphi + t, \psi)$ and $g\,e^{tT_3} =
g(\theta, \varphi, \psi + t)$. The right action is the one whose orbits are the Hopf circles (@sec-hopf).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Left and right translations are two commuting actions of the same group on itself. The first exercise checks this and
expresses conjugation through them.

::: {#exr-lg-left-right-commute}
#### Left and right translations commute

Show that $L_h \circ R_k = R_k \circ L_h$ for all $h, k \in G$, that $L_{h_1} \circ L_{h_2} = L_{h_1h_2}$ while $R_{k_1}
\circ R_{k_2} = R_{k_2k_1}$, and that conjugation $C_h(g) = hgh^{-1}$ is $L_h \circ R_{h^{-1}}$. Which of these maps fix
the identity?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$L_h(R_k(g)) = h(gk) = (hg)k = R_k(L_h(g))$ by associativity. $L_{h_1}(L_{h_2}(g)) = h_1h_2g$ and $R_{k_1}(R_{k_2}(g)) =
gk_2k_1$, so the right translations compose in the opposite order: $g \mapsto R_{k^{-1}}$ is the homomorphism that turns
them into a left action. $C_h(g) = hgh^{-1} = L_h(R_{h^{-1}}(g))$. A translation $L_h$ or $R_k$ fixes $e$ only if $h = e$
or $k = e$, while every $C_h$ fixes $e$; its derivative at $e$ is $\operatorname{Ad}_h$ of @def-adjoint.
:::

The shifts of the Euler angles in @exm-translation-su2 can be checked by multiplying matrices. The second exercise does
this and shows that translations by other generators are not shifts of a single angle.

::: {#exr-lg-translation-su2-euler}
#### Translations in Euler angles

With $g(\theta, \varphi, \psi) = e^{\varphi T_3}e^{\theta T_1}e^{\psi T_3}$ verify $e^{tT_3}g(\theta, \varphi, \psi) =
g(\theta, \varphi + t, \psi)$ and $g(\theta, \varphi, \psi)e^{tT_3} = g(\theta, \varphi, \psi + t)$. Does
$e^{tT_1}$ act by shifting $\theta$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both identities follow from $e^{tT_3}e^{\varphi T_3} = e^{(\varphi + t)T_3}$, applied to the left or the right factor.
Left translation by $e^{tT_1}$ shifts $\theta$ only at $\varphi = 0$, where $e^{tT_1}e^{\theta T_1} = e^{(\theta +
t)T_1}$; at other values of $\varphi$ the factor $e^{tT_1}$ must be moved past $e^{\varphi T_3}$, which changes all
three angles:

{{< sage exr-lg-translation-su2-euler >}}
:::

Left translations act on the group freely and transitively. The third exercise proves this and compares it with the
action of conjugations.

::: {#exr-lg-left-translation-free}
#### Translations act simply transitively

Show that for any $g, g' \in G$ there is exactly one $h$ with $L_hg = g'$, so that the action of $G$ on itself by left
translations is free and transitive. Show that conjugation is neither, unless $G$ is trivial, and describe the orbits
of conjugation in $SO(3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$hg = g'$ has the unique solution $h = g'g^{-1}$: existence is transitivity, uniqueness is freeness (the isotropy group
of every point is $\{e\}$). Conjugation fixes $e$, so it is not free unless $G = \{e\}$, and the orbit of $e$ is $\{e\}$,
so it is not transitive. In $SO(3)$ the conjugate $hR_n(\alpha)h^{-1}$ of the rotation by $\alpha$ about $n$ is the
rotation by $\alpha$ about $hn$, so the conjugation orbits are the sets of rotations with a fixed angle $\alpha \in [0,
\pi]$: two-spheres of axes, collapsed to a point at $\alpha = 0$ and to $\mathbb{RP}^2$ at $\alpha = \pi$.
:::
::::

A vector at the identity can be transported to every point by left translations. Fields obtained this way are the
left-invariant vector fields.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-left-invariant-field}
#### Left-invariant vector field

A vector field $X$ on $G$ is **left-invariant** if it is unchanged by every left translation, $dL_h(X_g) =
X_{hg}$. A left-invariant field is determined by its value $X_e \in T_eG = \mathfrak{g}$ at the identity, $X_g =
dL_g(X_e)$, so the left-invariant fields form a vector space isomorphic to $\mathfrak{g}$; their Lie brackets are
left-invariant, and the bracket of left-invariant fields agrees with the Lie algebra bracket of their values at
$e$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the affine group the left-invariant fields can be written down in the coordinates $(a, b)$. Their bracket reproduces
the structure constant of the affine algebra.

::: {#exm-invariant-field-affine}
#### The affine group

$X = a\,\partial_a$ and $Y = a\,\partial_b$ are left-invariant on the affine group: the Jacobian of $(a, b) \mapsto
(a_0a, a_0b + b_0)$ is $\operatorname{diag}(a_0, a_0)$, which sends $(a, 0)$ at $(a, b)$ to $(a_0a, 0)$, the value of
$X$ at the image point, and likewise for $Y$ (@fig-affine-group-fields). Their bracket is $[X, Y] = Y$, the
structure of @exm-structure-affine.
:::

On the circle left-invariance means constant coefficients in the angle coordinate. The left-invariant fields are then
also the Killing fields of the round metric.

::: {#exm-invariant-field-u1}
#### $\partial_\varphi$ on the circle

$\partial_\varphi$ is left-invariant on $U(1)$, since rotations shift $\varphi$ by a constant; every
left-invariant field on the circle is $c\,\partial_\varphi$, a one-dimensional space, as $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ is.
These are also the Killing fields, since the metric $d\varphi^2$ is invariant.
:::

On $SU(2)$ the left-invariant fields are generated by right multiplication with the basis of the Lie algebra. They form
a global frame of the three-sphere.

::: {#exm-invariant-field-su2}
#### Left-invariant fields on $SU(2)$

The three fields $\xi_a$ with $\xi_a(g) = gT_a$ (the velocity at $g$ of $t \mapsto g\,e^{tT_a}$) are left-invariant,
with brackets $[\xi_a, \xi_b] = \epsilon_{abc}\xi_c$; they are the dual frame of the forms @eq-su2-forms, and a
nowhere-vanishing frame of $S^3$ (@exm-frame-group). They generate right translations, so they are Killing fields of
the bi-invariant metric.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The figure draws the two left-invariant fields of the affine group on the half-plane. Both grow linearly with the
coordinate $a$, the factor that compensates the dilations of left translation.

![Left-invariant vector fields on the affine group of the line, coordinates $(a, b)$ on the half-plane $a > 0$:
$X = a\,\partial_a$ (blue) and $Y = a\,\partial_b$ (red) are the fields through the identity $(1, 0)$ transported
by left translations, and SageManifolds computes $[X, Y] = Y$. Generated by
`figures/affine_group_fields.sage`.](figures/affine_group_fields.svg){#fig-affine-group-fields width=55%}

For a matrix group the left-invariant field with value $A$ at the identity is $g \mapsto gA$. The first exercise
computes these fields for the Heisenberg group and their brackets.

::: {#exr-lg-heisenberg-fields}
#### Left-invariant fields on the Heisenberg group

For $g = h(x, y, z)$ of @exr-lg-heisenberg-group compute the velocities of $t \mapsto ge^{tA}$ for $A = E_{12}, E_{23},
E_{13}$ in the coordinates $(x, y, z)$, check that the resulting fields $X$, $Y$, $Z$ are invariant under left
translations, and compute their brackets.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$gE_{12}$ has a single entry $1$ in the $x$ slot, $gE_{23}$ has entries $1$ in the $y$ slot and $x$ in the $z$ slot, and
$gE_{13}$ has $1$ in the $z$ slot: $X = \partial_x$, $Y = \partial_y + x\,\partial_z$, $Z = \partial_z$. Left translation
by $h(a, b, c)$ is $(x, y, z) \mapsto (x + a, y + b, z + c + ay)$, whose Jacobian maps each field at $g$ to the same field
at $hg$. The only non-zero bracket is $[X, Y] = [\partial_x, \partial_y + x\,\partial_z] = \partial_z = Z$, matching
$[E_{12}, E_{23}] = E_{13}$ as @def-left-invariant-field requires:

{{< sage exr-lg-heisenberg-fields >}}
:::

The flow of a left-invariant field is a family of right translations. The second exercise proves this and checks it on
the affine group.

::: {#exr-lg-invariant-field-flow}
#### Flows of left-invariant fields

Let $\xi$ be the left-invariant field of a matrix group with $\xi(g) = gA$. Show that its flow (@def-flow) is
$\Phi_t(g) = ge^{tA}$, that $\Phi_t$ commutes with every left translation, and compute the flow of $X = a\,\partial_a$
and $Y = a\,\partial_b$ on the affine group.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{d}{dt}(ge^{tA}) = ge^{tA}A = \xi(ge^{tA})$ with initial value $g$, so $t \mapsto ge^{tA}$ is the integral curve
through $g$, and $\Phi_t = R_{e^{tA}}$. It commutes with left translations by @exr-lg-left-right-commute, as it must,
since the field is left-invariant. On the affine group $g = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $ge^{tX} =
\begin{pmatrix} ae^t & b \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $ge^{tY} = \begin{pmatrix} a & b + ta \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$: the
flow of $a\,\partial_a$ is $(a, b) \mapsto (ae^t, b)$ and that of $a\,\partial_b$ is $(a, b) \mapsto (a, b + ta)$, as
solving $\dot a = a$ and $\dot b = a$ confirms.
:::

The affine group was described abstractly in the examples. The third exercise represents it by matrices and recovers its
Lie algebra, bracket and one-parameter subgroups from them.

::: {#exr-affine-left-invariant}
#### The affine group as matrices

Represent the maps $x \mapsto ax + b$ by the matrices $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, compute the
product, the Lie algebra, the bracket $[X, Y]$ and the exponentials $e^{tX}$, $e^{tY}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-affine-left-invariant >}}

The left-invariant fields $a\,\partial_a$ and $a\,\partial_b$ are the images of $X$ and $Y$ under $dL_g$ with
$g = (a, b)$, and $[a\,\partial_a, a\,\partial_b] = a\,\partial_b$ reproduces $[X, Y] = Y$
(`figures/affine_group_fields.sage`).
:::
::::

The forms dual to the left-invariant fields are invariant under left translations as well. The definition states this
duality and the resulting basis of one-forms.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-left-invariant-form}
#### Left-invariant one-form

A one-form $\sigma$ on $G$ is **left-invariant** if $L_h^*\sigma = \sigma$ for every $h$ (@def-pullback). The
left-invariant one-forms are the duals of the left-invariant fields: for a basis $T_A$ of $\mathfrak{g}$ with
left-invariant fields $\xi_A$, the left-invariant forms $\sigma^A$ with $\sigma^A(\xi_B) = \delta^A_B$ form a
basis, and $\sigma^A$ is determined by its value $T^A \in \mathfrak{g}^*$ at the identity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the circle the left-invariant form is the differential of the angle. It is the component of the Maurer-Cartan form
of the circle group.

::: {#exm-invariant-form-u1}
#### $d\varphi$ on the circle

$d\varphi$ is left-invariant on $U(1)$, dual to $\partial_\varphi$; it is the Maurer-Cartan form $g^{-1}dg$ of
@def-maurer-cartan-form for $g = e^{i\varphi}$, since $e^{-i\varphi}\,d(e^{i\varphi}) = i\,d\varphi$.
:::

On the affine group the left-invariant forms have the coordinate $a$ in the denominator, to compensate the dilation of
left translations. Their exterior derivatives are an example of the Maurer-Cartan equation.

::: {#exm-invariant-form-affine}
#### The affine group

$\sigma^X = da/a$ and $\sigma^Y = db/a$ are left-invariant on the affine group, dual to $X = a\,\partial_a$ and
$Y = a\,\partial_b$: under $(a, b) \mapsto (a_0a, a_0b + b_0)$, $da/a \mapsto a_0\,da/(a_0a) = da/a$ and $db/a \mapsto
a_0\,db/(a_0a) = db/a$. Their exterior derivatives are $d\sigma^X = 0$ and $d\sigma^Y = -da \wedge db/a^2 =
-\sigma^X \wedge \sigma^Y$, the Maurer-Cartan equation for $[X, Y] = Y$.
:::

For $SU(2)$ in Euler angles the left-invariant forms are trigonometric combinations of the coordinate differentials.
They build the bi-invariant metric and the connection of the Hopf fibration.

::: {#exm-invariant-form-su2}
#### The left-invariant forms of $SU(2)$

In Euler angles the left-invariant forms are
$$
\sigma^1 = \cos\psi\, d\theta + \sin\theta\sin\psi\, d\varphi, \qquad
\sigma^2 = -\sin\psi\, d\theta + \sin\theta\cos\psi\, d\varphi, \qquad
\sigma^3 = d\psi + \cos\theta\, d\varphi
$$ {#eq-su2-forms}
(@exr-su2-forms-metric, @prp-su2-forms), and $\tfrac14\sum_a \sigma^a\sigma^a$ is the bi-invariant metric
@eq-su2-metric: the invariant inner product $-\kappa/2 = \delta_{ab}$ on the Lie algebra (@exm-killing-so3),
transported over the group by left translations. The first two forms are, up to the rotation by $\psi$, the round
metric's $d\theta$ and $\sin\theta\,d\varphi$ of the sphere; the third, $d\psi + \cos\theta\,d\varphi$, is the
connection of the Hopf fibration (@sec-hopf).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The left-invariant forms of the Heisenberg group are as simple as its fields. The first exercise computes them from
$g^{-1}dg$ and checks their invariance and their exterior derivatives.

::: {#exr-lg-invariant-form-heisenberg}
#### Left-invariant forms on the Heisenberg group

Compute $g^{-1}\partial_xg$, $g^{-1}\partial_yg$, $g^{-1}\partial_zg$ for $g = h(x, y, z)$ and read off forms
$\sigma^X$, $\sigma^Y$, $\sigma^Z$ along $E_{12}$, $E_{23}$, $E_{13}$. Check that they are invariant under left
translations, dual to the fields of @exr-lg-heisenberg-fields, and that $d\sigma^Z = -\sigma^X \wedge \sigma^Y$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g^{-1}dg = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & dx & dz - x\,dy \\ 0 & 0 & dy \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, so $\sigma^X = dx$, $\sigma^Y =
dy$, $\sigma^Z = dz - x\,dy$. Under $(x, y, z) \mapsto (x + a, y + b, z + c + ay)$, $dz - x\,dy \mapsto dz + a\,dy - (x + a)
dy = dz - x\,dy$. The pairings with $\partial_x$, $\partial_y + x\,\partial_z$, $\partial_z$ give the identity matrix,
and $d\sigma^Z = -dx \wedge dy = -\sigma^X \wedge \sigma^Y$, the Maurer-Cartan equation for $[X, Y] = Z$:

{{< sage exr-lg-invariant-form-heisenberg >}}
:::

A left-invariant form and a left-invariant field pair to a function that is the same at every point. The second
exercise proves this and uses it to test candidate forms.

::: {#exr-lg-invariant-form-pairing}
#### Pairings are constant

Show that $\sigma(\xi)$ is a constant function on $G$ whenever $\sigma$ is a left-invariant one-form and $\xi$ a
left-invariant vector field. Use this to decide which of $da/a$, $da$, $db/a$, $db/a^2$ are left-invariant on the affine
group.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sigma_{hg}(\xi_{hg}) = \sigma_{hg}(dL_h\xi_g) = (L_h^*\sigma)_g(\xi_g) = \sigma_g(\xi_g)$, and since left translations
act transitively the function is constant. A left-invariant form must therefore pair to constants with $X =
a\,\partial_a$ and $Y = a\,\partial_b$. $da/a$ gives $(1, 0)$ and $db/a$ gives $(0, 1)$, constants; $da$ gives $(a,
0)$ and $db/a^2$ gives $(0, 1/a)$, not constant, so these two are not left-invariant. Since the left-invariant forms
are the constant combinations of $\sigma^X$ and $\sigma^Y$, the test is also sufficient here.
:::

Wedging all the left-invariant one-forms gives a left-invariant volume form, a Haar measure. The third exercise
computes it for $SU(2)$ and the affine group and integrates it over $SU(2)$.

::: {#exr-lg-haar-measure}
#### Invariant volume forms

Compute $\sigma^1 \wedge \sigma^2 \wedge \sigma^3$ for the forms @eq-su2-forms and its integral over $0 < \theta < \pi$,
$0 < \varphi < 2\pi$, $0 < \psi < 4\pi$. Compare with the volume of the metric $\tfrac14\sum_a\sigma^a\sigma^a$ and with
the volume $2\pi^2$ of the unit three-sphere. Compute also $\sigma^X \wedge \sigma^Y$ on the affine group and check its
invariance.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sigma^1 \wedge \sigma^2 = (\cos^2\psi + \sin^2\psi)\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi = \sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge
d\varphi$, and wedging with $\sigma^3 = d\psi + \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ keeps only $d\psi$: $\sigma^1 \wedge \sigma^2 \wedge
\sigma^3 = \sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi \wedge d\psi$, with integral $2 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 4\pi = 16\pi^2$. The
metric $\tfrac14\sum\sigma^a\sigma^a$ has the orthonormal coframe $\tfrac12\sigma^a$ and hence the volume form
$\tfrac18\sigma^1 \wedge \sigma^2 \wedge \sigma^3$, with volume $2\pi^2$, that of the unit $S^3$, as it must be since the
metric is the round one. On the affine group $\sigma^X \wedge \sigma^Y = da \wedge db/a^2$, invariant by
@exm-invariant-form-affine:

{{< sage exr-lg-haar-measure >}}
:::
::::

#### The Maurer-Cartan form and equation

The left-invariant one-forms can be packaged into a single form with values in the Lie algebra. For a matrix group
this form has a compact expression, $g^{-1}dg$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-maurer-cartan-form}
#### Maurer-Cartan form

The **Maurer-Cartan form** of a matrix Lie group is the $\mathfrak{g}$-valued one-form $g^{-1}dg$: at $g$ it sends
a tangent vector $\dot g$ to $g^{-1}\dot g \in \mathfrak{g}$. It is left-invariant, since $(hg)^{-1}d(hg) =
g^{-1}dg$, and its components in a basis, $g^{-1}dg = \sigma^A T_A$, are the left-invariant one-forms of
@def-left-invariant-form; for a basis normalised by $\operatorname{tr}(T_AT_B) = -\tfrac12\delta_{AB}$ they are read
off as $\sigma^A = -2\operatorname{tr}(T_A\,g^{-1}dg)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the circle the Maurer-Cartan form has a single component. It is the differential of the angle, times the generator
$i$.

::: {#exm-mc-form-u1}
#### The circle

For $g = e^{i\varphi}$, $g^{-1}dg = i\,d\varphi$: the single component $\sigma = d\varphi$ along the generator $i$
of $\mathfrak{u}(1)$, with $d\sigma = 0$ as the abelian Maurer-Cartan equation requires.
:::

For the affine group the Maurer-Cartan form is a $2 \times 2$ matrix of one-forms. Its entries are the left-invariant
forms found earlier.

::: {#exm-mc-form-affine}
#### The affine group

For $g = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $g^{-1}dg = \begin{pmatrix} da/a & db/a \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
= \sigma^X X + \sigma^Y Y$ with $X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $Y = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}$: the forms of @exm-invariant-form-affine (@exr-affine-left-invariant).
:::

For $SU(2)$ the Maurer-Cartan form is computed from the Euler-angle matrix by projecting on the generators. The result
is the list of left-invariant forms @eq-su2-forms.

::: {#exm-mc-form-su2}
#### $SU(2)$ in Euler angles

With $g$ from @eq-euler-matrix and $g^{-1} = g^\dagger$, the components $\sigma^a = -2\operatorname{tr}(T_a\,
g^{-1}dg)$ are @eq-su2-forms; the computation in @exr-su2-forms-metric takes the three partial derivatives
$\partial_\theta g$, $\partial_\varphi g$, $\partial_\psi g$ and projects each on the basis $T_a$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The double cover relates the Maurer-Cartan forms of $SU(2)$ and $SO(3)$. The first exercise computes the form of $SO(3)$
in Euler angles and finds the same components.

::: {#exr-lg-mc-form-so3}
#### The Maurer-Cartan form of $SO(3)$

For $R = e^{\varphi L_3}e^{\theta L_1}e^{\psi L_3}$ compute $\sigma^a = -\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(L_aR^{-1}dR)$ and
compare with @eq-su2-forms. Explain the factor $-\tfrac12$ and why the components agree with those of $SU(2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{tr}(L_aL_b) = -2\delta_{ab}$ (@prp-so3-killing-form), so the component of $X = x_bL_b$ along $L_a$ is
$-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(L_aX)$, the analogue of $-2\operatorname{tr}(T_aX)$ for the normalisation $-\tfrac12\delta$.
The result is exactly @eq-su2-forms. The reason is that $\operatorname{Ad} : SU(2) \to SO(3)$ is a homomorphism with
derivative $T_a \mapsto L_a$ that maps the Euler-angle element $g$ to $R$ (@exr-lg-int-su2-so3): it maps $g^{-1}dg =
\sigma^aT_a$ to $R^{-1}dR = \sigma^aL_a$ with the same components.

{{< sage exr-lg-mc-form-so3 >}}
:::

Multiplying by the differential on the other side gives a right-invariant form. The second exercise relates the two
forms through the adjoint representation.

::: {#exr-lg-mc-right}
#### The right-invariant Maurer-Cartan form

Show that $\theta^R = dg\,g^{-1}$ is invariant under right translations, that $\theta^R = \operatorname{Ad}_g(g^{-1}dg)$,
and compute it for the affine group. Do the two forms coincide for $U(1)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$d(gk)(gk)^{-1} = dg\,kk^{-1}g^{-1} = dg\,g^{-1}$ for constant $k$, and $dg\,g^{-1} = g(g^{-1}dg)g^{-1}$. For the affine
group $dg\,g^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} da & db \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1/a & -b/a \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} =
\begin{pmatrix} da/a & db - b\,da/a \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, so the right-invariant forms are $da/a$ and $db - b\,da/a$,
different from the left-invariant $db/a$. For an abelian group $\operatorname{Ad}_g = 1$ and the two forms agree:
$e^{-i\varphi}d(e^{i\varphi}) = d(e^{i\varphi})e^{-i\varphi} = i\,d\varphi$.
:::

The Maurer-Cartan form of a product of two group-valued functions has a simple expression. The third exercise derives
it and recognises the transformation law of a gauge field.

::: {#exr-lg-mc-product}
#### The Maurer-Cartan form of a product

For matrix-valued functions $h$ and $k$ on a manifold, with values in $G$, show that $(hk)^{-1}d(hk) =
k^{-1}(h^{-1}dh)k + k^{-1}dk$. Use it to explain why $\sigma^3$ of @eq-su2-forms contains $d\psi$ with coefficient one
and $d\varphi$ with coefficient $\cos\theta$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$d(hk) = dh\,k + h\,dk$, so $(hk)^{-1}d(hk) = k^{-1}h^{-1}dh\,k + k^{-1}dk$. Writing $A = h^{-1}dh$, this is $A \mapsto
k^{-1}Ak + k^{-1}dk$, the gauge transformation of a connection (@sec-connections). For $g = e^{\varphi T_3}e^{\theta
T_1}e^{\psi T_3}$, take $h = e^{\varphi T_3}e^{\theta T_1}$ and $k = e^{\psi T_3}$: $k^{-1}dk = d\psi\,T_3$ contributes
$d\psi$ to $\sigma^3$, and $h^{-1}dh = d\varphi\,e^{-\theta T_1}T_3e^{\theta T_1} + d\theta\,T_1$ contributes, after
conjugation by $k$, the component $\cos\theta\,d\varphi$ along $T_3$, since $\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{-\theta T_1}}$ rotates
$T_3$ by $-\theta$ about the first axis and $\operatorname{Ad}_{k^{-1}}$ does not change the $T_3$ component.
:::
::::

The exterior derivative of the Maurer-Cartan form is again expressed through the form itself. The theorem gives this
equation, whose coefficients are the structure constants.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-maurer-cartan}
#### Maurer-Cartan equation

Differentiating $g^{-1}dg$ with $d(g^{-1}) = -g^{-1}\,dg\,g^{-1}$ gives $d(g^{-1}dg) = -g^{-1}dg \wedge g^{-1}dg$, that
is, in components,
$$
d\sigma^C = -\tfrac12 f_{AB}{}^C\, \sigma^A \wedge \sigma^B ,
$$ {#eq-maurer-cartan}
with $d$ and $\wedge$ the exterior derivative and wedge product of @sec-forms. *Proved in the text by the
computation above; verified on $SU(2)$ in* @prp-su2-forms.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For $SU(2)$ the equation relates each form to the wedge of the other two. The third form gives the simplest check.

::: {#exm-mc-equation-su2}
#### $SU(2)$

For $f_{ab}{}^c = \epsilon_{abc}$ the equation reads $d\sigma^1 = -\sigma^2 \wedge \sigma^3$, $d\sigma^2 = -\sigma^3
\wedge \sigma^1$, $d\sigma^3 = -\sigma^1 \wedge \sigma^2$; for @eq-su2-forms, $d\sigma^3 = d(\cos\theta\,d\varphi) =
-\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$ and $\sigma^1 \wedge \sigma^2 = \sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$
(@exr-maurer-cartan-check, @prp-su2-forms).
:::

For abelian groups every structure constant is zero and the right side vanishes. The left-invariant forms are then
closed, and locally they are differentials of coordinates.

::: {#exm-mc-equation-abelian}
#### Abelian groups

For the torus $T^2$ with $\sigma^1 = da$, $\sigma^2 = db$ all structure constants vanish and the equation says
$d(da) = d(db) = 0$: the left-invariant forms of an abelian group are closed, and locally exact.
:::

Read as a connection, the Maurer-Cartan form has zero curvature. This is the meaning of the equation in gauge theory.

::: {#exm-mc-equation-curvature}
#### A flat connection

Read as a connection one-form (@sec-connections), $A = g^{-1}dg$ has curvature $F = dA + A \wedge A = 0$ by the
Maurer-Cartan equation: the Maurer-Cartan form is the prototype of a **pure gauge** field, and the Yang-Mills
field strength of Part II measures the failure of a gauge field to be of this form.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The theorem has a short proof in matrix notation. The first exercise fills in the step from the matrix equation to the
component form.

::: {#exr-lg-mc-derivation}
#### From matrices to components

Show that $d(g^{-1}) = -g^{-1}dg\,g^{-1}$, that $d(g^{-1}dg) = -g^{-1}dg \wedge g^{-1}dg$, and that with $g^{-1}dg =
\sigma^AT_A$ the right side is $-\tfrac12f_{AB}{}^C\sigma^A \wedge \sigma^BT_C$, giving @eq-maurer-cartan.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Differentiating $g^{-1}g = 1$ gives $d(g^{-1})g + g^{-1}dg = 0$. Then $d(g^{-1}dg) = d(g^{-1}) \wedge dg = -g^{-1}dg\,g^{-1}
\wedge dg = -g^{-1}dg \wedge g^{-1}dg$, since $d(dg) = 0$. With $\theta = \sigma^AT_A$, $\theta \wedge \theta =
\sigma^A \wedge \sigma^B\,T_AT_B$; exchanging the summation labels and using $\sigma^B \wedge \sigma^A = -\sigma^A \wedge
\sigma^B$ gives $\tfrac12\sigma^A \wedge \sigma^B[T_A, T_B] = \tfrac12f_{AB}{}^C\sigma^A \wedge \sigma^BT_C$. Comparing
the coefficients of $T_C$ on both sides gives $d\sigma^C = -\tfrac12f_{AB}{}^C\sigma^A \wedge \sigma^B$.
:::

The affine group is small enough to check the theorem in both forms by hand. The second exercise compares the matrix
equation with the component equation.

::: {#exr-lg-mc-affine}
#### The Maurer-Cartan equation of the affine group

With $\theta = g^{-1}dg = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma^X & \sigma^Y \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ compute $d\theta$ and $\theta
\wedge \theta$ entry by entry, and check that $d\theta = -\theta \wedge \theta$ is the component equation with
$f_{XY}{}^Y = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$d\theta$ has entries $d\sigma^X = d(da/a) = 0$ and $d\sigma^Y = d(db/a) = -\tfrac{1}{a^2}da \wedge db$. The matrix
product $\theta \wedge \theta$ has upper left entry $\sigma^X \wedge \sigma^X = 0$ and upper right entry $\sigma^X \wedge
\sigma^Y + \sigma^Y \wedge 0 = \sigma^X \wedge \sigma^Y = \tfrac{1}{a^2}da \wedge db$, so $d\theta = -\theta \wedge
\theta$ holds entrywise. In components, $d\sigma^Y = -\tfrac12(f_{XY}{}^Y\sigma^X \wedge \sigma^Y + f_{YX}{}^Y\sigma^Y
\wedge \sigma^X) = -\sigma^X \wedge \sigma^Y$ and $d\sigma^X = 0$ because no structure constant has upper index $X$, in
agreement with @exm-invariant-form-affine.
:::

Applying the exterior derivative once more gives an identity for the structure constants. The third exercise shows that
this identity is the Jacobi identity.

::: {#exr-lg-mc-jacobi}
#### $d^2 = 0$ implies Jacobi

Apply $d$ to @eq-maurer-cartan, use the equation again for $d\sigma^A$, and show that $d^2\sigma^C = 0$ is equivalent to
$f_{[AB}{}^Df_{E]D}{}^C = 0$, the Jacobi identity of @def-structure-constants.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$0 = d^2\sigma^C = -\tfrac12f_{AB}{}^C(d\sigma^A \wedge \sigma^B - \sigma^A \wedge d\sigma^B) = -f_{AB}{}^C\,d\sigma^A
\wedge \sigma^B$, using the antisymmetry of $f$ in $A, B$. Substituting $d\sigma^A = -\tfrac12f_{DE}{}^A\sigma^D \wedge
\sigma^E$ gives $\tfrac12f_{DE}{}^Af_{AB}{}^C\sigma^D \wedge \sigma^E \wedge \sigma^B = 0$. The three-forms $\sigma^D
\wedge \sigma^E \wedge \sigma^B$ are antisymmetric in $D, E, B$, so the condition is that the totally antisymmetrised
coefficient vanishes, $f_{DE}{}^Af_{AB}{}^C + f_{EB}{}^Af_{AD}{}^C + f_{BD}{}^Af_{AE}{}^C = 0$: the Jacobi identity. So
the Maurer-Cartan equation can only hold for structure constants of a Lie algebra.
:::
::::

The left-invariant forms of $SU(2)$ have been computed in several ways in this section. The proposition collects the
results: the explicit forms, the Maurer-Cartan equation they satisfy, and the metric they define.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-su2-forms}
#### The left-invariant forms of $SU(2)$ and the Maurer-Cartan equation

The forms $\sigma^a = -2\operatorname{tr}(T_a g^{-1}dg)$ of the Euler-angle matrix are @eq-su2-forms, they satisfy
$d\sigma^c = -\tfrac12\epsilon_{abc}\sigma^a \wedge \sigma^b$, and $\tfrac14\sum_a\sigma^a \otimes \sigma^a$ is the
metric @eq-su2-metric.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The identification of the metric with the Euler-angle Gram matrix is the theorem `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.su2_gram` of
@prp-su2-metric.

**Sage.** Computed symbolically (@exr-su2-forms-metric, @exr-maurer-cartan-check, with SageManifolds'
`exterior_derivative` and `wedge`).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Squaring and adding the forms gives the metric in Euler angles explicitly. The cross term between $d\varphi$ and $d\psi$
comes from $\sigma^3$ alone.

::: {#exm-lg-su2-metric-expansion}
#### The metric in Euler angles

$(\sigma^1)^2 + (\sigma^2)^2 = d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$, since the $\psi$-dependence cancels as
$\cos^2\psi + \sin^2\psi = 1$, and $(\sigma^3)^2 = d\psi^2 + 2\cos\theta\,d\varphi\,d\psi + \cos^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$.
Adding, $\tfrac14\sum_a(\sigma^a)^2 = \tfrac14(d\theta^2 + d\varphi^2 + d\psi^2 + 2\cos\theta\,d\varphi\,d\psi)$, the
metric @eq-su2-metric of the unit three-sphere.
:::

The equation for $\sigma^3$ has a geometric meaning on the two-sphere. Its right side is, up to sign, the area form of
the unit sphere.

::: {#exm-lg-su2-hopf-curvature}
#### The curvature of the Hopf connection

$d\sigma^3 = -\sigma^1 \wedge \sigma^2 = -\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$ depends only on the coordinates
$(\theta, \varphi)$ of the base $S^2$ of the Hopf fibration, and it is minus the area form of the unit sphere, with
integral $-4\pi$. The form $\sigma^3 = d\psi + \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ is the connection of the fibration, and its
curvature is the field of a magnetic monopole at the centre of the sphere.
:::

The vector fields dual to the forms of the proposition are the left-invariant fields of @exm-invariant-field-su2. One
of them can be read off without computation.

::: {#exm-lg-su2-dual-fields}
#### The dual frame

Since $\sigma^1(\partial_\psi) = \sigma^2(\partial_\psi) = 0$ and $\sigma^3(\partial_\psi) = 1$, the dual field $\xi_3$
is $\partial_\psi$, the generator of right translations by $e^{tT_3}$ (@exm-translation-su2). Inverting the matrix of
components gives the other two, $\xi_1 = \cos\psi\,\partial_\theta + \frac{\sin\psi}{\sin\theta}(\partial_\varphi -
\cos\theta\,\partial_\psi)$ and $\xi_2 = -\sin\psi\,\partial_\theta + \frac{\cos\psi}{\sin\theta}(\partial_\varphi -
\cos\theta\,\partial_\psi)$ (@exr-lg-su2-dual-frame).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the forms of the proposition from the Euler-angle matrix by projecting on the generators. It
then checks the bi-invariant metric they define.

::: {#exr-su2-forms-metric}
#### The left-invariant forms and the metric

Compute $\sigma^a = -2\operatorname{tr}(T_a g^{-1} dg)$ for the Euler-angle matrix and verify that
$\tfrac14\sum_a \sigma^a \otimes \sigma^a$ is the metric @eq-su2-metric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each $\sigma^a = \sigma^a_\theta d\theta + \sigma^a_\varphi d\varphi + \sigma^a_\psi d\psi$ has components
$-2\operatorname{tr}(T_a g^\dagger \partial_i g)$. The result is @eq-su2-forms, and the Gram-like sum
$\tfrac14\sum_a \sigma^a_i \sigma^a_j$ reproduces the matrix @eq-su2-metric. In Sage:

{{< sage exr-su2-forms-metric >}}
:::

The second exercise checks the Maurer-Cartan equation of the proposition with SageManifolds. The exterior derivatives
and wedge products are computed in the Euler-angle chart.

::: {#exr-maurer-cartan-check}
#### The Maurer-Cartan equation on $SU(2)$

Define the three forms @eq-su2-forms as SageManifolds one-forms and check $d\sigma^c = -\tfrac12\epsilon_{abc}
\sigma^a \wedge \sigma^b$ for $c = 1, 2, 3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-maurer-cartan-check >}}
:::

The left-invariant fields satisfy the bracket relations of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, with the sign opposite to that of the
forms' equation. The third exercise computes them from the forms and checks the brackets.

::: {#exr-lg-su2-dual-frame}
#### The left-invariant frame of $SU(2)$

Invert the matrix of components of the forms @eq-su2-forms to obtain the dual fields $\xi_a$, and check with
SageManifolds that $[\xi_a, \xi_b] = \epsilon_{abc}\xi_c$. Derive this sign from $d\sigma(\xi, \eta) =
\xi(\sigma(\eta)) - \eta(\sigma(\xi)) - \sigma([\xi, \eta])$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The pairings $\sigma^c(\xi_b) = \delta^c_b$ are constant, so the formula gives $d\sigma^c(\xi_a, \xi_b) = -
\sigma^c([\xi_a, \xi_b])$. By the proposition $d\sigma^c(\xi_a, \xi_b) = -\tfrac12\epsilon_{dec}(\sigma^d \wedge
\sigma^e)(\xi_a, \xi_b) = -\epsilon_{abc}$, so $\sigma^c([\xi_a, \xi_b]) = \epsilon_{abc}$ and $[\xi_a, \xi_b] =
\epsilon_{abc}\xi_c$, the brackets of the $T_a$, as @def-left-invariant-field requires:

{{< sage exr-lg-su2-dual-frame >}}
:::
::::

#### Angular velocity

The left-invariant forms of $SO(3)$ have a mechanical meaning. If $R(t)$ is the orientation of a rigid body turning
about a fixed point, the Maurer-Cartan form evaluated on $\dot R$ is the angular velocity seen from the body, and the
right-invariant form gives the angular velocity seen from space. This unit defines the two angular velocities and
expresses them in Euler angles, which recovers the kinematic equations of rigid-body dynamics [@sinha2023rigid, Secs.
1.1.28-1.1.31].

A body turning about a fixed point $O$ is described by the rotation $R(t)$ that carries it from its position at time
$0$ to its position at time $t$: a point of the body that starts at $x_0$ is at $x(t) = R(t)x_0$. The definition
extracts a vector from the derivative of $R$, in two ways.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-lg-angular-velocity}
#### Angular velocity

Let $R(t)$ be a differentiable curve in $SO(3)$. Its **angular velocity in space** $\Omega(t)$ and its **angular
velocity in the body** $\omega(t)$ are the vectors of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with
$$
\dot R R^{-1} = \Omega \cdot L, \qquad R^{-1}\dot R = \omega \cdot L ,
$$ {#eq-lg-angular-velocity}
where $\Omega \cdot L = \Omega_aL_a$; both matrices lie in $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ (@exr-lg-angvel-antisymmetric). In terms of
@def-maurer-cartan-form, $\omega$ is the Maurer-Cartan form $R^{-1}dR$ and $\Omega$ the right-invariant form $dR\,R^{-1}$
(@exr-lg-mc-right) evaluated on the velocity $\dot R$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A rotation about a fixed axis at a variable rate is the case met in elementary mechanics. Both angular velocities then
point along the axis, and the velocity of a point is the familiar cross product.

::: {#exm-lg-angvel-fixed-axis}
#### Rotation about a fixed axis

For $R(t) = e^{f(t)n \cdot L}$ with a fixed unit vector $n$, $\dot R = \dot f\,(n \cdot L)R$ and $n \cdot L$ commutes with
$R$, so $\Omega = \omega = \dot f\,n$. A point $x(t) = R(t)x_0$ moves with $\dot x = \dot f\,(n \cdot L)x = \dot f\,n
\times x$ (@exm-lg-so3-cross), the velocity $\Omega \times x$ of a rigid rotation with angular speed $\dot f$; the case
$f(t) = t$, $n = e_3$ is @exm-lg-rotation-ode.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In general the two angular velocities differ, because they are one infinitesimal rotation written in the axes fixed in
space and in the axes carried by the body. The adjoint representation converts one into the other.

::: {#exm-lg-angvel-space-body}
#### Space and body components

$\dot RR^{-1} = R(R^{-1}\dot R)R^{-1} = R(\omega \cdot L)R^{-1} = (R\omega) \cdot L$, because a rotation preserves cross
products: $R(\omega \times R^{-1}y) = R\omega \times y$. So $\Omega = R\omega$, the adjoint action of @exm-adjoint-so3: the
components of $\Omega$ along the fixed axes $e_a$ are the components of $\omega$ along the body axes $Re_a$, which is why
$\omega$ is the angular velocity "in the body". In particular $|\Omega| = |\omega|$, and a point of the body moves with
$\dot x = \dot Rx_0 = \Omega \times x$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The left-invariant forms computed in this section therefore give the angular velocity of a body directly. The third
example states the dictionary, which @prp-lg-euler-kinematic below writes out.

::: {#exm-lg-angvel-mc-forms}
#### Angular velocity from the Maurer-Cartan form

For $SO(3)$, $R^{-1}dR = \sigma^aL_a$ with the components @eq-su2-forms (@exr-lg-mc-form-so3). Along a curve of Euler
angles $(\theta(t), \varphi(t), \psi(t))$ the velocity is $\dot\theta\,\partial_\theta + \dot\varphi\,\partial_\varphi +
\dot\psi\,\partial_\psi$, and $\omega_a = \sigma^a(\dot\theta\,\partial_\theta + \dot\varphi\,\partial_\varphi + \dot\psi\,
\partial_\psi)$; for instance $\omega_3 = \dot\psi + \cos\theta\,\dot\varphi$. The dual fields $\xi_a$ of
@exm-lg-su2-dual-fields are the velocities with $\omega = e_a$: unit rotation about the $a$-th axis of the body.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The definition asserts that the two matrices are antisymmetric. The first exercise proves it from $R^{\mathsf{T}}R = 1$
and computes how points move, as seen from space and from the body.

::: {#exr-lg-angvel-antisymmetric}
#### Angular velocities are antisymmetric

Differentiate $R^{\mathsf{T}}R = 1$ and $RR^{\mathsf{T}} = 1$ to show that $R^{-1}\dot R$ and $\dot RR^{-1}$ are
antisymmetric. Show that $x(t) = R(t)x_0$ satisfies $\dot x = \Omega \times x$, and that the body coordinates
$R^{-1}y$ of a point $y$ fixed in space move with $\frac{d}{dt}(R^{-1}y) = -\omega \times R^{-1}y$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$0 = \frac{d}{dt}(R^{\mathsf{T}}R) = \dot R^{\mathsf{T}}R + R^{\mathsf{T}}\dot R = (R^{\mathsf{T}}\dot R)^{\mathsf{T}} +
R^{\mathsf{T}}\dot R$ with $R^{\mathsf{T}} = R^{-1}$, and likewise $0 = \dot RR^{\mathsf{T}} + (\dot RR^{\mathsf{T}})^{\mathsf
{T}}$. Then $\dot x = \dot RR^{-1}x = (\Omega \cdot L)x = \Omega \times x$. Since $\frac{d}{dt}R^{-1} = -R^{-1}\dot RR^{-1}$,
$\frac{d}{dt}(R^{-1}y) = -(R^{-1}\dot R)R^{-1}y = -\omega \times R^{-1}y$: from the body, the fixed point turns with the
opposite angular velocity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A line that moves relative to the body sweeps an angle made of its own motion and of the rotation of the body. The
second exercise computes this angle to first order in time, a classical problem on rotating axes [@sinha2023rigid,
Sec. 1.1.33].

::: {#exr-lg-angvel-moving-line}
#### The angle swept by a moving line

A line through $O$ has unit direction $u(t)$ in body coordinates, so that its direction in space is $R(t)u(t)$. Show
that $\frac{d}{dt}(Ru) = R(\dot u + \omega \times u)$, and that the angle between the positions of the line at times
$t$ and $t + \delta t$ is $\delta t\,|\dot u + \omega \times u| + O(\delta t^2)$. Write the result in components for
$u = (l, m, n)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{d}{dt}(Ru) = \dot Ru + R\dot u = R(R^{-1}\dot Ru + \dot u) = R(\omega \times u + \dot u)$. The two positions are
unit vectors, so the angle $\delta$ between them satisfies $2\sin\frac\delta2 = |R(t + \delta t)u(t + \delta t) -
R(t)u(t)| = \delta t\,|R(\dot u + \omega \times u)| + O(\delta t^2)$, and $R$ preserves lengths. In components the
angle is $\delta t$ times the length of $(\dot l - m\omega_3 + n\omega_2,\ \dot m - n\omega_1 + l\omega_3,\ \dot n -
l\omega_2 + m\omega_1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Angular velocities of composed motions add, after one of them is turned into the frame of the other. The third
exercise derives the rule from the Maurer-Cartan form of a product, and the proposition that follows applies it twice.

::: {#exr-lg-angvel-product}
#### Adding angular velocities

For $R(t) = R_1(t)R_2(t)$ show that $\omega = R_2^{-1}\omega_1 + \omega_2$ and $\Omega = \Omega_1 + R_1\Omega_2$, where
$\omega_i$, $\Omega_i$ are the angular velocities of $R_i$. Compute $\omega$ and $\Omega$ for $R = e^{\varphi(t)L_3}
e^{\theta_0L_1}$ with constant $\theta_0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @exr-lg-mc-product, $(R_1R_2)^{-1}\frac{d}{dt}(R_1R_2) = R_2^{-1}(\omega_1 \cdot L)R_2 + \omega_2 \cdot L$, and
$R_2^{-1}(\omega_1 \cdot L)R_2 = (R_2^{-1}\omega_1) \cdot L$ by @exm-lg-angvel-space-body. Likewise $\frac{d}{dt}(R_1R_2)
(R_1R_2)^{-1} = \Omega_1 \cdot L + R_1(\Omega_2 \cdot L)R_1^{-1}$ gives $\Omega = \Omega_1 + R_1\Omega_2$. For $R =
e^{\varphi L_3}e^{\theta_0L_1}$ the second factor is constant, so $\Omega = \dot\varphi\,e_3$ and $\omega = R^{-1}\Omega =
\dot\varphi\,e^{-\theta_0L_1}e_3 = \dot\varphi\,(0, \sin\theta_0, \cos\theta_0)$: a body precessing about the vertical
sees its angular velocity fixed, inclined at $\theta_0$ to its third axis.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

Applying the rule twice to the Euler-angle product $e^{\varphi L_3}e^{\theta L_1}e^{\psi L_3}$ expresses both angular
velocities through the rates of the three angles. The proposition states the result, which mechanics calls Euler's
kinematic (or geometrical) equations [@sinha2023rigid, Secs. 1.1.30-1.1.31].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-lg-euler-kinematic}
#### Euler's kinematic equations

For $R(t) = e^{\varphi L_3}e^{\theta L_1}e^{\psi L_3}$ with Euler angles depending on $t$, the angular velocity in the
body is
$$
\omega_1 = \dot\theta\cos\psi + \dot\varphi\sin\theta\sin\psi, \quad \omega_2 = -\dot\theta\sin\psi +
\dot\varphi\sin\theta\cos\psi, \quad \omega_3 = \dot\psi + \dot\varphi\cos\theta ,
$$ {#eq-lg-euler-body}
the left-invariant forms @eq-su2-forms evaluated on the velocity, and the angular velocity in space is
$$
\Omega_1 = \dot\theta\cos\varphi + \dot\psi\sin\theta\sin\varphi, \quad \Omega_2 = \dot\theta\sin\varphi -
\dot\psi\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \quad \Omega_3 = \dot\varphi + \dot\psi\cos\theta ,
$$ {#eq-lg-euler-space}
with $\Omega = R\omega$ and $|\omega|^2 = |\Omega|^2 = \dot\theta^2 + \dot\varphi^2 + \dot\psi^2 +
2\cos\theta\,\dot\varphi\dot\psi$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest motion that involves all three angles is steady precession, in which the axis of a top turns uniformly
about the vertical at a fixed inclination while the top spins about that axis. The first example evaluates the
proposition for it.

::: {#exm-lg-ek-precession}
#### Steady precession

For $\theta = \theta_0$, $\varphi = \mu t$ and $\psi = \nu t$, @eq-lg-euler-space gives $\Omega = \mu\,e_3 + \nu\,(\sin
\theta_0\sin\mu t, -\sin\theta_0\cos\mu t, \cos\theta_0) = \mu\,e_3 + \nu\,Re_3$, the precession about the vertical plus
the spin about the moving axis $Re_3$ of the top (@exr-lg-ek-axis). In the body, $\omega = (\mu\sin\theta_0\sin\nu t,
\mu\sin\theta_0\cos\nu t, \nu + \mu\cos\theta_0)$ turns about the third body axis, and $|\omega|^2 = \mu^2 + \nu^2 +
2\mu\nu\cos\theta_0$ is constant.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Euler chart degenerates at $\theta = 0$, and the kinematic equations show it. Books on rigid bodies often use a
different convention for the middle rotation, and the second example also translates between the two.

::: {#exm-lg-ek-pole}
#### The pole of the chart and the z-y-z convention

The matrix of coefficients of $(\dot\theta, \dot\varphi, \dot\psi)$ in @eq-lg-euler-body has determinant $\sin\theta$,
so at $\theta = 0$ the rates cannot be recovered from $\omega$, and there $\omega_3 = \dot\varphi + \dot\psi$ sees only
the sum, as in @exm-exponential-euler (@exr-lg-ek-inverse). The z-y-z convention $e^{\varphi'L_3}e^{\theta L_2}e^{\psi'
L_3}$ [@sinha2023rigid, Sec. 1.1.29] describes the same rotation as ours with $\varphi = \varphi' + \frac\pi2$ and $\psi
= \psi' - \frac\pi2$, since $e^{\theta L_2} = e^{\frac\pi2L_3}e^{\theta L_1}e^{-\frac\pi2L_3}$; substituting, $\omega_1 =
\dot\theta\sin\psi' - \dot\varphi'\sin\theta\cos\psi'$, $\omega_2 = \dot\theta\cos\psi' + \dot\varphi'\sin\theta\sin\psi'$
and $\omega_3 = \dot\psi' + \dot\varphi'\cos\theta$, the form in which @sinha2023rigid [Sec. 1.1.30] states them, with his
$\psi$, $\varphi$ in the roles of our $\varphi'$, $\psi'$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The kinetic energy of a body turning about a fixed point is a quadratic form in its angular velocity in the body. For
a body with equal moments of inertia it is the bi-invariant metric of the group, which gives the metric of the
three-sphere a mechanical meaning.

::: {#exm-lg-ek-top-energy}
#### The kinetic energy of a top

A body whose principal moments of inertia about its body axes are $I_1 = I_2$ and $I_3$ has kinetic energy
$\frac12I_1(\omega_1^2 + \omega_2^2) + \frac12I_3\omega_3^2 = \frac12I_1(\dot\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,\dot\varphi^2) +
\frac12I_3(\dot\psi + \cos\theta\,\dot\varphi)^2$, by the computation of @exm-lg-su2-metric-expansion. For a spherical
top, $I_1 = I_3 = I$, it is $\frac12I|\omega|^2$, which is $2I$ times the metric @eq-su2-metric evaluated on the
velocity: the free spherical top moves along the geodesics of the bi-invariant metric.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The proposition can be checked by differentiating the product of three rotation matrices. The first exercise lets Sage
do it, and derives the space components by hand from the addition rule.

::: {#exr-lg-ek-check}
#### Euler's equations with Sage

With Sage, compute $R^{-1}\dot R$ and $\dot RR^{-1}$ for $R(t) = e^{\varphi(t)L_3}e^{\theta(t)L_1}e^{\psi(t)L_3}$, read off
$\omega$ and $\Omega$, and confirm @eq-lg-euler-body, @eq-lg-euler-space, $\Omega = R\omega$ and the value of
$|\omega|^2$. Derive @eq-lg-euler-space by hand from @exr-lg-angvel-product.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Applying $\Omega = \Omega_1 + R_1\Omega_2$ twice, $\Omega = \dot\varphi\,e_3 + e^{\varphi L_3}\bigl(\dot\theta\,e_1 +
e^{\theta L_1}\dot\psi\,e_3\bigr) = \dot\varphi\,e_3 + \dot\theta\,(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi, 0) + \dot\psi\,
e^{\varphi L_3}(0, -\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$, and $e^{\varphi L_3}(0, -\sin\theta, \cos\theta) = (\sin\theta\sin\varphi,
-\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \cos\theta)$, which is @eq-lg-euler-space. The rule $\omega = R_2^{-1}\omega_1 + \omega_2$ gives
@eq-lg-euler-body the same way:

{{< sage exr-lg-ek-check >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Given the angular velocity, the Euler angles are found by integrating the kinematic equations. The second exercise
solves them for the rates, wherever the chart allows.

::: {#exr-lg-ek-inverse}
#### Rates from the angular velocity

Solve @eq-lg-euler-body for $\dot\theta$, $\dot\varphi$, $\dot\psi$ when $\sin\theta \neq 0$, and compare the result with
the dual frame of @exm-lg-su2-dual-fields.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\omega_1\cos\psi - \omega_2\sin\psi = \dot\theta$ and $\omega_1\sin\psi + \omega_2\cos\psi = \dot\varphi\sin\theta$, so
$\dot\varphi = (\omega_1\sin\psi + \omega_2\cos\psi)/\sin\theta$ and $\dot\psi = \omega_3 - \cos\theta\,\dot\varphi$. The
velocity is then $\dot\theta\,\partial_\theta + \dot\varphi\,\partial_\varphi + \dot\psi\,\partial_\psi = \omega_1\bigl(\cos
\psi\,\partial_\theta + \frac{\sin\psi}{\sin\theta}(\partial_\varphi - \cos\theta\,\partial_\psi)\bigr) + \omega_2\bigl(-\sin
\psi\,\partial_\theta + \frac{\cos\psi}{\sin\theta}(\partial_\varphi - \cos\theta\,\partial_\psi)\bigr) + \omega_3\,
\partial_\psi = \omega_a\xi_a$, the dual frame: the velocity with body angular velocity $\omega$ is $\omega_a\xi_a$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The axis of a top is its third body axis, the point $Re_3$ of the unit sphere. The third exercise follows that point
and finds that the spin does not move it.

::: {#exr-lg-ek-axis}
#### The motion of the axis

Show that $Re_3 = (\sin\theta\sin\varphi, -\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \cos\theta)$, so that its spherical angles are
$(\theta, \varphi - \frac\pi2)$, that $\frac{d}{dt}(Re_3) = \Omega \times Re_3$, and that its speed on the sphere is
$(\dot\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,\dot\varphi^2)^{1/2}$, independent of $\dot\psi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{\psi L_3}e_3 = e_3$, so $Re_3 = e^{\varphi L_3}e^{\theta L_1}e_3 = e^{\varphi L_3}(0, -\sin\theta, \cos\theta) =
(\sin\theta\sin\varphi, -\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \cos\theta)$. By @exr-lg-angvel-antisymmetric with $x_0 = e_3$,
$\frac{d}{dt}(Re_3) = \Omega \times Re_3$, whose length is $|R(\omega \times e_3)| = (\omega_1^2 + \omega_2^2)^{1/2} =
(\dot\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,\dot\varphi^2)^{1/2}$ by @exm-lg-su2-metric-expansion. The spin $\dot\psi$ turns the body
about $Re_3$ and leaves the axis in place.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
