### Exercises {#sec-lie-groups-algebras-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Three exercises that combine the four sections of this chapter: the double cover $SU(2) \to SO(3)$ followed from the
group to the Lie algebra and back, the affine group of the line taken through every construction of the chapter, and
the Heisenberg group, a nilpotent counterpart of both.

The first integrative exercise builds the double cover on the whole group rather than on one subgroup. It uses the
Euler angles, the adjoint representation, the Killing form and the exponential map together.

::: {#exr-lg-int-su2-so3}
#### The double cover from end to end

For the Euler-angle element $g(\theta, \varphi, \psi)$ of @eq-euler-matrix compute the matrix of
$\operatorname{Ad}_g$ in the basis $T_a$. Show that it is the rotation $e^{\varphi L_3}e^{\theta L_1}e^{\psi L_3}$, that
it is orthogonal of determinant one, that $\operatorname{Ad}_{-g} = \operatorname{Ad}_g$, that its derivative is
$\operatorname{ad}_{T_a} = L_a$ with Killing form $-2\delta_{ab}$, and that $(\theta, \varphi, \psi) = (0, 0, 2\pi)$
gives $g = -1$ and $\operatorname{Ad}_g = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{Ad}$ is a homomorphism, so $\operatorname{Ad}_g = \operatorname{Ad}_{e^{\varphi T_3}}\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{\theta
T_1}}\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{\psi T_3}}$, and each factor is $\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{tT_a}} = e^{t\operatorname{ad}_{T_a}} =
e^{tL_a}$ (@exr-lg-ad-exp, @exr-lg-su2-so3-isomorphism). Orthogonality follows from the invariance of the Killing form
$-2\delta_{ab}$ (@exr-lg-killing-invariance), and the determinant is one because $\operatorname{Ad}_g$ is connected to
the identity through $\operatorname{Ad}_{g(t\theta, t\varphi, t\psi)}$. Conjugation by $-g$ equals conjugation by $g$,
and $g(0, 0, 2\pi) = e^{2\pi T_3} = -1$ covers the identity rotation: the kernel $\{\pm 1\}$ of the double cover is the
centre of @exr-lg-centre-su2. Every rotation is an Euler-angle product, so $\operatorname{Ad}$ is onto $SO(3)$:

{{< sage exr-lg-int-su2-so3 >}}
:::

The second integrative exercise takes the affine group through every construction of the chapter. It is the smallest
non-abelian example, and its Killing form shows what changes when the group is not semisimple.

::: {#exr-lg-int-affine}
#### The affine group throughout

For the affine group $\{x \mapsto ax + b,\ a > 0\}$: (a) build its Lie algebra in Sage's `LieAlgebra` module and compute
its Killing form; (b) compute the exponential map $e^{xX + yY}$ and show that it is a bijection from $\mathfrak{g}$ onto
the group; (c) compute $g^{-1}dg$, check the Maurer-Cartan equation, and find the left-invariant volume form.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $[X, Y] = Y$, and the Killing form is $\kappa(X, X) = 1$, all other components zero (@exm-killing-abelian): degenerate,
so the algebra is not semisimple; it is solvable. (b) $e^{xX + yY} = \begin{pmatrix} e^x & y(e^x - 1)/x \\ 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}$ (@exr-lg-one-param-affine). Given $a > 0$ and $b$, $x = \log a$ is forced by the diagonal, and then $y =
bx/(a - 1)$ (or $y = b$ when $a = 1$), since $(e^x - 1)/x > 0$: the exponential map is a bijection, unlike that of
$SU(2)$ or $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ (@exm-exponential-su2, @exr-lg-exp-not-surjective). (c) $g^{-1}dg = \sigma^XX + \sigma^YY$
with $\sigma^X = da/a$, $\sigma^Y = db/a$ (@exm-mc-form-affine), $d\sigma^Y = -\sigma^X \wedge \sigma^Y$ (@exr-lg-mc-affine),
and the left-invariant volume form is $\sigma^X \wedge \sigma^Y = da \wedge db/a^2$ (@exr-lg-haar-measure):

{{< sage exr-lg-int-affine >}}
:::

The third integrative exercise repeats the analysis for the Heisenberg group, whose Lie algebra is nilpotent rather than
solvable. Every construction of the chapter becomes polynomial.

::: {#exr-lg-int-heisenberg}
#### The Heisenberg group throughout

For the Heisenberg group of @exr-lg-heisenberg-group: (a) show that its Lie algebra is $\mathfrak{n}_3$, with $[X, Y] = Z$
central, and that the adjoint representation and the Killing form are as in @exr-lg-ad-heisenberg; (b) compute $e^N$ for
$N = xE_{12} + yE_{23} + zE_{13}$ and show that the exponential map is a diffeomorphism $\mathfrak{n}_3 \to H$; (c) verify
that $e^{X}e^{Y} = e^{X + Y + \frac12[X, Y]}$ exactly, and relate the Maurer-Cartan equation $d\sigma^Z = -\sigma^X \wedge
\sigma^Y$ to the bracket.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) A curve $h(x(t), y(t), z(t))$ through the identity has velocity $\dot x E_{12} + \dot yE_{23} + \dot zE_{13}$, so the Lie
algebra is $\mathfrak{n}_3$ (@exr-lg-upper-triangular), with $[E_{12}, E_{23}] = E_{13}$ central
(@exr-lg-heisenberg-structure); every $\operatorname{ad}$ is nilpotent and $\kappa = 0$. (b) $N^2 = xyE_{13}$ and $N^3 = 0$,
so $e^N = 1 + N + \tfrac12N^2 = h(x, y, z + \tfrac12xy)$; the inverse map $h(x, y, z) \mapsto (x, y, z - \tfrac12xy)$ is
polynomial, so $\exp$ is a diffeomorphism. (c) $e^{E_{12}}e^{E_{23}} = h(1, 0, 0)h(0, 1, 0) = h(1, 1, 1)$, while $e^{E_{12} +
E_{23} + \frac12E_{13}} = h(1, 1, \tfrac12 + \tfrac12) = h(1, 1, 1)$: the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff series of
@exr-lg-exp-noncommuting stops after the commutator because all higher brackets vanish. The Maurer-Cartan equation
$d\sigma^Z = -\sigma^X \wedge \sigma^Y$ of @exr-lg-invariant-form-heisenberg is @eq-maurer-cartan for the single structure
constant $f_{XY}{}^Z = 1$, and $d\sigma^X = d\sigma^Y = 0$ because $X$ and $Y$ never appear as brackets.
:::
::::


## Representations of Lie algebras {#sec-lie-representations}

A representation lets a Lie algebra act on a vector space by matrices, and the finite-dimensional representations of
the compact Lie algebras are classified by a small amount of combinatorial data: weights, roots and highest weights.
This chapter has three sections. Weights and the representations of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ introduces Cartan subalgebras
and weights, builds the spin-$j$ representations from ladder operators, exponentiates them to the rotation matrices
of spin $j$ and decomposes tensor products with the Clebsch-Gordan rule. Roots and $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ runs the same programme in rank two, with the Gell-Mann basis, the
hexagon of roots, highest weights, simple roots and the Cartan matrix. Branching rules restricts representations to
subalgebras, works the branching of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ under $\mathfrak{su}(2) \times \mathfrak{u}(1)$ and splits
$\mathfrak{so}(4)$ into two commuting copies of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$. Every statement is followed by three examples and
three exercises with hidden solutions, and many of the computations use Sage's `WeylCharacterRing` and `RootSystem`.

### Weights and the representations of su(2) {#sec-weights-su2}

The representations of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ are the spins of quantum mechanics, and they are classified by a single
number because a diagonalisable generator, $J_3$, labels the states and two ladder operators move between them.
The same mechanism, with a Cartan subalgebra in place of $J_3$ and roots in place of the ladder operators,
classifies the representations of every compact Lie algebra, and @sec-roots-su3 runs it for $\mathfrak{su}(3)$.

#### Cartan subalgebras and weights

To label the vectors of a representation by numbers we need operators that can be diagonalised simultaneously, and
the largest commuting family inside the Lie algebra is the natural choice. The definition below names this family and
its dimension, the single integer that organises everything else in the chapter.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-cartan-subalgebra}
#### Cartan subalgebra

A **Cartan subalgebra** $\mathfrak{h}$ of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ is a maximal abelian subalgebra whose
elements act diagonalisably in every finite-dimensional representation (for compact Lie algebras, a maximal
abelian subalgebra); its dimension is the **rank** of $\mathfrak{g}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ any two independent generators fail to commute, so a Cartan subalgebra is a single line. The
choice of that line is the choice of a quantisation axis in quantum mechanics.

::: {#exm-cartan-su2}
#### $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ has rank one

$\mathfrak{h} = \operatorname{span}(T_3)$: no other generator commutes with $T_3$, since $[T_3, T_1] = T_2$ and
$[T_3, T_2] = -T_1$. Every Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ is the span of some $n_aT_a$, a choice of
axis.
:::

For the unitary algebras the diagonal matrices are the obvious commuting family. Tracelessness removes one dimension,
which is why $\mathfrak{su}(n)$ has rank one less than the size of its matrices.

::: {#exm-cartan-su3}
#### $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ has rank two

$\mathfrak{h} = \operatorname{span}(\lambda_3, \lambda_8)$, the diagonal traceless matrices, which commute with
each other (@sec-roots-su3); $\mathfrak{su}(n)$ has rank $n - 1$, its Cartan subalgebra being the diagonal
traceless matrices.
:::

At the other extreme every element of an abelian algebra commutes with every other. The rank then equals the
dimension, and for a direct sum of algebras the ranks of the summands add.

::: {#exm-cartan-abelian}
#### Abelian algebras and $\mathfrak{so}(4)$

An abelian Lie algebra is its own Cartan subalgebra, with rank equal to its dimension; $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ has
rank one and the torus algebra $\mathbb{R}^n$ rank $n$. $\mathfrak{so}(4) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus
\mathfrak{su}(2)$ (@sec-branching) has rank $2$, one $T_3$ from each factor.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks by a direct computation that a Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ cannot be enlarged,
and that any axis serves as well as the third one. The cross product of vectors does all the work.

::: {#exr-lrep-cartan-axis}
#### The commutant of an axis

Find all $X = x_aT_a \in \mathfrak{su}(2)$ with $[T_3, X] = 0$, and more generally with $[n_aT_a, X] = 0$ for a unit
vector $n$. Conclude that $\operatorname{span}(n_aT_a)$ is a maximal abelian subalgebra.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
From $[T_a, T_b] = \epsilon_{abc}T_c$, $[n_aT_a, x_bT_b] = \epsilon_{abc}n_ax_bT_c = (n \times x)_cT_c$. This vanishes
exactly when $x$ is parallel to $n$, so the commutant of $n_aT_a$ is the line it spans; for $n = e_3$ the condition
reads $x_1T_2 - x_2T_1 = 0$, so $x_1 = x_2 = 0$. A line is abelian, and since nothing outside it commutes with $n_aT_a$
it is maximal: the rank of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ is one, whichever axis is chosen.
:::

For $\mathfrak{su}(n)$ the second exercise shows that the diagonal traceless matrices cannot be enlarged either. A
single diagonal matrix with distinct entries already forces every matrix commuting with it to be diagonal, which Sage
confirms by solving the linear equations for $n \leq 5$.

::: {#exr-lrep-cartan-sun}
#### The rank of $\mathfrak{su}(n)$

Show that the traceless matrices commuting with $H = \operatorname{diag}(h_1, \dots, h_n)$, $h_i$ distinct, are
diagonal, so that the diagonal traceless matrices form a Cartan subalgebra of dimension $n - 1$. Check with Sage for
$n = 2, \dots, 5$ by computing the dimension of the centraliser.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[H, X]_{ij} = (h_i - h_j)X_{ij}$, so $[H, X] = 0$ forces $X_{ij} = 0$ for $i \neq j$: $X$ is diagonal. The diagonal
traceless matrices commute among themselves and nothing else commutes with a generic one, so they form a maximal
abelian subalgebra, of dimension $n - 1$ (the anti-Hermitian ones are $i$ times real diagonal traceless matrices,
with the same dimension over $\mathbb{R}$):

{{< sage exr-lrep-cartan-sun >}}
:::

The orthogonal algebras behave differently, since their generators are rotations in planes and two rotations commute
when their planes are orthogonal. The third exercise finds the rank of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ this way and generalises to
every $\mathfrak{so}(N)$.

::: {#exr-lrep-cartan-so4}
#### The rank of $\mathfrak{so}(N)$

With the rotation generators $(M_{ij})_{kl} = \delta_{ik}\delta_{jl} - \delta_{il}\delta_{jk}$ of $\mathbb{R}^4$, show
that $M_{01}$ and $M_{23}$ commute and that every element of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ commuting with both lies in their
span. Deduce that $\mathfrak{so}(N)$ has rank $\lfloor N/2 \rfloor$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$M_{01}$ and $M_{23}$ rotate the orthogonal planes $(x_0, x_1)$ and $(x_2, x_3)$, so they commute (by the bracket
formula of @exr-so4-coset, the pairs share no index). An antisymmetric $X$ commuting with $M_{01}$ preserves its
kernel, the plane $(x_2, x_3)$, and its image, the plane $(x_0, x_1)$, so $X$ is block diagonal with two antisymmetric
$2 \times 2$ blocks: $X = aM_{01} + bM_{23}$. In $\mathbb{R}^N$ one can fit $\lfloor N/2 \rfloor$ orthogonal planes,
and the same argument shows that $M_{01}, M_{23}, M_{45}, \dots$ span a maximal abelian subalgebra; for $N = 3$ this
gives rank one, as for $\mathfrak{su}(2) \cong \mathfrak{so}(3)$.
:::
::::

Once a Cartan subalgebra is fixed, its elements can be diagonalised together in any representation. The common
eigenvalues are the labels we were looking for, and the definition below names them and counts their repetitions.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-weight}
#### Weight

In a representation $V$ of $\mathfrak{g}$ the simultaneous eigenvalues of the Cartan subalgebra are the
**weights** of $V$: for a basis $H_1, \dots, H_r$ of $\mathfrak{h}$ a weight is the vector $\mu = (\mu_1, \dots,
\mu_r)$ of eigenvalues of a common eigenvector, and the number of independent eigenvectors with weight $\mu$ is
its **multiplicity**. The **weight diagram** is the set of weights with multiplicities (@fig-su2-weights).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The smallest non-trivial case is the two-dimensional representation of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$. Using the Hermitian
generator $J_3 = iT_3$ makes the eigenvalues real, and they are the familiar spin projections.

::: {#exm-weight-spinor}
#### The spinor representation

With $H = J_3 = iT_3 = \tfrac12\sigma_3$, the representation on $\mathbb{C}^2$ has weights $+\tfrac12$ and
$-\tfrac12$, the eigenvalues of $\tfrac12\sigma_3$, each of multiplicity one: spin up and spin down.
:::

The rotation generators of $\mathbb{R}^3$ are real antisymmetric, so their eigenvectors are complex. After
complexifying, the generator of rotations about the third axis has three eigenvalues, one for each direction.

::: {#exm-weight-vector}
#### The vector representation

On $\mathbb{R}^3 \otimes \mathbb{C}$, $iL_3$ has eigenvalues $1, 0, -1$ (@exm-charges-sphere of
@sec-reductive, where the eigenvectors $L_1 \pm iL_2$ and $L_3$ of $\operatorname{ad}_{L_3}$ are found): the weights
of spin $1$, each once.
:::

Every Lie algebra acts on itself by the bracket, and the weights of this adjoint representation deserve a name of
their own. They are the subject of @sec-roots-su3, and the example records the first two cases.

::: {#exm-weight-adjoint}
#### Roots as weights of the adjoint

The weights of the adjoint representation are the **roots** (the non-zero ones) together with the zero weight,
whose multiplicity is the rank: for $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ the roots are $\pm 1$ (the weights of $\operatorname{ad}_{J_3}$
on $J_\pm$) and $0$ has multiplicity one; for $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ the roots form a hexagon and $0$ has
multiplicity two (@sec-roots-su3).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![Weight diagrams of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ from Sage's `WeylCharacterRing`. Left: the weights $m = j, j - 1, \dots, -
j$ of spin $j$, each of multiplicity one. Right: the weights of $1 \otimes 1$ with multiplicities $1, 2, 3, 2, 1$,
which decompose as spin $2$, spin $1$ and spin $0$. Generated by
`figures/su2_weights.sage`.](figures/su2_weights.svg){#fig-su2-weights width=90%}

The first exercise finds the weights of the vector representation explicitly, eigenvectors included. The
eigenvectors $(1, \pm i, 0)$ are the circular polarisations familiar from optics.

::: {#exr-lrep-weight-spin1}
#### Weights of the vector representation

With $(L_a)_{bc} = -\epsilon_{abc}$, find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $iL_3$ on $\mathbb{C}^3$, check $[L_1,
L_2] = L_3$, and confirm the weights $1, 0, -1$ with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$L_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, so $iL_3(1, \pm i, 0) = i(\mp i, 1, 0) =
\pm(1, \pm i, 0)$ and $iL_3e_3 = 0$: the weights are $+1$ on $(1, i, 0)$, $-1$ on $(1, -i, 0)$ and $0$ on $e_3$, each
once.

{{< sage exr-lrep-weight-spin1 >}}
:::

Weights behave simply under the two basic constructions of new representations from old, the tensor product and the
dual. The second exercise derives the rules, which turn the decomposition of tensor products into arithmetic with
weights.

::: {#exr-lrep-weight-tensor}
#### Weights of tensor products and duals

A Lie algebra acts on $V \otimes W$ by $X(v \otimes w) = Xv \otimes w + v \otimes Xw$ and on the dual $V^*$ by
$-X^{\mathsf{T}}$. Show that the weights of $V \otimes W$ are the sums $\mu + \nu$ of weights of $V$ and $W$ (with
multiplicities multiplied), and that those of $V^*$ are the negatives $-\mu$. Apply this to $\tfrac12 \otimes
\tfrac12$ and to the dual of spin $j$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $Hv = \mu(H)v$ and $Hw = \nu(H)w$ for all $H \in \mathfrak{h}$, then $H(v \otimes w) = (\mu(H) + \nu(H))v \otimes w$;
products of weight bases form a weight basis of $V \otimes W$, so the multiplicity of a weight $\lambda$ is
$\sum_{\mu + \nu = \lambda}m_V(\mu)m_W(\nu)$. In the dual basis, $-H^{\mathsf{T}}$ is diagonal with entries $-\mu(H)$. For
$\tfrac12 \otimes \tfrac12$ the weights are $\pm\tfrac12 \pm \tfrac12 = 1, 0, 0, -1$ (@exm-clebsch-spinors). The
weights $j, \dots, -j$ of spin $j$ are symmetric under $m \to -m$, so the dual has the same weights: every spin-$j$
representation is equivalent to its dual.
:::

The third exercise is the first rank-two computation. Complex conjugation of the matrices gives a second
three-dimensional representation of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, and its weights show that it is not equivalent to the first.

::: {#exr-lrep-weight-su3-fund}
#### The conjugate representation of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$

$\mathfrak{su}(3)$ acts on $\mathbb{C}^3$ by $T_A = -\tfrac{i}{2}\lambda_A$ and, in the **conjugate representation**
$\bar{\mathbf{3}}$, by the complex conjugates $\bar T_A$. Show that in $\bar{\mathbf{3}}$ the Hermitian matrices
$\lambda_A$ act as $-\bar\lambda_A$, and find the weights with respect to $(\lambda_3, \lambda_8)$. Why are
$\mathbf{3}$ and $\bar{\mathbf{3}}$ inequivalent?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\bar T_A = \tfrac{i}{2}\bar\lambda_A = -\tfrac{i}{2}(-\bar\lambda_A)$, so $\lambda_A$ is represented by $-\bar\lambda_A$.
Since $\lambda_3$ and $\lambda_8$ are real and diagonal, their eigenvalues change sign: the weights of
$\bar{\mathbf{3}}$ are $(-1, -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3})$, $(1, -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3})$, $(0, \tfrac{2}{\sqrt3})$, the triangle of
@fig-su3-weights turned upside down. Equivalent representations have the same weights, and the two triangles differ,
so $\bar{\mathbf{3}} \not\cong \mathbf{3}$; unlike the spins of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, the fundamental representation of
$\mathfrak{su}(3)$ is not self-dual.
:::
::::

#### The spin-$j$ representations

The weights of a representation of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ are found by moving between eigenvectors of $J_3$. The
operators that perform the moves are complex combinations of the two remaining generators, defined below.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-ladder-operators}
#### Ladder operators

For $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with $J_3 = iT_3$, the **ladder operators** are $J_\pm = iT_1 \mp T_2$; the brackets
@eq-su2-brackets become $[J_3, J_\pm] = \pm J_\pm$ and $[J_+, J_-] = 2J_3$, so $J_\pm$ raise and lower the
$J_3$-eigenvalue by one: if $J_3 v = mv$ then $J_3(J_\pm v) = (m \pm 1)J_\pm v$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In the two smallest representations the ladder operators are matrices with a single line of ones or square roots
above or below the diagonal. The examples show them moving the weight vectors along the chain of weights.

::: {#exm-ladder-matrices}
#### Spin $\tfrac12$ and spin $1$

In the spinor representation $J_+ = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $J_- = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\
1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ send spin down to spin up and back, and $J_+$ kills spin up: $\tfrac12$ is the highest weight.
In the vector representation $J_\pm$ connect the three weights $1, 0, -1$ in a chain.
:::

The ladder operators are elements of the complexified Lie algebra itself, so the adjoint representation sees them too.
There they are eigenvectors of $J_3$, which is the defining property of root vectors.

::: {#exm-ladder-adjoint}
#### Ladder operators as root vectors

$J_\pm$ are eigenvectors of $\operatorname{ad}_{J_3}$ with eigenvalues $\pm 1$: they are the **root vectors** of
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$, and $[J_3, J_\pm] = \pm J_\pm$ is the statement that the roots are $\pm 1$. For
$\mathfrak{su}(3)$ there are six root vectors, three raising and three lowering (@sec-roots-su3).
:::

In quantum mechanics the same operators act on wave functions on the sphere. Their action on the spherical
harmonics is the standard example of a ladder.

::: {#exm-ladder-harmonic}
#### Angular momentum

In quantum mechanics $J_\pm = J_1 \pm iJ_2$ act on the spherical harmonics $Y_{lm}$ as $J_\pm Y_{lm} \propto
Y_{l, m \pm 1}$: the functions on the sphere decompose into the spin-$l$ representations of @def-spin-j, which is
the harmonic expansion of fields on $S^2$ used in Part IV.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the ladder brackets from the structure constants of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$. It is a short
computation, but every later statement about spin uses it.

::: {#exr-ladder-brackets}
#### The ladder brackets

Derive $[J_3, J_\pm] = \pm J_\pm$ and $[J_+, J_-] = 2J_3$ from $[T_a, T_b] = \epsilon_{abc}T_c$ with $J_3 = iT_3$,
$J_\pm = iT_1 \mp T_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[J_3, J_\pm] = i[T_3, iT_1 \mp T_2] = i(iT_2 \mp (-T_1)) = -T_2 \pm iT_1 = \pm(iT_1 \mp T_2) = \pm J_\pm$, using
$[T_3, T_1] = T_2$ and $[T_3, T_2] = -T_1$. $[J_+, J_-] = [iT_1 - T_2, iT_1 + T_2] = i[T_1, T_2] - i[T_2, T_1] =
2iT_3 = 2J_3$.
:::

The second exercise builds the ladder operators of the vector representation from the real rotation generators. Sage
checks the brackets and follows $J_+$ up the chain until it annihilates the top vector.

::: {#exr-lrep-ladder-spin1}
#### The ladder of the vector representation

With $(L_a)_{bc} = -\epsilon_{abc}$, form $J_3 = iL_3$ and $J_\pm = iL_1 \mp L_2$, verify the brackets of
@def-ladder-operators, and show that $J_+$ maps the weight-$m$ eigenvector of $J_3$ to a multiple of the weight-$(m +
1)$ eigenvector and kills the weight-$1$ one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The brackets follow from $[L_a, L_b] = \epsilon_{abc}L_c$ exactly as in @exr-ladder-brackets. By
@def-ladder-operators, $J_+$ raises the weight by one, and since there is no weight $2$ it must kill the weight-$1$
vector; so $J_+^2 \neq 0$ but $J_+^3 = 0$:

{{< sage exr-lrep-ladder-spin1 >}}
:::

The third exercise introduces the quadratic Casimir operator, which commutes with the whole algebra and therefore takes
one value on an irreducible representation. Writing it in terms of the ladder operators gives that value at once.

::: {#exr-lrep-ladder-casimir}
#### The Casimir operator

With $J_a = iT_a$, show that $[J_a, J_b] = i\epsilon_{abc}J_c$, that $C = J_1^2 + J_2^2 + J_3^2$ commutes with every
$J_a$, and that $C = J_-J_+ + J_3^2 + J_3$. Evaluate $C$ on a vector $v$ with $J_+v = 0$, $J_3v = jv$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[J_a, J_b] = -[T_a, T_b] = -\epsilon_{abc}T_c = i\epsilon_{abc}J_c$, since $T_c = -iJ_c$. Then $[C, J_a] =
\sum_b(J_b[J_b, J_a] + [J_b, J_a]J_b) = i\epsilon_{bac}(J_bJ_c + J_cJ_b) = 0$, a contraction of an antisymmetric
with a symmetric tensor. With $J_\pm = J_1 \pm iJ_2$ (which is $iT_1 \mp T_2$), $J_-J_+ = J_1^2 + J_2^2 + i[J_1, J_2] =
J_1^2 + J_2^2 - J_3$, so $C = J_-J_+ + J_3^2 + J_3$. On a highest-weight vector $Cv = (j^2 + j)v = j(j + 1)v$, the
familiar eigenvalue of the squared angular momentum.
:::
::::

The ladder operators and the Casimir operator together determine every finite-dimensional irreducible representation
of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$. The definition below describes the outcome: start at the top and step down until the chain
stops.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-spin-j}
#### Spin-$j$ representation

Starting from a **highest weight** vector $v$ with $J_+ v = 0$ and $J_3 v = jv$ and applying $J_-$ repeatedly gives
vectors of weights $j, j - 1, j - 2, \dots$; in a finite-dimensional representation the chain must end, and
$[J_+, J_-] = 2J_3$ forces it to end at $-j$, so $2j$ is a non-negative integer. The resulting irreducible
representation of dimension $2j + 1$ is the **spin-$j$ representation**, $j = 0, \tfrac12, 1, \tfrac32, \dots$,
with weights $j, j - 1, \dots, -j$ each of multiplicity one (@fig-su2-weights); every irreducible representation of
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$ is one of these.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first three spins are representations already met in this book. Each is identified by its dimension and by the
list of its weights.

::: {#exm-spin-low}
#### Spins $0$, $\tfrac12$, $1$

Spin $0$ is the trivial representation; spin $\tfrac12$ the spinor representation $T_a$ on $\mathbb{C}^2$; spin $1$
the vector representation $L_a$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, equivalently the adjoint. Their dimensions $1, 2, 3$ and
weights are checked in @exr-su2-clebsch.
:::

The spins split into two families according to how a rotation by $2\pi$ acts. This is the distinction between the
group $SU(2)$ and the rotation group $SO(3)$ that it covers twice.

::: {#exm-spin-half-integer}
#### Representations of $SU(2)$ that are not representations of $SO(3)$

$e^{2\pi T_3}$ acts on the weight-$m$ vector as $e^{-2\pi i m} = (-1)^{2j}$: for half-integer $j$ the element $-1
\in SU(2)$ acts as $-1$, so the half-integer spins are representations of $SU(2)$ but not of $SO(3) = SU(2)/\{\pm
1\}$ (@exm-cover-su2). Spinors in physics are the half-integer spins.
:::

The functions on the sphere form an infinite-dimensional representation of the rotations. It splits into the
integer spins, each appearing once, with the spherical harmonics as weight vectors.

::: {#exm-spin-harmonics}
#### Spherical harmonics

The functions on the sphere decompose as $\bigoplus_{l \geq 0}(\text{spin } l)$, each integer spin once, with the
$2l + 1$ spherical harmonics $Y_{lm}$ as weight vectors; a field on $M_4 \times S^2$ expanded in $Y_{lm}$ becomes a
tower of four-dimensional fields in the spin-$l$ representations of the gauge group $SO(3)$ (Part IV).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The definition asserted that the chain of weights stops exactly at $-j$. The first exercise proves it with the
Casimir operator of @exr-lrep-ladder-casimir, by computing the length of each vector in the chain.

::: {#exr-lrep-spinj-norm}
#### Why the chain stops at $-j$

In a unitary representation $J_3$ is Hermitian and $J_+^\dagger = J_-$. For the chain $v_m = J_-^{j - m}v$ below a
highest-weight vector $v$, show that $\|J_-v_m\|^2 = (j + m)(j - m + 1)\|v_m\|^2$, and deduce that the chain ends at
$m = -j$ and that $2j$ is a non-negative integer.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
As in @exr-lrep-ladder-casimir, $J_+J_- = J_1^2 + J_2^2 + J_3 = C - J_3^2 + J_3$, and $C = j(j + 1)$ on the whole
chain because $C$ commutes with $J_-$. Hence $\|J_-v_m\|^2 = \langle v_m, J_+J_-v_m\rangle = (j(j + 1) - m^2 +
m)\|v_m\|^2 = (j + m)(j - m + 1)\|v_m\|^2$. The factor vanishes for $m = -j$, so $J_-v_{-j} = 0$ and the chain can stop
there. If the weights $j, j - 1, \dots$ skipped $-j$, some $m < -j$ with $v_m \neq 0$ would occur, and then $(j + m)(j -
m + 1) < 0$ would make a squared norm negative. So $j - k = -j$ for some integer $k \geq 0$: $2j = k$.
:::

The second exercise writes down the spin-$j$ matrices for any $j$, with the square roots that the norms of the first
exercise produce. Sage checks the brackets and the value of the Casimir up to $j = 3$.

::: {#exr-lrep-spinj-matrices}
#### The spin-$j$ matrices

In the basis $v_m$ normalised to unit length, show that $J_3 = \operatorname{diag}(j, \dots, -j)$ and $J_+v_m =
\sqrt{j(j + 1) - m(m + 1)}\,v_{m + 1}$, $J_- = J_+^{\mathsf{T}}$. Check the brackets and $C = j(j + 1)\mathbb{1}$ for $j
\leq 3$, and write out $J_+$ for $j = \tfrac32$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @exr-lrep-spinj-norm, $\|J_+v_m\|^2 = \langle v_m, J_-J_+v_m\rangle = (j(j + 1) - m^2 - m)\|v_m\|^2$, using $J_-J_+ =
C - J_3^2 - J_3$; with real positive phases this gives the stated matrix elements, and $J_- = J_+^\dagger =
J_+^{\mathsf{T}}$ since they are real. For $j = \tfrac32$ the entries are $\sqrt3, 2, \sqrt3$:

{{< sage exr-lrep-spinj-matrices >}}
:::

The third exercise packages the weights of spin $j$ into a single function, the character. Its value at a rotation by
$2\pi$ recovers the sign of @exm-spin-half-integer.

::: {#exr-lrep-spinj-character}
#### The character of spin $j$

Show that $\chi_j(\theta) = \operatorname{tr}e^{i\theta J_3} = \sum_{m = -j}^{j}e^{im\theta} = \frac{\sin((j +
\frac12)\theta)}{\sin(\theta/2)}$ and that $\chi_j(2\pi) = (-1)^{2j}(2j + 1)$. Check with Sage for $j \leq \tfrac52$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The sum is geometric: multiplying by $e^{i\theta/2} - e^{-i\theta/2}$ telescopes it to $e^{i(j + \frac12)\theta} -
e^{-i(j + \frac12)\theta}$, and dividing by $2i$ on both sides gives the quotient of sines. At $\theta = 2\pi$ every
term $e^{2\pi im}$ equals $(-1)^{2j}$ (all $m$ differ from $j$ by integers), so $\chi_j(2\pi) = (-1)^{2j}(2j + 1)$:
$e^{2\pi iJ_3}$ is $-\mathbb{1}$ on half-integer spins.

{{< sage exr-lrep-spinj-character >}}
:::
::::

The spin-$j$ representation of the Lie algebra exponentiates to a representation of the group $SU(2)$, through
$\rho(e^X) = e^{\rho(X)}$ of @def-exponential-map. Its matrices are the rotation matrices of quantum mechanics: they
turn a state of spin $j$ as $e^{tn \cdot L}$ turns a vector, and they are the simplest way to rotate any object
numerically [@boudreau2018applied, Secs. 14.2 and 14.4].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-lrep-rotation-matrix}
#### Rotation matrices of spin $j$

Let $J_a$ be the Hermitian spin-$j$ matrices of @exr-lrep-spinj-matrices in the weight basis $v_j, \dots, v_{-j}$, so
that $T_a$ is represented by $-iJ_a$. The **rotation matrix of spin $j$** of $g = e^{tn \cdot T} \in SU(2)$ is the
unitary $(2j + 1) \times (2j + 1)$ matrix $D^j(g) = e^{-itn \cdot J}$, and $D^j(gh) = D^j(g)D^j(h)$. For the
Euler-angle element @eq-euler-angles its entries are
$$
D^j_{m'm}(\varphi, \theta, \psi) = e^{-im'\varphi}\,d^j_{m'm}(\theta)\,e^{-im\psi}, \qquad d^j(\theta) = e^{-i\theta J_1} .
$$ {#eq-lrep-wigner}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For spin one-half the rotation matrices are the elements of $SU(2)$ themselves. The first example compares
@eq-lrep-wigner with the Euler-angle matrix and with the tables found in quantum mechanics books.

::: {#exm-lrep-dj-half}
#### Spin one-half

For $j = \frac12$, $J_a = \frac12\sigma_a$, so $-itn \cdot J = tn \cdot T$ and $D^{1/2}(g) = g$: @eq-lrep-wigner is
@eq-euler-matrix, with $d^{1/2}(\theta) = e^{\theta T_1}$ of @eq-exp-t3-t1 and, for instance, $D^{1/2}_{\frac12\frac12} =
e^{-i\varphi/2}\cos\frac\theta2\,e^{-i\psi/2}$. The middle rotation is about the first axis because the Euler angles of
this book use $T_1$; most tables of $d^j$ use $e^{-i\theta J_2}$, and since $e^{-i\theta J_2} = e^{-i\frac\pi2J_3}e^{-i
\theta J_1}e^{i\frac\pi2J_3}$ the two differ by phases, $d^j_{m'm} = i^{m' - m}(e^{-i\theta J_2})_{m'm}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For spin one the rotation matrices must be the rotations of space in disguise, since the spin-one representation is
the vector representation. The second example finds the basis that removes the disguise [@boudreau2018applied, Sec.
14.4.1].

::: {#exm-lrep-dj-spherical-basis}
#### Spin one and the spherical basis

In the vector representation $J_a = iL_a$ (@exm-lg-so3-angular-momentum), and the vectors $e_{+1} = -(e_1 + ie_2)/
\sqrt2$, $e_0 = e_3$, $e_{-1} = (e_1 - ie_2)/\sqrt2$ satisfy $J_3e_m = me_m$, $J_+e_{-1} = \sqrt2\,e_0$ and $J_+e_0 =
\sqrt2\,e_{+1}$, the normalisation of @exr-lrep-spinj-matrices: they are the weight basis. Hence the matrix of the
rotation $e^{tn \cdot L}$ in this basis is $D^1(e^{tn \cdot T})$. A vector $x = \sum_mx^me_m$ has the spherical components
$x^{\pm1} = \mp(x_1 \mp ix_2)/\sqrt2$ and $x^0 = x_3$; multiplying $(x^{+1}, x^0, x^{-1})$ by $D^1$ and reading the
Cartesian components off again rotates $x$, which is how a program that only knows the $D^j$ rotates ordinary vectors.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Computing $e^{-itn \cdot J}$ from its power series is wasteful when the eigenvalues of the exponent are known. The third
example uses them, as numerical libraries do [@boudreau2018applied, eq. 14.3].

::: {#exm-lrep-dj-diagonalise}
#### Exponentiating by diagonalisation

For $h \in SU(2)$ whose rotation $\operatorname{Ad}(h)$ carries $e_3$ to the unit vector $n$, $D^j(h)J_3D^j(h)^{-1} = n
\cdot J$ (the spin-$j$ form of @exm-lg-angvel-space-body, @exr-lrep-dj-spin-vector). So $n \cdot J$ has the eigenvalues
$j, j - 1, \dots, -j$, evenly spaced and never degenerate, and with $U = D^j(h)$, $D^j(e^{tn \cdot T}) = U\operatorname{diag}
(e^{-ijt}, \dots, e^{ijt})U^\dagger$: the exponential of a diagonal matrix is taken entry by entry. At $t = 2\pi$ every
entry is $e^{\mp 2\pi im} = (-1)^{2j}$, so $D^j(e^{2\pi n \cdot T}) = (-1)^{2j}$, the sign of @exm-spin-half-integer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Rotating a state of definite weight mixes in all the other weights. The first exercise follows the probabilities and
the amplitudes as the angle of rotation grows [@boudreau2018applied, Exercise 14.3].

::: {#exr-lrep-dj-spin32}
#### A rotated spin-$\tfrac32$ state

Rotate the highest-weight state $v_{3/2}$ of spin $\frac32$ by $\theta$ about the first axis. With Sage, compute the
amplitudes $\langle v_m, d^{3/2}(\theta)v_{3/2}\rangle$ and show that the probabilities of the four weights are
$\binom{3}{3/2 - m}\cos^{3 + 2m}\frac\theta2\,\sin^{3 - 2m}\frac\theta2$. Which quantities have period $2\pi$ in $\theta$
and which only $4\pi$? Repeat for spin $2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The state $v_j$ is the product of $2j$ spin-up states of spin one-half, the highest weight of $(\frac12)^{\otimes 2j}$
(@def-clebsch-gordan), and each factor is turned into $\cos\frac\theta2\,{\uparrow} - i\sin\frac\theta2\,{\downarrow}$
by $e^{\theta T_1}$. Expanding the product and projecting on the normalised symmetric state with $j + m$ factors up gives
the amplitude $\binom{2j}{j - m}^{1/2}\cos^{j + m}\frac\theta2\,(-i\sin\frac\theta2)^{j - m}$, so the probabilities form
a binomial distribution with $p = \cos^2\frac\theta2$. The probabilities have period $2\pi$; for half-integer $j$ the
amplitudes change sign at $\theta = 2\pi$ and return at $4\pi$, while for spin $2$ they have period $2\pi$:

{{< sage exr-lrep-dj-spin32 >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For integer spin the rotation matrices contain the spherical harmonics. The second exercise finds them in the column of
weight zero, a convenient way of computing harmonics numerically [@boudreau2018applied, Exercise 14.1].

::: {#exr-lrep-dj-harmonics}
#### Spherical harmonics from rotation matrices

For integer $l$ show that the column $m = 0$ of $D^l(\varphi, \theta, \psi)$ does not depend on $\psi$, and check with
Sage for $l \leq 3$ that $\sqrt{(2l + 1)/(4\pi)}\,\overline{D^l_{m0}(\varphi, \theta, \psi)} = Y_{lm}(\theta, \varphi -
\frac\pi2)$, with the Condon-Shortley phases, where $(\theta, \varphi - \frac\pi2)$ are the spherical angles of the axis
$Re_3$ (@exr-lg-ek-axis).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{-i\psi J_3}v_0 = v_0$, so the column is $e^{-im\varphi}d^l_{m0}(\theta)$, independent of $\psi$: it is a function of
the point $Re_3$ of the sphere alone, and by $D^l(gh) = D^l(g)D^l(h)$ the $2l + 1$ functions transform among themselves
in the spin-$l$ representation, as the harmonics of @exm-spin-harmonics do. Sage confirms that, with the normalisation
$\sqrt{(2l + 1)/(4\pi)}$, they are exactly the harmonics at $Re_3$:

{{< sage exr-lrep-dj-harmonics >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The expectation values of the spin matrices form a vector that turns with the state. The third exercise proves this
for spin one-half and finds the direction of every spin state [@boudreau2018applied, eq. 14.5].

::: {#exr-lrep-dj-spin-vector}
#### The spin vector of a state

For a unit vector $\xi \in \mathbb{C}^2$ let $s(\xi) = \xi^\dagger J\xi$ with $J = \frac12\sigma$. Show that $g^\dagger
\sigma_ag = R_{ab}\sigma_b$ with $R = \operatorname{Ad}(g)$, hence $s(g\xi) = Rs(\xi)$, and that $\xi = (\cos\frac\beta2,
e^{i\alpha}\sin\frac\beta2)$ has $s = \frac12(\sin\beta\cos\alpha, \sin\beta\sin\alpha, \cos\beta)$, so that every state
of spin one-half points in a definite direction, with $|s| = \frac12$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By definition of the adjoint matrix, $g\sigma_bg^\dagger = R_{cb}\sigma_c$; multiplying by $R_{ab}$, summing over $b$ and
using $RR^{\mathsf{T}} = 1$ gives $\sigma_a = R_{ab}\,g\sigma_bg^\dagger$, that is $g^\dagger\sigma_ag = R_{ab}\sigma_b$. Then
$s_a(g\xi) = \xi^\dagger g^\dagger J_ag\xi = R_{ab}s_b(\xi)$. For the given $\xi$, $\xi^\dagger\sigma_3\xi = \cos^2\frac\beta2 -
\sin^2\frac\beta2 = \cos\beta$ and $\xi^\dagger(\sigma_1 + i\sigma_2)\xi = 2\cos\frac\beta2\sin\frac\beta2\,e^{i\alpha} =
\sin\beta\,e^{i\alpha}$, which gives $s$. Every unit vector of $\mathbb{C}^2$ is of this form up to a phase, which does not
change $s$; the same identity with $D^j$ in place of $g$ makes $\langle J\rangle$ a vector for every spin.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

Products of representations appear whenever two systems are combined, for instance two particles with spin. The
definition below states how such a product splits into spins, and the weights explain why.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-clebsch-gordan}
#### Clebsch-Gordan decomposition

The tensor product of two representations (@def-direct-sum-rep) decomposes into irreducibles; for
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$,
$$
j_1 \otimes j_2 = (j_1 + j_2) \oplus (j_1 + j_2 - 1) \oplus \dots \oplus |j_1 - j_2| ,
$$ {#eq-clebsch-gordan}
read off from the weights: the weights of the product are all sums $m_1 + m_2$, and peeling off the highest weight
and its string repeatedly gives the list. Sage's `WeylCharacterRing` performs this decomposition
(@prp-clebsch-sage).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The most famous instance combines two spin-$\tfrac12$ particles. Its four states split into the triplet and the
singlet of atomic physics.

::: {#exm-clebsch-spinors}
#### $\tfrac12 \otimes \tfrac12 = 1 \oplus 0$

Two spinors have weights $\pm\tfrac12 \pm \tfrac12 = 1, 0, 0, -1$: a triplet (the symmetric combinations) and a
singlet (the antisymmetric one): two spin-$\tfrac12$ particles combine to spin $1$ or spin $0$.
:::

Two vectors give nine states, and the weights now have multiplicities up to three. Peeling off strings of weights
produces three spins, which are the symmetric traceless, antisymmetric and trace parts of a two-index tensor.

::: {#exm-clebsch-vectors}
#### $1 \otimes 1 = 2 \oplus 1 \oplus 0$

Two vectors have weights $\{1, 0, -1\} + \{1, 0, -1\}$ with multiplicities $1, 2, 3, 2, 1$ (@fig-su2-weights):
spin $2$ (the symmetric traceless tensors), spin $1$ (the antisymmetric tensors, $\mathbb{R}^3 \wedge \mathbb{R}^3
\cong \mathbb{R}^3$, the adjoint again) and spin $0$ (the trace), the decomposition $3 \otimes 3 = 5 \oplus 3 \oplus
1$ of @exm-tensor-spins. In CSDR the scalars live in tensor products of this kind, and the Higgs potential is built
from the invariant (spin $0$) parts.
:::

Combining an integer and a half-integer spin gives only half-integer spins, since every weight of the product is a
half-integer. The orbital angular momentum $1$ of an electron combined with its spin is the standard example.

::: {#exm-clebsch-mixed}
#### $1 \otimes \tfrac12 = \tfrac32 \oplus \tfrac12$

Weights $\{1, 0, -1\} + \{\pm\tfrac12\} = \tfrac32, \tfrac12, \tfrac12, -\tfrac12, -\tfrac12, -\tfrac32$: the string of
spin $\tfrac32$ leaves one copy of $\pm\tfrac12$ (@exr-clebsch); likewise $\tfrac32 \otimes \tfrac12 = 2 \oplus 1$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise carries out the peeling procedure of the definition by hand. It is the computation behind
@exm-clebsch-mixed, done once in full.

::: {#exr-clebsch}
#### A tensor product by hand

Decompose $1 \otimes \tfrac12$ and $\tfrac32 \otimes \tfrac12$ of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ from their weights.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$1 \otimes \tfrac12$ has weights $\{1, 0, -1\} + \{\pm\tfrac12\} = \tfrac32, \tfrac12, \tfrac12, -\tfrac12, -\tfrac12, -
\tfrac32$: the string $\tfrac32, \dots, -\tfrac32$ (spin $\tfrac32$) leaves $\tfrac12, -\tfrac12$ (spin
$\tfrac12$), so $1 \otimes \tfrac12 = \tfrac32 \oplus \tfrac12$. Likewise $\tfrac32 \otimes \tfrac12 = 2 \oplus 1$, in
agreement with @eq-clebsch-gordan.
:::

A decomposition must preserve dimensions, and this gives a quick consistency check of @eq-clebsch-gordan. The second
exercise performs the check in general, as a sum of an arithmetic progression.

::: {#exr-lrep-cg-dimension}
#### Counting dimensions

Show that $\sum_{J = |j_1 - j_2|}^{j_1 + j_2}(2J + 1) = (2j_1 + 1)(2j_2 + 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Take $j_1 \geq j_2$ and write $J = j_1 - j_2 + k$, $k = 0, \dots, 2j_2$. Then $\sum_k(2j_1 - 2j_2 + 1 + 2k) = (2j_2 +
1)(2j_1 - 2j_2 + 1) + 2j_2(2j_2 + 1) = (2j_2 + 1)(2j_1 + 1)$. For example $1 \otimes 1$: $5 + 3 + 1 = 9$, and
$\tfrac32 \otimes \tfrac12$: $5 + 3 = 8$.
:::

Products of three or more spins are decomposed by applying the rule repeatedly, and a spin can then occur more than
once. The third exercise counts the multiplicities and the invariants, with Sage as a check.

::: {#exr-lrep-cg-three-spinors}
#### Three and four spins

Decompose $\tfrac12 \otimes \tfrac12 \otimes \tfrac12$, $1 \otimes 1 \otimes 1$ and $\tfrac12^{\otimes 4}$ by applying
@eq-clebsch-gordan twice or three times, count the singlets, and identify the singlet of $1 \otimes 1 \otimes 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tfrac12 \otimes \tfrac12 \otimes \tfrac12 = (1 \oplus 0) \otimes \tfrac12 = \tfrac32 \oplus \tfrac12 \oplus \tfrac12$,
with no singlet (a half-integer total cannot be $0$). $1 \otimes 1 \otimes 1 = (2 \oplus 1 \oplus 0) \otimes 1 = (3
\oplus 2 \oplus 1) \oplus (2 \oplus 1 \oplus 0) \oplus 1 = 3 \oplus 2 \cdot 2 \oplus 3 \cdot 1 \oplus 0$; its single
singlet is the triple product $\epsilon_{abc}u_av_bw_c$ of three vectors. $\tfrac12^{\otimes 4} = (1 \oplus 0)
\otimes (1 \oplus 0) = 2 \oplus 3 \cdot 1 \oplus 2 \cdot 0$, with two singlets. In Sage, `A1(n)` is spin $n/2$:

{{< sage exr-lrep-cg-three-spinors >}}
:::
::::

The decompositions above were obtained by hand from the weights. The proposition records the ones used later,
together with the weights of the spin-$j$ representation.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-clebsch-sage}
#### Clebsch-Gordan decompositions

$\tfrac12 \otimes \tfrac12 = 1 \oplus 0$ and $1 \otimes 1 = 2 \oplus 1 \oplus 0$, and spin $j$ has the $2j + 1$ weights
$j, \dots, -j$ each once.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation: `WeylCharacterRing` in `figures/su2_weights.sage` and @exr-su2-clebsch.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The character ring identifies the summands, but not the vectors that span them. For two spinors the vectors are easy
to write down, and the ladder operators check which combination belongs to which spin.

::: {#exm-lrep-cg-singlet}
#### The triplet and the singlet

On $\tfrac12 \otimes \tfrac12$ the ladder operators act as $J_\pm \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes J_\pm$. Starting from the
highest vector ${\uparrow\uparrow}$, $J_-$ gives ${\uparrow\downarrow} + {\downarrow\uparrow}$ and then
$2\,{\downarrow\downarrow}$: the triplet is symmetric. The orthogonal vector ${\uparrow\downarrow} -
{\downarrow\uparrow}$ is killed by $J_+$ (both terms give ${\uparrow\uparrow}$ with opposite signs) and by $J_-$: it
is the singlet, and it is antisymmetric.
:::

The peeling procedure can be watched on the weight multiplicities alone. The example does this for $1 \otimes 1$, the
right panel of @fig-su2-weights.

::: {#exm-lrep-cg-peeling}
#### Peeling the weights of $1 \otimes 1$

The multiplicities of the weights $2, 1, 0, -1, -2$ are $1, 2, 3, 2, 1$. The highest weight $2$ starts a string of
spin $2$ with multiplicities $1, 1, 1, 1, 1$; subtracting leaves $0, 1, 2, 1, 0$, whose highest weight $1$ starts a
spin-$1$ string; subtracting $0, 1, 1, 1, 0$ leaves $0, 0, 1, 0, 0$, a spin $0$. This is the algorithm that the
character ring runs in @prp-clebsch-sage.
:::

The examples so far suggest that symmetry under exchange of the two factors separates the summands. For two copies
of the same spin this is a general rule, illustrated here for spins $\tfrac12$ and $1$.

::: {#exm-lrep-cg-symmetry}
#### Symmetric and antisymmetric parts

For $j \otimes j$ the summands alternate in symmetry, starting with the symmetric spin $2j$: $\operatorname{Sym}^2(\tfrac12)
= 1$ and $\Lambda^2(\tfrac12) = 0$ (@exm-lrep-cg-singlet), while $\operatorname{Sym}^2(1) = 2 \oplus 0$, of dimension
$6$, and $\Lambda^2(1) = 1$, of dimension $3$ (@exm-clebsch-vectors). The dimensions $j(2j + 1)$ of $\Lambda^2$ and
$(j + 1)(2j + 1)$ of $\operatorname{Sym}^2$ agree with these counts.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise repeats the computation behind the proposition with Sage, including the weights of $1 \otimes 1$
and the dimension formula. It is the reference computation for the summary table at the end of the chapter.

::: {#exr-su2-clebsch}
#### Tensor products with the Weyl character ring

With Sage's `WeylCharacterRing("A1")`, decompose $\tfrac12 \otimes \tfrac12$, $1 \otimes 1$, $1 \otimes \tfrac12$ and
$\tfrac32 \otimes \tfrac12$, list the weights of $1 \otimes 1$ with multiplicities, and check $\dim(\text{spin } j) =
2j + 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In coroot style `A1((n,))` is the irreducible character of spin $n/2$ and products are decomposed automatically:

{{< sage exr-su2-clebsch >}}
:::

The second exercise finds the singlet of $1 \otimes 1$ as an explicit vector, by solving $J_+w = 0$ on the zero-weight
space. The same linear algebra recovers the singlet of two spinors from @exm-lrep-cg-singlet.

::: {#exr-lrep-cg-highest-vector}
#### The singlet as a kernel

With the spin-$j$ matrices of @exr-lrep-spinj-matrices, find the vectors of weight $0$ in $j \otimes j$ that are
killed by $J_+ \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes J_+$, for $j = \tfrac12$ and $j = 1$. Explain why their number is the number of
spin-$0$ summands.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each irreducible summand contains exactly one highest-weight vector, so the vectors of weight $\mu$ killed by $J_+$
count the summands of spin $\mu$. For $j = 1$, with $J_+|{-1}\rangle = \sqrt2|0\rangle$ and $J_+|0\rangle =
\sqrt2|1\rangle$, applying $J_+$ to $a|1\rangle|{-1}\rangle + b|0\rangle|0\rangle + c|{-1}\rangle|1\rangle$ gives
$\sqrt2(a + b)|1\rangle|0\rangle + \sqrt2(b + c)|0\rangle|1\rangle$, so $(a, b, c) \propto (1, -1, 1)$: one singlet.
For $j = \tfrac12$ the singlet is $|\tfrac12\rangle|{-\tfrac12}\rangle - |{-\tfrac12}\rangle|\tfrac12\rangle$:

{{< sage exr-lrep-cg-highest-vector >}}
:::

The third exercise proves @eq-clebsch-gordan in general by peeling weights, and lets Sage confirm it for all spins up
to $3$. It generalises @exm-lrep-cg-peeling.

::: {#exr-lrep-cg-general}
#### The Clebsch-Gordan series in general

Show that for $j_1 \geq j_2$ the weight $m$ of $j_1 \otimes j_2$ has multiplicity $j_1 + j_2 - |m| + 1$ for $|m| \geq
j_1 - j_2$ and $2j_2 + 1$ for $|m| \leq j_1 - j_2$, and deduce @eq-clebsch-gordan. Check it with Sage for $j_1, j_2
\leq 3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The multiplicity of $m$ is the number of pairs $(m_1, m_2)$ with $m_1 + m_2 = m$, $|m_1| \leq j_1$, $|m_2| \leq j_2$:
$m_2$ ranges over $[\max(-j_2, m - j_1), \min(j_2, m + j_1)]$, which gives the two formulas. The multiplicities
therefore increase by one at each step from $m = j_1 + j_2$ down to $m = j_1 - j_2$ and are constant below. Peeling
off strings, each step down from the top starts one new string, at $J = j_1 + j_2, j_1 + j_2 - 1, \dots, j_1 - j_2$,
and nothing starts below $j_1 - j_2$: this is @eq-clebsch-gordan.

{{< sage exr-lrep-cg-general >}}
:::
::::

### Roots and su(3) {#sec-roots-su3}

With a Cartan subalgebra of rank two the weights become points in a plane, the roots a hexagon, and the whole
Lie algebra is encoded in a $2 \times 2$ integer matrix. $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ is the gauge algebra of the strong
interaction and the smallest simple Lie algebra of rank two, and this section works its roots, weights and Cartan
matrix explicitly, with Sage's root-system module alongside.

#### The Gell-Mann basis

Computations in $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ need a basis, and the standard one extends the Pauli matrices to three
dimensions. The definition fixes the eight matrices and their normalisation, which the rest of the section uses
throughout.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gell-mann}
#### Gell-Mann basis

$\mathfrak{su}(3)$ is the eight-dimensional algebra of traceless anti-Hermitian $3 \times 3$ matrices, with
basis $T_A = -\tfrac{i}{2}\lambda_A$ built from the **Gell-Mann matrices**
$$
\begin{gathered}
\lambda_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0&1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \
\lambda_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0&-i&0\\i&0&0\\0&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \
\lambda_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1&0&0\\0&-1&0\\0&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \
\lambda_4 = \begin{pmatrix} 0&0&1\\0&0&0\\1&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \\
\lambda_5 = \begin{pmatrix} 0&0&-i\\0&0&0\\i&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \
\lambda_6 = \begin{pmatrix} 0&0&0\\0&0&1\\0&1&0 \end{pmatrix}, \
\lambda_7 = \begin{pmatrix} 0&0&0\\0&0&-i\\0&i&0 \end{pmatrix}, \
\lambda_8 = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}\begin{pmatrix} 1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&-2 \end{pmatrix},
\end{gathered}
$$ {#eq-gell-mann}
normalised by $\operatorname{tr}(\lambda_A\lambda_B) = 2\delta_{AB}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The Gell-Mann matrices are `KaluzaKlein.gellMann`.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first three Gell-Mann matrices are the Pauli matrices placed in the upper left corner. They therefore close into
a copy of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, and two more copies sit in the other corners.

::: {#exm-gell-mann-su2}
#### The $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ subalgebra

$\lambda_{1, 2, 3}$ are the Pauli matrices in the upper block and span an $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ subalgebra, with
$[\lambda_1, \lambda_2] = 2i\lambda_3$ and cyclic permutations (@prp-branching-su3 of @sec-branching); $\lambda_{4, 5}$
and $\lambda_{6, 7}$ with the appropriate diagonal matrices span two further $\mathfrak{su}(2)$'s.
:::

Two of the eight matrices are diagonal, and diagonal matrices commute. They form the Cartan subalgebra of
@exm-cartan-su3 in the Gell-Mann normalisation.

::: {#exm-gell-mann-cartan}
#### The Cartan subalgebra

$\lambda_3$ and $\lambda_8$ are the diagonal traceless matrices, they commute, and no other generator commutes
with both: the Cartan subalgebra is $\operatorname{span}(\lambda_3, \lambda_8)$, rank $2$ (@def-cartan-subalgebra).
:::

The brackets of the Gell-Mann matrices define structure constants, the analogue of $\epsilon_{abc}$ for
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$. Only nine of them are independent and non-zero, and the example lists them.

::: {#exm-gell-mann-structure}
#### Structure constants

$[\lambda_A, \lambda_B] = 2if_{ABC}\lambda_C$ with totally antisymmetric $f_{ABC}$: $f_{123} = 1$, $f_{147} = f_{246} =
f_{257} = f_{345} = \tfrac12$, $f_{156} = f_{367} = -\tfrac12$, $f_{458} = f_{678} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$
(@exr-su3-structure); $f_{458} \neq 0$ is what makes $SU(3)/U(1) \times U(1)$ a non-symmetric coset
(@sec-reductive).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the properties of the basis claimed in the definition. The normalisation of the
anti-Hermitian generators is the one fixed in the conventions of the book.

::: {#exr-lrep-gm-trace}
#### Normalisation of the Gell-Mann basis

Check that the $\lambda_A$ are Hermitian and traceless with $\operatorname{tr}(\lambda_A\lambda_B) = 2\delta_{AB}$, and
deduce that the $T_A = -\tfrac{i}{2}\lambda_A$ are anti-Hermitian with $\operatorname{tr}(T_AT_B) = -
\tfrac12\delta_{AB}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each $\lambda_A$ has a Pauli matrix (or a real diagonal matrix) in a block and zeros elsewhere, so it is Hermitian and
traceless; two different $\lambda_A$ either occupy different entries or are orthogonal diagonal matrices, and each
squares to a matrix of trace $2$ ($\lambda_8^2 = \tfrac13\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, 4)$). Then $T_A^\dagger =
\tfrac{i}{2}\lambda_A = -T_A$ and $\operatorname{tr}(T_AT_B) = -\tfrac14\operatorname{tr}(\lambda_A\lambda_B) =
-\tfrac12\delta_{AB}$:

{{< sage exr-lrep-gm-trace >}}
:::

The second exercise makes the two further copies of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ of @exm-gell-mann-su2 explicit. The diagonal
matrix that completes each copy explains why $\lambda_8$ appears in the brackets of $\lambda_4$ and $\lambda_5$.

::: {#exr-lrep-gm-su2s}
#### Three copies of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$

Show that $\lambda_4, \lambda_5$ and $\tfrac12(\lambda_3 + \sqrt3\lambda_8)$ satisfy the Pauli relations $[\sigma_1,
\sigma_2] = 2i\sigma_3$ (and cyclic), and likewise $\lambda_6, \lambda_7$ and $\tfrac12(-\lambda_3 + \sqrt3\lambda_8)$.
Read off $f_{453}$ and $f_{458}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\lambda_4$ and $\lambda_5$ are $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ in rows and columns $1, 3$, and $\sigma_3$ in that block is
$\operatorname{diag}(1, 0, -1) = \tfrac12(\lambda_3 + \sqrt3\lambda_8)$, since $\lambda_3 + \sqrt3\lambda_8 =
\operatorname{diag}(2, 0, -2)$. Matrices supported in one block multiply as in that block, so the Pauli relations
hold. Similarly $\lambda_6, \lambda_7$ act in rows $2, 3$ with $\sigma_3 = \operatorname{diag}(0, 1, -1) =
\tfrac12(-\lambda_3 + \sqrt3\lambda_8)$. From $[\lambda_4, \lambda_5] = 2i \cdot \tfrac12(\lambda_3 + \sqrt3\lambda_8)$,
$f_{453} = \tfrac12$ and $f_{458} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, in agreement with $f_{345} = \tfrac12$ and @exm-gell-mann-structure.
:::

The third exercise computes all structure constants by machine and sorts them by the Cartan subalgebra. The sorting
anticipates the root decomposition defined next.

::: {#exr-su3-structure}
#### Structure constants of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$

Compute the structure constants $f_{ABC}$ in the Gell-Mann basis and split them according to the decomposition
$\mathfrak{su}(3) = \mathfrak{r} \oplus \mathfrak{k}$ with $\mathfrak{r} = \operatorname{span}(\lambda_3, \lambda_8)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-su3-structure >}}

The non-zero constants with all three indices in $\mathfrak{k}$ ($f_{147}$, $f_{156}$, $f_{246}$, $f_{257}$) are
what make the coset $SU(3)/U(1) \times U(1)$ non-symmetric (@sec-reductive).
:::
::::

#### Roots and weights of su(3)

The ladder operators of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ were eigenvectors of $\operatorname{ad}_{J_3}$. With a Cartan subalgebra of
higher rank the same idea gives a family of simultaneous eigenvectors, and their eigenvalue vectors are the roots.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-root}
#### Root

The **roots** of $\mathfrak{g}$ are the non-zero weights of the adjoint representation: the eigenvalue vectors
$\alpha$ of $\operatorname{ad}_{H_1}, \dots, \operatorname{ad}_{H_r}$ on common eigenvectors $E_\alpha \in
\mathfrak{g} \otimes \mathbb{C}$, the **root vectors**, with $[H_i, E_\alpha] = \alpha_iE_\alpha$. The roots come
in pairs $\pm\alpha$, each of multiplicity one, and $\mathfrak{g} \otimes \mathbb{C} = \mathfrak{h} \oplus
\bigoplus_\alpha \mathbb{C}E_\alpha$ (the **root decomposition**).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ the root decomposition is the splitting into $J_3$ and the two ladder operators. The two roots
are the numbers $\pm 1$.

::: {#exm-root-su2}
#### $\mathfrak{su}(2)$

The roots are $\pm 1$ with root vectors $J_\pm$ (@exm-ladder-adjoint): $\mathfrak{su}(2) \otimes \mathbb{C} =
\mathbb{C}J_3 \oplus \mathbb{C}J_+ \oplus \mathbb{C}J_-$.
:::

For $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ the root vectors are the ladder operators of the three copies of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$. Their
eigenvalues under the two diagonal Gell-Mann matrices are six vectors in a plane.

::: {#exm-root-su3}
#### The hexagon of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$

With $H = (\lambda_3, \lambda_8)$ the combinations $\lambda_1 \pm i\lambda_2$, $\lambda_4 \pm i\lambda_5$, $\lambda_6 \pm
i\lambda_7$ are eigenvectors of $\operatorname{ad}_{\lambda_3}$ and $\operatorname{ad}_{\lambda_8}$ with eigenvalue
pairs $\pm(2, 0)$, $\pm(1, \sqrt3)$, $\pm(-1, \sqrt3)$ (@prp-coset-su3 of @sec-reductive, @exr-su3-roots): the
vertices of a regular hexagon (@fig-su3-weights), and $\lambda_3, \lambda_8$ themselves have weight $(0, 0)$ with
multiplicity two.
:::

Sage knows the root systems of all simple Lie algebras by their type. In its notation $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ is type
$A_2$, and the roots are expressed in terms of two simple roots.

::: {#exm-root-sage}
#### Sage's root system

`RootSystem(["A", 2])` lists the simple roots $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$, the positive roots $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_1 +
\alpha_2$ and all six roots (@exr-su3-cartan); `WeylCharacterRing("A2")` gives the weights of any representation
with multiplicities, the adjoint having the zero weight twice.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![In one plane: the weights of the fundamental representation $\mathbf{3}$ of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ (blue squares,
an equilateral triangle) and the six roots (red arrows, a regular hexagon) with the double zero weight at the
origin, in the $(\lambda_3, \lambda_8)$-eigenvalue plane. Generated by
`figures/su3_weights.sage`.](figures/su3_weights.svg){#fig-su3-weights width=50%}

{{< interactive su3_weights 460 >}}

The interactive version shows the weight diagrams of $\mathbf{3}$, $\bar{\mathbf{3}}$, the adjoint $\mathbf{8}$ and the
decuplet $\mathbf{10}$ in the same plane, computed with Sage's `WeylCharacterRing`. Each representation can be switched
on and off in the legend, and hovering a weight shows its coordinates and its multiplicity.

The first exercise derives the roots from the Gell-Mann matrices and computes the Cartan matrix from them. It is the
computation behind @exm-root-su3, carried out symbolically in Sage.

::: {#exr-su3-roots}
#### Roots from the Gell-Mann matrices

Compute the $(\operatorname{ad}_{\lambda_3}, \operatorname{ad}_{\lambda_8})$ eigenvalues of the six combinations
$\lambda_1 \pm i\lambda_2$, $\lambda_4 \pm i\lambda_5$, $\lambda_6 \pm i\lambda_7$, choose simple roots and compute the
Cartan matrix, and read off the branching of @sec-branching.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The eigenvalues are $\pm(2,0)$, $\pm(1,\sqrt3)$, $\pm(-1,\sqrt3)$. With $\alpha_1 = (2, 0)$ and
$\alpha_2 = (-1, \sqrt3)$, $\alpha_1 \cdot \alpha_1 = \alpha_2 \cdot \alpha_2 = 4$ and $\alpha_1 \cdot \alpha_2 = -2$,
so $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. In Sage:

{{< sage exr-su3-roots >}}
:::

The definition claims that the roots come in pairs $\pm\alpha$. The second exercise proves this with Hermitian
conjugation, using that the $H_i$ are Hermitian matrices with real eigenvalues.

::: {#exr-lrep-root-pairs}
#### Roots come in pairs

Let the $H_i$ be Hermitian matrices (as $\lambda_3, \lambda_8$ are) and $[H_i, E] = \alpha_iE$ with $E \neq 0$. Show
that the $\alpha_i$ are real and that $[H_i, E^\dagger] = -\alpha_iE^\dagger$. Check this on $E = \lambda_1 + i\lambda_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With the inner product $\langle X, Y\rangle = \operatorname{tr}(X^\dagger Y)$ on matrices, $\operatorname{ad}_{H_i}$ is
Hermitian: $\operatorname{tr}(X^\dagger[H, Y]) = \operatorname{tr}([H, X]^\dagger Y)$ for $H = H^\dagger$. So its
eigenvalues $\alpha_i$ are real. Taking the adjoint of $[H_i, E] = \alpha_iE$ gives $[E^\dagger, H_i] =
\alpha_iE^\dagger$, that is $[H_i, E^\dagger] = -\alpha_iE^\dagger$. For $E = \lambda_1 + i\lambda_2 = 2E_{12}$ (root
$(2, 0)$), $E^\dagger = \lambda_1 - i\lambda_2 = 2E_{21}$, with root $(-2, 0)$.
:::

All the unitary algebras behave like $\mathfrak{su}(3)$: the root vectors are the off-diagonal matrix units. The third
exercise finds the twelve roots of $\mathfrak{su}(4)$ this way and compares them with Sage's root system of type
$A_3$.

::: {#exr-lrep-root-sun}
#### The roots of $\mathfrak{su}(n)$

For $H = \operatorname{diag}(h_1, \dots, h_n)$ show that $[H, E_{ij}] = (h_i - h_j)E_{ij}$ for the matrix units
$E_{ij}$, so that the roots of $\mathfrak{su}(n)$ are $e_i - e_j$, $i \neq j$. Count them, check $\dim\mathfrak{su}(n) =
\text{rank} + \#\text{roots}$, and compare with Sage for $n = 4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(HE_{ij})_{kl} = h_k\delta_{ki}\delta_{jl}$ and $(E_{ij}H)_{kl} = \delta_{ki}\delta_{jl}h_l$, so $[H, E_{ij}] = (h_i -
h_j)E_{ij}$: the root of $E_{ij}$ is the functional $e_i - e_j$. There are $n(n - 1)$ ordered pairs, and $(n - 1) +
n(n - 1) = n^2 - 1 = \dim\mathfrak{su}(n)$. For $n = 3$, $E_{12}, E_{13}, E_{23}$ are $\tfrac12(\lambda_1 +
i\lambda_2)$, $\tfrac12(\lambda_4 + i\lambda_5)$, $\tfrac12(\lambda_6 + i\lambda_7)$:

{{< sage exr-lrep-root-sun >}}
:::
::::

The weights of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ were ordered on a line, with a highest one at the top. In a plane there is no
natural order, so we choose a direction, and the definition below uses it to single out one weight of each
representation.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-highest-weight}
#### Highest weight

Choosing a direction in the weight space (a linear functional that vanishes on no root) splits the roots into
**positive** and **negative** ones; the **highest weight** of a representation is its weight with the largest
value, and an irreducible representation is determined by its highest weight. The highest weights are the
non-negative integer combinations of the **fundamental weights**, as many as the rank.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The fundamental representation of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ has three weights, read off from the diagonal entries of
$\lambda_3$ and $\lambda_8$. The highest of them is the first fundamental weight.

::: {#exm-highest-fundamental}
#### The fundamental representation $\mathbf{3}$

On $\mathbb{C}^3$ the weights are the diagonal entries of $(\lambda_3, \lambda_8)$: $(1, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3})$, $(-1,
\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3})$, $(0, -\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3})$, the corners of an equilateral triangle (@fig-su3-weights),
traditionally named $u, d, s$; with the direction of @exm-cartan-su3-matrix the highest weight is $(1,
\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3})$, the first fundamental weight.
:::

The adjoint representation has the roots as its non-zero weights, so its highest weight is the highest root. Sage
labels representations by the coefficients of their highest weights in the fundamental weights.

::: {#exm-highest-adjoint}
#### The adjoint $\mathbf{8}$

The highest weight of the adjoint is the highest root $(1, \sqrt3) = \alpha_1 + \alpha_2$, the sum of the two
fundamental weights; Sage writes it `A2(1,1)` (@exr-su3-cartan). The conjugate $\bar{\mathbf{3}}$ has highest
weight `A2(0,1)` and weights the negatives of those of $\mathbf{3}$, and $\mathbf{3} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{3}} =
\mathbf{8} \oplus \mathbf{1}$ (@exr-branching-levi).
:::

In rank one the general theory reduces to the spin-$j$ construction of the previous section. The example translates
between the two languages, where a highest weight is a single number.

::: {#exm-highest-su2}
#### Spin $j$ again

For $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ the fundamental weight is $\tfrac12$, the highest weights are $j = \tfrac12 n$, and the
highest-weight construction of @def-spin-j is the rank-one case of the general theory.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise fixes an explicit direction in the weight plane and finds the highest weights of the two
three-dimensional representations. Together they give the two fundamental weights.

::: {#exr-lrep-hw-3bar}
#### The fundamental weights of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$

Use the functional $\ell(\mu) = \mu_2 + \varepsilon\mu_1$ with small $\varepsilon > 0$. Check that it makes $(2, 0)$,
$(1, \sqrt3)$, $(-1, \sqrt3)$ positive, find the highest weights $\omega_1$ of $\mathbf{3}$ and $\omega_2$ of
$\bar{\mathbf{3}}$ (@exr-lrep-weight-su3-fund), and check that $\omega_1 + \omega_2$ is the highest root.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\ell(2, 0) = 2\varepsilon$, $\ell(1, \sqrt3) = \sqrt3 + \varepsilon$ and $\ell(-1, \sqrt3) = \sqrt3 - \varepsilon$ are
positive for $0 < \varepsilon < \sqrt3$. Among the weights of $\mathbf{3}$, $\ell$ is largest on $\omega_1 = (1,
\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3})$ (larger than $(-1, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3})$ by $2\varepsilon$), and among those of $\bar{\mathbf{3}}$ on
$\omega_2 = (0, \tfrac{2}{\sqrt3})$. Then $\omega_1 + \omega_2 = (1, \tfrac{3}{\sqrt3}) = (1, \sqrt3)$, the root on
which $\ell$ is largest, in agreement with @exm-highest-adjoint.
:::

The second exercise decomposes $\mathbf{3} \otimes \mathbf{3}$ using only weights. The antisymmetric part turns out to
be the conjugate representation, a fact special to $\mathfrak{su}(3)$.

::: {#exr-lrep-hw-6}
#### $\mathbf{3} \otimes \mathbf{3} = \mathbf{6} \oplus \bar{\mathbf{3}}$

Show that the weights of $\Lambda^2\mathbf{3}$ are the negatives of the weights of $\mathbf{3}$, so that
$\Lambda^2\mathbf{3} \cong \bar{\mathbf{3}}$, and that $\operatorname{Sym}^2\mathbf{3}$ has the six weights $w_a + w_b$,
$a \leq b$, with highest weight $2\omega_1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The weights $w_u, w_d, w_s$ of $\mathbf{3}$ add up to zero because $\lambda_3$ and $\lambda_8$ are traceless. The
weights of $\Lambda^2\mathbf{3}$ are $w_a + w_b$ with $a \neq b$, which equals $-w_c$ for the third index $c$: the
weights of $\bar{\mathbf{3}}$, and a three-dimensional representation with these weights is irreducible (its highest
weight $\omega_2$ generates it), so $\Lambda^2\mathbf{3} \cong \bar{\mathbf{3}}$. The symmetric part has weights $2w_u,
2w_d, 2w_s, w_u + w_d, w_u + w_s, w_d + w_s$, the highest being $2w_u = 2\omega_1 = (2, \tfrac{2}{\sqrt3})$: this is
the $\mathbf{6}$, Sage's `A2(2,0)` (@exr-lrep-hw-dimension).
:::

The third exercise uses Weyl's dimension formula for $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, which computes the dimension of an
irreducible representation from its highest weight alone. The exercise compares it with Sage's character ring on many
cases and finds which dimensions occur.

::: {#exr-lrep-hw-dimension}
#### Weyl's dimension formula for $\mathfrak{su}(3)$

The irreducible representation with highest weight $a\omega_1 + b\omega_2$ has dimension $\tfrac12(a + 1)(b + 1)(a + b +
2)$. Check this with Sage for $a, b < 8$, identify $\mathbf{6}$, $\mathbf{10}$, $\mathbf{27}$, verify
$\mathbf{3} \otimes \mathbf{3} = \mathbf{6} \oplus \bar{\mathbf{3}}$, and decide whether $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ has an
irreducible representation of dimension $9$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ give $3$, $(1, 1)$ gives $8$, $(2, 0)$ gives $6$, $(3, 0)$ gives $10$ and $(2, 2)$ gives $27$.
Dimension $9$ does not occur: for $a \leq b$, $a = 0$ needs $(b + 1)(b + 2) = 18$, $a = 1$ needs $(b + 1)(b + 3) = 9$,
$a = 2$ needs $(b + 1)(b + 4) = 6$, none with integer $b \geq a$, and larger $a$ give dimension at least $\tfrac12 \cdot 4
\cdot 4 \cdot 8 = 64$ (the formula is symmetric in $a, b$):

{{< sage exr-lrep-hw-dimension >}}
:::
::::

#### Simple roots and the Cartan matrix

Six roots are redundant: each is a combination of a few of them with integer coefficients. The definition below picks
out a basis of the root system, as many roots as the rank, in terms of which all others are sums.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-simple-roots}
#### Simple roots

The positive roots that are not sums of other positive roots are the **simple roots** $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_r$,
as many as the rank; every positive root is a non-negative integer combination of them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the hexagon of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, three roots are positive for the usual choice of direction, and one of them is
the sum of the other two. The remaining two are the simple roots.

::: {#exm-simple-su3}
#### $\mathfrak{su}(3)$

With the positive roots $(2, 0)$, $(1, \sqrt3)$, $(-1, \sqrt3)$, the simple roots are $\alpha_1 = (2, 0)$ and
$\alpha_2 = (-1, \sqrt3)$, and $\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 = (1, \sqrt3)$ is the third positive root (@exr-su3-cartan).
:::

The pattern of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ extends to every unitary algebra. In the orthogonal coordinates of the diagonal
entries the simple roots are differences of neighbouring basis vectors.

::: {#exm-simple-su2}
#### $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak{su}(n)$

$\mathfrak{su}(2)$ has the single simple root $\alpha = 1$ (or $2$ in the normalisation where $J_3$ has
eigenvalues $\pm 1$ on the root vectors); $\mathfrak{su}(n)$ has $n - 1$ simple roots $e_i - e_{i+1}$ in the
orthogonal basis Sage uses, and $\binom{n}{2}$ positive roots $e_i - e_j$, $i < j$.
:::

The set of simple roots depends on the direction chosen to define positivity. The dependence is harmless, because the
different choices are related by symmetries of the root diagram.

::: {#exm-simple-choice}
#### Dependence on the choice of direction

A different direction in the weight plane gives a different set of positive roots, related to the first by an
element of the **Weyl group**, the symmetry group of the root diagram, $S_3$ for the hexagon of
$\mathfrak{su}(3)$: the Cartan matrix below does not depend on the choice.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise carries out a change of direction explicitly. The new simple roots are found, and a reflection in
the Weyl group is identified that maps the old ones to the new ones.

::: {#exr-lrep-simple-direction}
#### Another choice of positive roots

Use $\ell(\mu) = \mu_1 + \varepsilon\mu_2$ with small $\varepsilon > 0$. Find the positive and the simple roots of
$\mathfrak{su}(3)$, and a reflection of the plane, preserving the hexagon, that maps $\alpha_1 = (2, 0)$, $\alpha_2 =
(-1, \sqrt3)$ to the new simple roots.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\ell$ is positive on $(2, 0)$, $(1, \sqrt3)$ and $(1, -\sqrt3)$. Since $(2, 0) = (1, \sqrt3) + (1, -\sqrt3)$, the simple
roots are $(1, \sqrt3)$ and $(1, -\sqrt3)$. The reflection in the line perpendicular to $\alpha_2$ (the line at
$30°$) sends a vector at angle $\theta$ to angle $60° - \theta$: $\alpha_1$ (at $0°$) goes to $(1, \sqrt3)$ and
$\alpha_2$ (at $120°$) to $(1, -\sqrt3)$. This reflection permutes the six roots, so it is an element of the Weyl
group (@exm-lrep-weyl-reflection).
:::

The second exercise proves a property of simple roots used repeatedly in the classification: the difference of two
simple roots is never a root. The argument uses only the definition.

::: {#exr-lrep-simple-difference}
#### Differences of simple roots

Show that $\alpha_i - \alpha_j$ is not a root for distinct simple roots, and check it on the hexagon of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every root is positive or negative. If $\beta = \alpha_i - \alpha_j$ were a positive root, then $\alpha_i = \beta +
\alpha_j$ would be a sum of positive roots, contradicting simplicity; if it were negative, $\alpha_j = (-\beta) +
\alpha_i$ would be. For $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, $\alpha_1 - \alpha_2 = (3, -\sqrt3)$ has length $\sqrt{12}$, while all
roots have length $2$.
:::

The third exercise looks at the next unitary algebra, $\mathfrak{su}(4)$ of type $A_3$, with three simple roots and six
positive ones. Sage writes each positive root in terms of the simple ones.

::: {#exr-lrep-simple-su4}
#### Simple roots of $\mathfrak{su}(4)$

With Sage's `RootSystem(["A", 3])`, list the simple roots, write every positive root as a non-negative integer
combination of them, and check that there are $\binom42 = 6$ positive roots.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The positive roots $e_i - e_j$, $i < j$, are the sums $\alpha_i + \alpha_{i + 1} + \dots + \alpha_{j - 1}$ of
consecutive simple roots $\alpha_k = e_k - e_{k + 1}$ (@exm-simple-su2):

{{< sage exr-lrep-simple-su4 >}}
:::
::::

The simple roots are determined up to rotation and scale by their lengths and the angles between them. The
definition below records these in an integer matrix, which turns out to determine the whole Lie algebra.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-cartan-matrix}
#### Cartan matrix

The **Cartan matrix** is $A_{ij} = 2(\alpha_i \cdot \alpha_j)/(\alpha_j \cdot \alpha_j)$, with the inner product
induced by the Killing form on $\mathfrak{h}$. Its diagonal entries are $2$, its off-diagonal entries are
non-positive integers, and it determines the Lie algebra up to isomorphism; its graph, with a node per simple
root and $A_{ij}A_{ji}$ lines between nodes $i$ and $j$, is the **Dynkin diagram**.
:::
