**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ the two simple roots have equal length and meet at $120°$. Their Cartan matrix is the simplest
non-diagonal one.

::: {#exm-cartan-su3-matrix}
#### The Cartan matrix of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$

All roots have length $2$ and $\alpha_1 \cdot \alpha_2 = -2$, so $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$,
the Cartan matrix of type $A_2$ (@prp-su3-root-system): two nodes joined by one line.
:::

When simple roots are orthogonal the off-diagonal entries vanish. The Lie algebra then splits, as the example shows
for $\mathfrak{so}(4)$.

::: {#exm-cartan-su2-matrix}
#### Type $A_1$ and $A_1 \times A_1$

$\mathfrak{su}(2)$ has the $1 \times 1$ Cartan matrix $(2)$, a single node; $\mathfrak{so}(4) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2)
\oplus \mathfrak{su}(2)$ has $\operatorname{diag}(2, 2)$, two disconnected nodes, and a disconnected Dynkin diagram
means a direct sum of Lie algebras.
:::

The possible Cartan matrices are severely restricted, and their complete list is the classification of simple Lie
algebras. The example names the families.

::: {#exm-cartan-classification}
#### The classification

The Cartan matrices of the simple Lie algebras fall into the series $A_n = \mathfrak{su}(n+1)$, $B_n =
\mathfrak{so}(2n+1)$, $C_n = \mathfrak{sp}(n)$, $D_n = \mathfrak{so}(2n)$ and the exceptional $G_2, F_4, E_6, E_7,
E_8$; $E_8$ is the gauge algebra of the heterotic string and $E_6$ a candidate unification group of Part V.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes a Cartan matrix with roots of two different lengths. It shows that the matrix need not be
symmetric and that the Dynkin diagram then has a double line.

::: {#exr-lrep-cartan-b2}
#### The Cartan matrix of $\mathfrak{so}(5)$

The simple roots of $B_2 = \mathfrak{so}(5)$ can be taken as $\alpha_1 = (1, -1)$ and $\alpha_2 = (0, 1)$. Compute the
Cartan matrix, the angle between the roots, the ratio of their lengths, and the number of lines in the Dynkin
diagram.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\alpha_1 \cdot \alpha_1 = 2$, $\alpha_2 \cdot \alpha_2 = 1$ and $\alpha_1 \cdot \alpha_2 = -1$, so $A_{12} = 2(-1)/1 = -
2$ and $A_{21} = 2(-1)/2 = -1$: $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, not symmetric. The angle has
$\cos\theta = -1/\sqrt2$, $\theta = 135°$; the long root is $\sqrt2$ times the short one, and $A_{12}A_{21} = 2$ gives a
double line.
:::

The second exercise explains why so few Cartan matrices exist. The product $A_{ij}A_{ji}$ is four times the squared
cosine of the angle between two simple roots, and integrality leaves only four possible angles.

::: {#exr-lrep-cartan-angles}
#### The allowed angles

Show that $A_{ij}A_{ji} = 4\cos^2\theta_{ij}$, deduce that $A_{ij}A_{ji} \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ for $i \neq j$, and list
the possible angles between simple roots and the possible ratios of their lengths.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$A_{ij}A_{ji} = 4(\alpha_i \cdot \alpha_j)^2/(|\alpha_i|^2|\alpha_j|^2) = 4\cos^2\theta_{ij}$. It is a product of
integers, and it is less than $4$ because $\alpha_i \neq \pm\alpha_j$; so it is $0, 1, 2$ or $3$. The off-diagonal entries are
non-positive (@def-cartan-matrix; an acute angle would make $\alpha_i - \alpha_j$ a root, which
@exr-lrep-simple-difference excludes), so $\theta_{ij} = 90°, 120°, 135°$ or
$150°$. When $A_{ij} \neq 0$, $|\alpha_i|^2/|\alpha_j|^2 = A_{ij}/A_{ji}$, which is $1$ for $120°$, $2$ or $\tfrac12$
for $135°$, $3$ or $\tfrac13$ for $150°$: these are $A_2$, $B_2$ and $G_2$.
:::

The third exercise computes Cartan matrices from Sage's simple roots with the formula of the definition. Sage's own
`CartanMatrix` uses the transposed convention $2(\alpha_i \cdot \alpha_j)/(\alpha_i \cdot \alpha_i)$, which matters
only when root lengths differ.

::: {#exr-lrep-cartan-b2-g2}
#### Cartan matrices with Sage

For the types $A_2$, $B_2$, $G_2$ and $A_3$, compute $A_{ij}$ from the simple roots of `RootSystem(...).ambient_space()`,
compare with `CartanMatrix`, and print the products $A_{12}A_{21}$, the determinants and the Dynkin diagrams.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The matrices agree with the transposes of Sage's, the products $A_{12}A_{21}$ are $1, 2, 3$ for $A_2, B_2, G_2$ (one,
two and three lines, @exr-lrep-cartan-angles), and the $B_2$ matrix is that of @exr-lrep-cartan-b2:

{{< sage exr-lrep-cartan-b2-g2 >}}
:::
::::

The proposition collects the data of the root system of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ found in this section. All of it is
determined by the type $A_2$, and the eigenvalue computations behind it return in a later chapter.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-su3-root-system}
#### The root system of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$

The simple roots are $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$, the positive roots $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_1 + \alpha_2$, the Cartan
matrix is $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, and the adjoint has dimension $8$ with the zero weight
of multiplicity $2$. The eigenvalues of $\operatorname{ad}_{\lambda_3}$ and $\operatorname{ad}_{\lambda_8}$ on the
root vectors are computed in @prp-coset-su3.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The eigenvalues of $\operatorname{ad}_{\lambda_3}$ and $\operatorname{ad}_{\lambda_8}$ on the root vectors are the
theorems of @prp-coset-su3.

**Sage.** Computed by Sage's `RootSystem` and `WeylCharacterRing` (@exr-su3-cartan).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The symmetry of the hexagon is generated by reflections in lines perpendicular to the roots. The Cartan matrix
describes how these reflections act on the simple roots.

::: {#exm-lrep-weyl-reflection}
#### Weyl reflections

The reflection in the line perpendicular to a root $\alpha$ is $s_\alpha(\mu) = \mu - \frac{2(\mu \cdot \alpha)}{\alpha
\cdot \alpha}\alpha$. On simple roots $s_{\alpha_j}(\alpha_i) = \alpha_i - A_{ij}\alpha_j$, so $s_{\alpha_1}(\alpha_2) =
\alpha_2 + \alpha_1$ and $s_{\alpha_1}(\alpha_1) = -\alpha_1$. The three reflections and the rotations by $\pm 120°$
form the Weyl group $S_3$ (@exm-simple-choice), which permutes the weights of every representation preserving their
multiplicities: it maps the triangle of $\mathbf{3}$ to itself (@exr-lrep-weyl-group).
:::

The dimension of a Lie algebra is visible in its root diagram: one dimension for each root and the rank for the
origin. The count recovers the familiar dimensions of the unitary algebras.

::: {#exm-lrep-adjoint-dimension}
#### Dimension from the roots

By the root decomposition, $\dim\mathfrak{g} = \text{rank} + \#\text{roots}$: $2 + 6 = 8$ for $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, $1 + 2 =
3$ for $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, and $(n - 1) + n(n - 1) = n^2 - 1$ for $\mathfrak{su}(n)$ (@exr-lrep-root-sun). The zero
weight of the adjoint has multiplicity equal to the rank, $2$ for $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, as in @prp-su3-root-system.
:::

Adding a root to another root repeatedly produces a string of roots, which breaks off after finitely many steps. The
length of the string is fixed by the Cartan matrix, and for $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ every string is short.

::: {#exm-lrep-root-strings}
#### Root strings

The $\alpha_1$-string through $\alpha_2$ consists of the roots $\alpha_2 + k\alpha_1$: $k = 0, 1$ give roots, while
$\alpha_2 - \alpha_1$ (@exr-lrep-simple-difference) and $\alpha_2 + 2\alpha_1 = (3, \sqrt3)$ are not roots. In general
the string $\beta - p\alpha, \dots, \beta + q\alpha$ has $p - q = 2(\beta \cdot \alpha)/(\alpha \cdot \alpha)$; here $p
= 0$, $q = 1$ and $A_{21} = -1$. Since $[E_\alpha, E_\beta]$ has root $\alpha + \beta$, the string says $[E_{\alpha_1},
E_{\alpha_2}] \neq 0$ but $[E_{\alpha_1}, [E_{\alpha_1}, E_{\alpha_2}]] = 0$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise is the Sage computation behind the proposition. It lists the roots, prints the Cartan matrix and the
Dynkin diagram, and gives the weights of $\mathbf{3}$ and $\mathbf{8}$.

::: {#exr-su3-cartan}
#### The root system with Sage

List the simple and positive roots of $A_2$ with `RootSystem`, print the Cartan matrix and Dynkin diagram, and
the weights of $\mathbf{3}$ and $\mathbf{8}$ with `WeylCharacterRing`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-su3-cartan >}}
:::

Sage writes weights of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ in orthogonal coordinates $(w_1, w_2, w_3)$, the diagonal entries, while
this section uses the eigenvalues of $\lambda_3$ and $\lambda_8$. The second exercise translates between the two, which
is also how the interactive figure is drawn.

::: {#exr-lrep-root-ambient}
#### From Sage's coordinates to the $(\lambda_3, \lambda_8)$ plane

Show that a weight with diagonal entries $(w_1, w_2, w_3)$ has $(\lambda_3, \lambda_8)$-eigenvalues $(w_1 - w_2, (w_1 + w_2 -
2w_3)/\sqrt3)$. Map Sage's simple roots $e_1 - e_2$, $e_2 - e_3$ and the weight $(\tfrac23, -\tfrac13, -\tfrac13)$, and
check that the Cartan matrix is the same in both coordinates.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(d_1, d_2, d_3)$ acts on the weight vector with eigenvalue $\sum_id_iw_i$; for
$\lambda_3$ and $\lambda_8$ this gives the stated formula. Then $e_1 - e_2 \mapsto (2, 0) = \alpha_1$, $e_2 - e_3 \mapsto
(-1, \sqrt3) = \alpha_2$ and $(\tfrac23, -\tfrac13, -\tfrac13) \mapsto (1, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}) = \omega_1$. In Sage's
coordinates the simple roots have squared length $2$ and inner product $-1$; in the plane $4$ and $-2$. The inner
products are scaled by $2$, and $A_{ij}$ is a ratio of inner products, so it is unchanged.
:::

The third exercise generates the Weyl group from the reflections in the simple roots and checks its properties with
Sage. The orbit of a single root is the whole hexagon.

::: {#exr-lrep-weyl-group}
#### The Weyl group of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$

With Sage, compute the order of the Weyl group of $A_2$, check $s_1(\alpha_2) = \alpha_1 + \alpha_2$, show that the orbit
of $\alpha_1$ is the set of all roots and that every element permutes the roots, and find the orbit of $\omega_1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The group has order $6$ and acts as $S_3$ on the three orthogonal coordinates, permuting $e_1, e_2, e_3$; it permutes
the roots $e_i - e_j$, and since every root is $e_i - e_j$ for some pair, the orbit of $e_1 - e_2$ is all six. The orbit
of $\omega_1$ is the three weights of $\mathbf{3}$ (@exm-lrep-weyl-reflection):

{{< sage exr-lrep-weyl-group >}}
:::
::::

### Branching rules {#sec-branching}

Restricting a representation to a subalgebra breaks it into smaller pieces, and the list of pieces, the branching
rule, is read off from the weights. Symmetry breaking in physics is governed by such rules: when a symmetry is reduced
to a subgroup, the states of one multiplet split into multiplets of the subgroup with definite charges. This section
defines restriction and branching, works the branchings of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ under $\mathfrak{su}(2) \times
\mathfrak{u}(1)$ and under its maximal torus, and proves the isomorphism $\mathfrak{so}(4) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2)
\oplus \mathfrak{su}(2)$ behind the isometries of the three-sphere.

#### Restriction and branching

A representation of a group is in particular a representation of each of its subgroups. The definition below names
this operation; its interest lies in how an irreducible representation falls apart under it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-restriction}
#### Restriction of a representation

Restricting a representation $\rho$ of $G$ (or $\mathfrak{g}$) to a subgroup $H$ (subalgebra $\mathfrak{h}$)
gives a representation $\rho|_H$ of $H$ on the same space, usually reducible even when $\rho$ is irreducible.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest case restricts the rotations of space to the rotations about one axis. The axis itself is fixed, and the
plane perpendicular to it rotates.

::: {#exm-restriction-so3-so2}
#### The vector of $SO(3)$ under $SO(2)$

Restricted to the rotations about the $Z$-axis, $\mathbb{R}^3$ splits into the fixed line $\{(0, 0, z)\}$ (charge
$0$) and the plane $\{(x, y, 0)\}$ on which $SO(2)$ rotates (charges $\pm 1$ after complexification): $\mathbf{3}
\to \mathbf{1}_0 \oplus \mathbf{1}_{1} \oplus \mathbf{1}_{-1}$ (@exm-invariant-rotation, @prp-coset-so3).
:::

The fundamental representation of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ restricted to the $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ of the upper left block
splits by the block structure. The first two basis vectors form a doublet and the third is left alone.

::: {#exm-restriction-su3-su2}
#### The fundamental of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ under $\mathfrak{su}(2)$

Restricted to the $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ of $\lambda_{1, 2, 3}$, $\mathbb{C}^3$ splits into the doublet $(e_1, e_2)$ and
the singlet $e_3$: $\mathbf{3} \to \mathbf{2} \oplus \mathbf{1}$ (@exr-branching-levi).
:::

Restricting all the way down to a Cartan subalgebra leaves only one-dimensional pieces. The branching rule is then
just the list of weights.

::: {#exm-restriction-spin}
#### Spin $j$ under $\mathfrak{u}(1)$

Restricted to $\operatorname{span}(J_3)$, spin $j$ splits into its $2j + 1$ weight lines, the charges $m = j, \dots, -
j$ of @def-weight: branching to a Cartan subalgebra is the weight decomposition.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise shows that the branching to $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ does not depend on which axis is chosen. The reason
is that any two axes are related by a rotation, and the rotation acts in the representation.

::: {#exr-lrep-restrict-axis}
#### Restriction to any axis

Show that the restriction of spin $j$ to the $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ generated by $n_aJ_a$, for a unit vector $n$, has the
same charges $j, \dots, -j$ as the restriction to $J_3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $R \in SO(3)$ be a rotation with $Re_3 = n$ and $U$ an element of $SU(2)$ covering it, acting on spin $j$ by
$\rho(U)$. Then $n_aJ_a = \rho(U)J_3\rho(U)^{-1}$ (the generators transform as a vector under conjugation), so $n_aJ_a$
and $J_3$ have the same eigenvalues, with eigenvectors $\rho(U)v_m$. All Cartan subalgebras of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ are
conjugate, and the branching to any of them is the weight decomposition.
:::

The second exercise restricts to one of the other copies of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ inside $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, found in
@exr-lrep-gm-su2s. The fundamental and the adjoint split in the same pattern as for the upper-left copy.

::: {#exr-lrep-restrict-other-su2}
#### Another $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ in $\mathfrak{su}(3)$

Restrict $\mathbf{3}$ and $\mathbf{8}$ to the $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ spanned by $\lambda_4, \lambda_5$ and $H' =
\tfrac12(\lambda_3 + \sqrt3\lambda_8)$, using the eigenvalues of $\tfrac12H'$ (the analogue of $J_3 = \tfrac12\sigma_3$).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tfrac12H' = \operatorname{diag}(\tfrac12, 0, -\tfrac12)$: on $\mathbf{3}$, $(e_1, e_3)$ is a doublet and $e_2$ a
singlet, $\mathbf{3} \to \mathbf{2} \oplus \mathbf{1}$. On the matrix units $[\tfrac12H', E_{ij}] = \tfrac12(h_i -
h_j)E_{ij}$ with $h = (1, 0, -1)$: $E_{13}, E_{31}$ have weights $\pm 1$, $E_{12}, E_{23}$ weight $\tfrac12$, $E_{21},
E_{32}$ weight $-\tfrac12$, and the Cartan subalgebra weight $0$ twice. So $\mathbf{8} \to \mathbf{3} \oplus \mathbf{2}
\oplus \mathbf{2} \oplus \mathbf{1}$, as for the upper-left $\mathfrak{su}(2)$: the two subalgebras are conjugate by a
permutation matrix exchanging $e_2$ and $e_3$.
:::

The third exercise restricts a representation of a direct sum $\mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{su}(2)$ to the
diagonal $\mathfrak{su}(2)$. It shows that the Clebsch-Gordan decomposition is itself a branching rule.

::: {#exr-lrep-restrict-diagonal}
#### Tensor products as restrictions

$\mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{su}(2)$ (@def-direct-sum-algebras) acts on $V_j \otimes V_k$ by $(X_1, X_2) \mapsto
\rho_j(X_1) \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes \rho_k(X_2)$, a representation $(j, k)$ of dimension $(2j + 1)(2k + 1)$. Show that
its restriction to the diagonal $\{(X, X)\}$ is $j \otimes k$, and compute it with Sage for several $(j, k)$, including
the vector of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ restricted to $\mathfrak{so}(3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On the diagonal, $X$ acts as $\rho_j(X) \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes \rho_k(X)$, which is the tensor product representation, so
the restriction is $j \otimes k$, decomposed by @eq-clebsch-gordan. For $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ this is $1 \oplus 0$: the
vector of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ restricted to $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ is $\mathbb{R}^3 \oplus \mathbb{R}$
(@exm-lrep-so4-diagonal). Sage gives the same through the branching rule from $D_2$ to $B_1$:

{{< sage exr-lrep-restrict-diagonal >}}
:::
::::

Restriction gives a reducible representation, and the next step is to decompose it into irreducibles of the
subalgebra. The definition below names the result and explains how weights compute it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-branching-rule}
#### Branching rule

The decomposition of a restricted representation into irreducibles of $H$, written $\rho \to \bigoplus_i
\rho_i$, is the **branching rule** for $G \supset H$. It is computed from the weights: the weights of $\rho|_H$
are the weights of $\rho$ projected onto the Cartan subalgebra of $H$ (plus the charges under any $\mathfrak{u}(1)$
factors), and they are sorted into weight diagrams of irreducibles of $H$ (@fig-branching-su3).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The main example of the section branches the adjoint of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ under the subalgebra generated by the
upper-left $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\lambda_8$. The eight generators fall into four multiplets with definite charges.

::: {#exm-branching-su3-su2-u1}
#### $\mathfrak{su}(3) \supset \mathfrak{su}(2) \times \mathfrak{u}(1)$

Take $\mathfrak{su}(2) = \operatorname{span}(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3)$ and $\mathfrak{u}(1) =
\operatorname{span}(\lambda_8)$, which commute. The adjoint $\mathbf{8}$ splits into $\lambda_{1,2,3}$ (a triplet of
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with $\lambda_8$-charge $0$, since $[\lambda_8, \lambda_a] = 0$), $\lambda_8$ (a singlet of charge
$0$), $\lambda_4 \pm i\lambda_5$ and $\lambda_6 \pm i\lambda_7$ (two doublets, with $\lambda_3$-weights $\pm 1$ and
$\lambda_8$-charges $+\sqrt3$ and $-\sqrt3$):
$$
\mathbf{8} \to \mathbf{3}_0 \oplus \mathbf{1}_0 \oplus \mathbf{2}_{\sqrt3} \oplus \mathbf{2}_{-\sqrt3}
$$ {#eq-branching-su3}
(@prp-branching-su3, @fig-branching-su3). This is the branching used in Part V when $SU(3)$ is reduced over $S^2$
with $R = U(1)$ embedded along $\lambda_8$: the gauge group $SU(2) \times U(1)$ is the commutant of the embedding
and the doublets are the Higgs fields.
:::

Restricting to the maximal torus instead splits everything into one-dimensional pieces. The branching rule is then the
weight diagram of the adjoint itself.

::: {#exm-branching-torus}
#### $\mathfrak{su}(3) \supset \mathfrak{u}(1) \times \mathfrak{u}(1)$

Under the maximal torus every weight is its own one-dimensional representation: $\mathbf{8} \to 2 \cdot (0, 0)
\oplus \bigoplus_{\text{roots}} \alpha$, eight charge vectors, the hexagon plus the double origin of
@fig-su3-weights. This is the branching used for $SU(3)/U(1) \times U(1)$ in @sec-reductive.
:::

Sage implements branching rules for many pairs of algebras. For the upper-left $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ the relevant rule is
called `levi`, after the Levi subalgebras obtained by deleting nodes of the Dynkin diagram.

::: {#exm-branching-sage}
#### Branching with Sage

`WeylCharacterRing("A2")(1,1).branch(WeylCharacterRing("A1"), rule="levi")` returns the $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ content
$\mathbf{1} \oplus 2 \cdot \mathbf{2} \oplus \mathbf{3}$ of the adjoint, and the $\mathbf{3} \to \mathbf{2} \oplus
\mathbf{1}$ of the fundamental (@exr-branching-levi); the $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ charges are read from the
$\lambda_8$-components of the weights.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Computed in `figures/branching_su3.sage`.

![The branching of the adjoint of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ under $\mathfrak{su}(2) \times \mathfrak{u}(1)$: the eight
weights in the $(\lambda_3, \lambda_8)$ plane grouped by $\lambda_8$-charge. The row at charge $0$ is the triplet
plus the singlet (the double point at the origin), the rows at charge $\pm\sqrt3$ are the two doublets.
Generated by `figures/branching_su3.sage` with Sage's branching

The first exercise runs Sage's branching rule on the three smallest representations. It also confirms the tensor
product $\mathbf{3} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{3}}$, which relates the fundamental to the adjoint.

::: {#exr-branching-levi}
#### Branching with the Weyl character ring

Branch $\mathbf{3}$, $\bar{\mathbf{3}}$ and $\mathbf{8}$ of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ to the Levi subalgebra
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with Sage, and check $\mathbf{3} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{3}} = \mathbf{8} \oplus \mathbf{1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-branching-levi >}}
:::

Sage's `levi` rule gives the $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ content but not the $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ charges. The second exercise
computes the charges from the weights by hand, for the fundamental and then for the adjoint.

::: {#exr-branching-charges}
#### Charges from weights

From the weights of $\mathbf{3}$ in @fig-su3-weights, compute the $\lambda_8$-charges and $\lambda_3$-weights of the
doublet and singlet of $\mathbf{3} \to \mathbf{2}_{1/\sqrt3} \oplus \mathbf{1}_{-2/\sqrt3}$, and check that the
charges of $\mathbf{8} \subset \mathbf{3} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{3}}$ are differences of charges of $\mathbf{3}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The weights $(1, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3})$ and $(-1, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3})$ form the doublet (charge $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$,
$\lambda_3$-weights $\pm 1$) and $(0, -\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3})$ the singlet. Differences of $\mathbf{3}$-weights give
$\lambda_8$-charges $0$ (within the doublet) and $\pm(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3} + \tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}) = \pm\sqrt3$ (doublet
minus singlet), exactly the charges of @eq-branching-su3.
:::

The third exercise branches the six-dimensional representation of @exr-lrep-hw-6 with charges. Its weights are sums
of two weights of $\mathbf{3}$, so the charges are sums as well.

::: {#exr-lrep-branch-6}
#### Branching the $\mathbf{6}$

Branch $\mathbf{6} = \operatorname{Sym}^2\mathbf{3}$ under $\mathfrak{su}(2) \times \mathfrak{u}(1)$ with the
$\lambda_8$-charges, and compare with Sage's `levi` branching of `A2(2,0)`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With the charges $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ of $u, d$ and $-\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$ of $s$: $uu, ud, dd$ have charge
$\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$ and $\lambda_3$-weights $2, 0, -2$ (a triplet); $us, ds$ have charge $-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ (a
doublet); $ss$ has charge $-\tfrac{4}{\sqrt3}$. So $\mathbf{6} \to \mathbf{3}_{2/\sqrt3} \oplus \mathbf{2}_{-1/\sqrt3}
\oplus \mathbf{1}_{-4/\sqrt3}$, the symmetric square of $\mathbf{2}_{1/\sqrt3} \oplus \mathbf{1}_{-2/\sqrt3}$:

{{< sage exr-lrep-branch-6 >}}
:::
::::

The proposition isolates the brackets that make @eq-branching-su3 true. They are finitely many identities between
Gell-Mann matrices, each a commutator of two of the eight matrices of @eq-gell-mann.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-branching-su3}
#### The branching of the adjoint of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$

$[\lambda_8, \lambda_a] = 0$ for $a = 1, 2, 3$ and $[\lambda_1, \lambda_2] = 2i\lambda_3$ (with cyclic permutations): the
triplet and singlet are neutral and close into $\mathfrak{su}(2)$; the doublets' charges $\pm\sqrt3$ and
$\lambda_3$-weights $\pm 1$ are @prp-coset-su3 of @sec-reductive.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Representations.su3_branching_neutral` and `KaluzaKlein.Representations.su3_su2_subalgebra`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Representations.su3_branching_neutral >}}

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The neutral generators of the proposition form a subalgebra of their own, the set of all elements commuting with
$\lambda_8$. It is a direct sum of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak{u}(1)$.

::: {#exm-lrep-branch-commutant}
#### The commutant of $\lambda_8$

$\lambda_8 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$ has a repeated eigenvalue, and the matrices commuting with
it are block diagonal with blocks of sizes $2$ and $1$. In $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ these are spanned by $\lambda_1,
\lambda_2, \lambda_3$ and $\lambda_8$: the commutant is $\mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1) \cong \mathfrak{u}(2)$,
exactly the neutral part $\mathbf{3}_0 \oplus \mathbf{1}_0$ of @eq-branching-su3.
:::

The conjugate representation branches like the fundamental with the charges reversed. The example records it,
because $\mathbf{3} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{3}}$ is used to build the adjoint.

::: {#exm-lrep-branch-3bar}
#### The branching of $\bar{\mathbf{3}}$

The weights of $\bar{\mathbf{3}}$ are the negatives of those of $\mathbf{3}$ (@exr-lrep-weight-su3-fund), so
$\bar{\mathbf{3}} \to \mathbf{2}_{-1/\sqrt3} \oplus \mathbf{1}_{2/\sqrt3}$; the doublet $\bar{\mathbf{2}} \cong
\mathbf{2}$ of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ is self-conjugate (@exr-lrep-weight-tensor), only the charges change sign.
:::

In particle physics the $\lambda_8$-charge is rescaled to the hypercharge of the quark model. The example shows the
familiar fractional values emerging from the branching rules.

::: {#exm-lrep-branch-hypercharge}
#### Hypercharge

With $Y = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\lambda_8 = \tfrac13\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$, the branching $\mathbf{3} \to
\mathbf{2}_{1/3} \oplus \mathbf{1}_{-2/3}$ gives the hypercharges $\tfrac13$ of the $u, d$ quarks and $-\tfrac23$ of
$s$, and @eq-branching-su3 becomes $\mathbf{8} \to \mathbf{3}_0 \oplus \mathbf{1}_0 \oplus \mathbf{2}_1 \oplus
\mathbf{2}_{-1}$: the pions and $\eta$ at $Y = 0$ and the kaon doublets at $Y = \pm 1$ of the meson octet.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the brackets of the proposition by direct matrix computation in Sage. It also computes the
charges and weights of the four doublet generators.

::: {#exr-lrep-branch-neutral}
#### The brackets of the proposition

With Sage, check $[\lambda_8, \lambda_a] = 0$ for $a = 1, 2, 3$, $[\lambda_1, \lambda_2] = 2i\lambda_3$ and its cyclic
permutations, and compute the $\lambda_8$-charges and $\lambda_3$-weights of $\lambda_4 \pm i\lambda_5$ and $\lambda_6
\pm i\lambda_7$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\lambda_8$ is a multiple of the identity on the upper block, where $\lambda_{1, 2, 3}$ live, so it commutes with them.
The doublet $(\lambda_4 + i\lambda_5, \lambda_6 + i\lambda_7) = (2E_{13}, 2E_{23})$ has charge $\sqrt3$ (from $h_i - h_3 =
\tfrac{3}{\sqrt3}$) and $\lambda_3$-weights $\pm 1$:

{{< sage exr-lrep-branch-neutral >}}
:::

Every branching found so far has charges that add up to zero. The second exercise explains why: $\lambda_8$ is a
combination of commutators, and the trace of a commutator vanishes in any representation.

::: {#exr-lrep-branch-trace}
#### Charges add up to zero

Write $\lambda_8$ as a combination of $[\lambda_1, \lambda_2]$ and $[\lambda_4, \lambda_5]$ (@exr-lrep-gm-su2s), and
deduce that the $\lambda_8$-charges of any finite-dimensional representation, counted with multiplicity, add up to
zero. Check this on $\mathbf{3}$, $\mathbf{8}$ and $\mathbf{6}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[\lambda_1, \lambda_2] = 2i\lambda_3$ and $[\lambda_4, \lambda_5] = i(\lambda_3 + \sqrt3\lambda_8)$, so $\lambda_8 =
\tfrac{1}{i\sqrt3}([\lambda_4, \lambda_5] - \tfrac12[\lambda_1, \lambda_2])$. In a representation $\rho$,
$\operatorname{tr}\rho([X, Y]) = \operatorname{tr}[\rho(X), \rho(Y)] = 0$, so $\operatorname{tr}\rho(\lambda_8) = 0$,
which is the sum of the charges. Checks: $\mathbf{3}$: $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3} + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3} - \tfrac{2}{\sqrt3} = 0$;
$\mathbf{8}$: $2\sqrt3 - 2\sqrt3 = 0$; $\mathbf{6}$ (@exr-lrep-branch-6): $3 \cdot \tfrac{2}{\sqrt3} - 2 \cdot
\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3} - \tfrac{4}{\sqrt3} = 0$.
:::

The third exercise asks what changes when the $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ is embedded along $\lambda_3$ instead of $\lambda_8$.
The commutant is then much smaller, and the comparison shows which diagonal generators give a non-abelian commutant.

::: {#exr-lrep-branch-other-u1}
#### Embedding the $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ elsewhere

Find the commutant of $\lambda_3$ in $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ and branch $\mathbf{8}$ under the $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ it generates.
More generally, describe the commutant of $\operatorname{diag}(h_1, h_2, h_3)$ in terms of the multiplicities of the
$h_i$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[H, X]_{ij} = (h_i - h_j)X_{ij}$, so $X$ commutes with $H$ exactly when $X_{ij} = 0$ whenever $h_i \neq h_j$: the
commutant is block diagonal, one block for each distinct eigenvalue, $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{u}(n_1) \oplus \dots)$ for
eigenvalue multiplicities $n_1, \dots$. For $\lambda_3 = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0)$ the eigenvalues are distinct and
the commutant is the Cartan subalgebra $\operatorname{span}(\lambda_3, \lambda_8)$, abelian. Under the $\mathfrak{u}(1)$
of $\lambda_3$ the charges $h_i - h_j$ give $\mathbf{8} \to \mathbf{1}_{2} \oplus \mathbf{1}_{-2} \oplus 2 \cdot
\mathbf{1}_{1} \oplus 2 \cdot \mathbf{1}_{-1} \oplus 2 \cdot \mathbf{1}_{0}$. A non-abelian commutant needs a repeated
eigenvalue, as for $\lambda_8$ (@exm-lrep-branch-commutant).
:::
::::

#### The splitting of so(4)

Some Lie algebras are built from smaller ones that do not interact at all. The definition below makes this precise,
and the rest of the section shows that the rotations of four-dimensional space are of this kind.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-direct-sum-algebras}
#### Direct sum of Lie algebras

The **direct sum** $\mathfrak{g}_1 \oplus \mathfrak{g}_2$ of two Lie algebras is their direct sum as vector spaces
with $[X_1 + X_2, Y_1 + Y_2] = [X_1, Y_1] + [X_2, Y_2]$: elements of the two summands commute. A Lie algebra that is
a direct sum of simple ones is **semisimple**, and its Dynkin diagram is disconnected (@exm-cartan-su2-matrix).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest direct sums are abelian, and the gauge algebra of the electroweak theory is the standard non-abelian
example. Both appeared already in the branching of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$.

::: {#exm-direct-sum-torus}
#### $\mathfrak{u}(1) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1)$

The Lie algebra of the torus $T^2$ is $\mathfrak{u}(1) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1)$, abelian; the gauge algebra of the
electroweak theory is $\mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1)$, with the $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ commuting with the
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$, which is the structure of the commutant in @exm-branching-su3-su2-u1.
:::

The six rotation generators of $\mathbb{R}^4$ can be recombined into two commuting triples. Each triple satisfies the
brackets of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, so $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ is a direct sum.

::: {#exm-direct-sum-so4}
#### Self-dual and anti-self-dual rotations

With the generators $M_{ij}$ of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ (@sec-reductive), the combinations
$$
J_a = -\tfrac12\left(\epsilon_{abc}M_{bc} + M_{a3}\right), \qquad K_a = -\tfrac12\left(\epsilon_{abc}M_{bc} - M_{a3}\right)
$$ {#eq-so4-split}
(with $a, b, c \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ labelling the first three axes and $3$ the fourth, axes numbered $0, 1, 2, 3$ as in
@exr-lrep-so4-matrices) satisfy $[J_a, J_b] = \epsilon_{abc}J_c$, $[K_a, K_b] = \epsilon_{abc}K_c$ and $[J_a, K_b] = 0$
(@prp-so4-split): the six-dimensional $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ is the direct sum of two commuting copies of
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$, the self-dual and anti-self-dual parts, so named because $J$ and $K$ are the $\pm 1$
eigenspaces of the Hodge star (@sec-forms) on antisymmetric matrices.
:::

The splitting of the Lie algebra has a counterpart for groups and for the geometry of the three-sphere. The
three-sphere is itself the group $SU(2)$, which can be multiplied from the left and from the right.

::: {#exm-direct-sum-s3}
#### Isometries of the three-sphere

At the group level $SO(4) \cong (SU(2) \times SU(2))/\mathbb{Z}_2$: $S^3 = SU(2)$ has isometry group $SU(2) \times
SU(2)$ acting by left and right multiplication (@exm-isometry-su2), and the decomposition $\mathfrak{so}(4) =
\mathfrak{so}(3) \oplus \mathfrak{k}$ of @sec-reductive is the diagonal $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ plus its complement.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise splits the unitary algebra $\mathfrak{u}(2)$ into its trace part and its traceless part. It is the
commutant of @exm-lrep-branch-commutant seen on its own.

::: {#exr-lrep-dsum-u2}
#### $\mathfrak{u}(2) = \mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1)$

Show that every anti-Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrix is uniquely $X = X_0 + \tfrac12(\operatorname{tr}X)\mathbb{1}$ with
$X_0 \in \mathfrak{su}(2)$, and that this decomposition is a direct sum of Lie algebras. Is $\mathfrak{u}(2)$
semisimple?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$X_0 = X - \tfrac12(\operatorname{tr}X)\mathbb{1}$ is traceless and anti-Hermitian (the trace of an anti-Hermitian matrix
is imaginary, so $\tfrac12(\operatorname{tr}X)\mathbb{1}$ is anti-Hermitian too), and the decomposition is unique since
$\mathfrak{su}(2) \cap i\mathbb{R}\mathbb{1} = 0$. The identity commutes with everything, and $[X, Y] = [X_0, Y_0]$ is
traceless, so the brackets are those of $\mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1)$. It is not semisimple: the summand
$\mathfrak{u}(1)$ is abelian, not simple. Its centre $i\mathbb{R}\mathbb{1}$ is the obstruction.
:::

The second exercise describes the irreducible representations of a direct sum. They are tensor products of
irreducible representations of the summands, and their dimensions multiply.

::: {#exr-lrep-dsum-reps}
#### Representations of a direct sum

Given representations $\rho_1$ of $\mathfrak{g}_1$ on $V_1$ and $\rho_2$ of $\mathfrak{g}_2$ on $V_2$, show that $\rho(X_1 +
X_2) = \rho_1(X_1) \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes \rho_2(X_2)$ is a representation of $\mathfrak{g}_1 \oplus \mathfrak{g}_2$.
Find the dimensions and the weights, with respect to $(J_3, K_3)$, of the representations $(j, k)$ of $\mathfrak{su}(2)
\oplus \mathfrak{su}(2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[\rho(X_1 + X_2), \rho(Y_1 + Y_2)] = [\rho_1(X_1), \rho_1(Y_1)] \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes [\rho_2(X_2), \rho_2(Y_2)]$, since the
cross terms $\rho_1(X_1) \otimes \rho_2(Y_2)$ appear twice with opposite signs; this is $\rho([X_1, Y_1] + [X_2, Y_2])$.
The representation $(j, k)$ has dimension $(2j + 1)(2k + 1)$ and the weights $(m, n)$ with $|m| \leq j$, $|n| \leq k$
(steps of one), each once: a rectangle in the weight plane. For example $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ has the four weights
$(\pm\tfrac12, \pm\tfrac12)$ (@exm-lrep-so4-vector).
:::

The third exercise reads the direct-sum structure off the Cartan matrix and the Dynkin diagram, using Sage. The
Cartan type $D_2$ of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ turns out to be $A_1 \times A_1$.

::: {#exr-lrep-dsum-cartan}
#### Disconnected Dynkin diagrams

With Sage, print the Cartan matrices of the types $A_1 \times A_1$, $D_2$ and $A_2 \times A_1$, check that their Dynkin
diagrams are disconnected, and compute the dimensions of the representations $(\mathbf{3}, \mathbf{2})$ and
$(\mathbf{8}, \mathbf{3})$ of $\mathfrak{su}(3) \oplus \mathfrak{su}(2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The simple roots of the two summands are orthogonal, so the Cartan matrix is block diagonal; $D_2$ has the same matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(2, 2)$ as $A_1 \times A_1$, which is $\mathfrak{so}(4) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus
\mathfrak{su}(2)$ at the level of root systems. The dimensions multiply (@exr-lrep-dsum-reps): $3 \cdot 2 = 6$ and $8
\cdot 3 = 24$:

{{< sage exr-lrep-dsum-cartan >}}
:::
::::

The proposition states the splitting of @exm-direct-sum-so4 as a list of matrix identities. Each of them can be
checked entry by entry on $4 \times 4$ matrices.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-so4-split}
#### $\mathfrak{so}(4) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{su}(2)$

The matrices @eq-so4-split satisfy the $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ relations separately and commute with each other.
:::

`KaluzaKlein.Representations.JK_of_M4`, entry by entry, with the axes numbered $0, 1, 2, 3$.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Representations.so4_splits_commute >}}

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The defining representation of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ on $\mathbb{C}^4$ has four weights. Under the splitting they form
the representation $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$, a doublet of each $\mathfrak{su}(2)$.

::: {#exm-lrep-so4-vector}
#### The vector of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ is $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$

Take the Cartan generators $J_3 = -\tfrac12(M_{01} + M_{23})$ and $K_3 = -\tfrac12(M_{01} - M_{23})$ of @exr-so4-jk.
$iM_{01}$ has eigenvalues $\pm 1$ on the plane $(x_0, x_1)$ and $0$ on $(x_2, x_3)$, and $iM_{23}$ the reverse. So
$(iJ_3, iK_3)$ has the weights $\mp(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ on the first plane and $\mp(\tfrac12, -\tfrac12)$ on the second:
the four weights $(\pm\tfrac12, \pm\tfrac12)$ of $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$, of dimension $2 \cdot 2 = 4$
(@exr-lrep-so4-matrices).
:::

The adjoint representation of a direct sum is the sum of the adjoints of the summands. For $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ this
splits the six generators into the two triples.

::: {#exm-lrep-so4-adjoint}
#### The adjoint of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$

The $J_a$ span a triplet of the first $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ on which the second acts trivially, and the $K_a$ the
reverse: the adjoint is $(1, 0) \oplus (0, 1)$, of dimension $3 + 3 = 6$. In the language of forms, the
antisymmetric matrices, or two-forms on $\mathbb{R}^4$, split into self-dual and anti-self-dual parts
(@exm-direct-sum-so4).
:::

The rotations of the first three axes form a subalgebra $\mathfrak{so}(3) \subset \mathfrak{so}(4)$. In terms of the
splitting it is the diagonal $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, and the branchings follow from Clebsch-Gordan.

::: {#exm-lrep-so4-diagonal}
#### The diagonal $\mathfrak{so}(3)$

From @eq-so4-split, $J_a + K_a$ involves only the $M_{bc}$ with $b, c$ among the first three axes: the diagonal
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$ is the $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ fixing the fourth axis. Restricted to it, $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12) \to
\tfrac12 \otimes \tfrac12 = 1 \oplus 0$, which is $\mathbb{R}^4 = \mathbb{R}^3 \oplus \mathbb{R}$, and $(1, 0) \oplus
(0, 1) \to 1 \oplus 1$, which is $\mathfrak{so}(4) = \mathfrak{so}(3) \oplus \mathfrak{k}$ with $\mathfrak{k}$ spanned by
the $M_{a3}$ (@exr-lrep-restrict-diagonal).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks two of the brackets of the proposition by hand. It uses the general bracket formula of the
rotation generators.

::: {#exr-so4-jk}
#### Checking the splitting by hand

Verify $[J_3, K_3] = 0$ and $[J_1, J_2] = J_3$ from the brackets of the $M_{ij}$ computed in @exr-so4-coset.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$J_3 = -\tfrac12(M_{01} + M_{23})$ and $K_3 = -\tfrac12(M_{01} - M_{23})$ (in the labels of @sec-reductive, where
the axes are $0, 1, 2, 3$), and $[M_{01}, M_{23}] = 0$ since the pairs share no index, so $[J_3, K_3] =
\tfrac14([M_{01}, -M_{23}] + [M_{23}, M_{01}]) = 0$. For $[J_1, J_2]$ expand the four brackets with
$[M_{ij}, M_{kl}] = \delta_{jk}M_{il} - \delta_{ik}M_{jl} - \delta_{jl}M_{ik} + \delta_{il}M_{jk}$ and collect:
the result is $-\tfrac12(M_{01} + M_{23}) = J_3$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The bracket $[J_1, J_2] = J_3$ is part of the theorem `KaluzaKlein.Representations.so4_splits_brackets`.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The second exercise repeats the whole computation in Sage with explicit $4 \times 4$ matrices, with the axes numbered
$0, 1, 2, 3$. It also computes the weights of @exm-lrep-so4-vector.

::: {#exr-lrep-so4-matrices}
#### The splitting with explicit matrices

With $(M_{ij})_{kl} = \delta_{ik}\delta_{jl} - \delta_{il}\delta_{jk}$ on axes $0, 1, 2, 3$, define $J_a = -\tfrac12(M_{bc} +
M_{a3})$ and $K_a = -\tfrac12(M_{bc} - M_{a3})$ for $(a, b, c)$ a cyclic permutation of $(0, 1, 2)$. Check all
brackets of @prp-so4-split, write $J_0$ in terms of the $M_{ij}$, and find the simultaneous eigenvalues of
$(iJ_2, iK_2)$ on $\mathbb{C}^4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In these labels $J_2 = -\tfrac12(M_{01} + M_{23})$ is the $J_3$ of @exr-so4-jk. All brackets hold, $J_0 = -\tfrac12(M_{12} +
M_{03})$, and the weights are $(\pm\tfrac12, \pm\tfrac12)$:

{{< sage exr-lrep-so4-matrices >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The labels and matrices are those of the Lean file: $J_0$ is the matrix of
`KaluzaKlein.Representations.JK_of_M4`.

**Sage.** The computation in the solution above.
:::

The third exercise justifies the names self-dual and anti-self-dual. The Hodge star acts on antisymmetric $4 \times 4$
matrices, and the $J_a$ and $K_a$ are its eigenvectors.

::: {#exr-lrep-so4-hodge}
#### Self-dual and anti-self-dual

Define $(\star M)_{ij} = \tfrac12\epsilon_{ijkl}M_{kl}$ with $\epsilon_{0123} = 1$. Show that $\star M_{01} = M_{23}$,
$\star M_{12} = M_{03}$, $\star M_{02} = -M_{13}$ and $\star^2 = 1$, and deduce that, in the labels of
@exr-lrep-so4-matrices, $\star J_a = J_a$ and $\star K_a = -K_a$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\star M_{01})_{ij} = \tfrac12(\epsilon_{ij01} - \epsilon_{ij10}) = \epsilon_{ij01}$, non-zero only for $\{i, j\} = \{2,
3\}$, with $\epsilon_{2301} = 1$ (the permutation $(02)(13)$ is even): $\star M_{01} = M_{23}$. Likewise $\epsilon_{0312}
= 1$ (a $3$-cycle) gives $\star M_{12} = M_{03}$, and $\epsilon_{1302} = -1$ (a $4$-cycle) gives $\star M_{02} =
-M_{13}$. Applying the same computation to the images shows $\star^2 = 1$. Then $J_2 = -\tfrac12(M_{01} + M_{23})$ and
$J_0 = -\tfrac12(M_{12} + M_{03})$ are fixed by $\star$, and $J_1 = -\tfrac12(M_{20} + M_{13}) = -\tfrac12(-M_{02} +
M_{13})$ is mapped to $-\tfrac12(M_{13} - M_{02}) = J_1$; the $K_a$, with the opposite relative sign, change sign.
:::
::::

### Exercises {#sec-representations-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Three exercises that combine the three sections of this chapter: the octet of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ seen through weights,
roots and branching at once, the full root-system analysis of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$, and the decuplet with its weights,
highest weight and branching.

The first integrative exercise builds the adjoint of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ from the fundamental in three independent
ways. The final check is that restriction commutes with tensor products, so the branching of the octet follows from
that of the triplet.

::: {#exr-lrep-int-octet}
#### The octet three ways

(a) Check with the Weyl character ring that $\mathbf{3} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{3}} = \mathbf{8} \oplus \mathbf{1}$. (b)
Using @exr-lrep-weight-tensor, show that the weights of $\mathbf{3} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{3}}$ are the six roots and the
zero weight three times. (c) Using the branchings of $\mathbf{3}$ and $\bar{\mathbf{3}}$ (@exr-branching-charges,
@exm-lrep-branch-3bar) and @eq-clebsch-gordan, branch $\mathbf{3} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{3}}$ under $\mathfrak{su}(2)
\times \mathfrak{u}(1)$ and recover @eq-branching-su3.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) is a one-line computation in Sage. (b) The weights are $w_a - w_b$; for $a = b$ this is $0$ three times, and for $a
\neq b$ the differences of the corners of the triangle, which are the six roots (also checked in
`figures/su3_weights.sage`). Removing one zero weight for the singlet leaves the weights of the adjoint
(@exm-weight-adjoint). (c) $(\mathbf{2}_{1/\sqrt3} \oplus \mathbf{1}_{-2/\sqrt3}) \otimes (\mathbf{2}_{-1/\sqrt3} \oplus
\mathbf{1}_{2/\sqrt3})$: charges add and spins combine by Clebsch-Gordan, giving $\mathbf{2} \otimes \mathbf{2} =
\mathbf{3}_0 \oplus \mathbf{1}_0$, $\mathbf{2}_{1/\sqrt3} \otimes \mathbf{1}_{2/\sqrt3} = \mathbf{2}_{\sqrt3}$,
$\mathbf{1}_{-2/\sqrt3} \otimes \mathbf{2}_{-1/\sqrt3} = \mathbf{2}_{-\sqrt3}$ and $\mathbf{1}_0$. Removing the singlet
$\mathbf{1}_0$ of (a) leaves @eq-branching-su3:

{{< sage exr-lrep-int-octet >}}
:::

The second integrative exercise treats $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ as a rank-two algebra in its own right. Its Cartan subalgebra,
roots and Cartan matrix are computed from the splitting, and the result is compared with the hexagon of
$\mathfrak{su}(3)$.

::: {#exr-lrep-int-so4}
#### The root system of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$

Using @prp-so4-split: (a) show that $\operatorname{span}(J_3, K_3)$ is a Cartan subalgebra; (b) find the roots with
respect to $(iJ_3, iK_3)$, with root vectors built from the ladder operators of the two copies of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$;
(c) choose simple roots and compute the Cartan matrix; (d) compare the number of roots and the dimension with
$\mathfrak{su}(3)$, which also has rank two.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $J_3$ and $K_3$ commute by @prp-so4-split, and an element $\sum_a(x_aJ_a + y_aK_a)$ commuting with both has $x
\parallel e_3$ and $y \parallel e_3$ by @exr-lrep-cartan-axis applied to each summand: the span is maximal abelian, rank
$2$ (@exm-cartan-abelian). (b) The ladder operators $J_\pm$ of the first copy commute with $K_3$ and have $iJ_3$-weights
$\pm 1$ (@exm-ladder-adjoint), so their roots are $(\pm 1, 0)$; those of the second copy give $(0, \pm 1)$. Four roots
and rank two make $\dim = 6$, as it should. (c) With a direction such as $\ell(\mu) = \mu_1 + 2\mu_2$ the positive roots
are $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$, both simple and orthogonal, so $A = \operatorname{diag}(2, 2)$, the disconnected diagram of
type $A_1 \times A_1 = D_2$ (@exm-cartan-su2-matrix, @exr-lrep-dsum-cartan). (d) $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ has six roots
forming a hexagon, at angles of $60°$, and dimension $8$; the four roots of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ form a square whose
simple roots meet at $90°$, the case $A_{12}A_{21} = 0$ of @exr-lrep-cartan-angles.
:::

The third integrative exercise studies the decuplet $\mathbf{10}$, which appears in $\mathbf{3} \otimes \mathbf{3} \otimes
\mathbf{3}$. Its weights form a large triangle, shown in the interactive version of @fig-su3-weights, and its
branching is a tower of spins.

::: {#exr-lrep-int-decuplet}
#### The decuplet

(a) Decompose $\mathbf{3} \otimes \mathbf{3} \otimes \mathbf{3}$ with Sage. (b) List the weights of $\mathbf{10} =
\operatorname{Sym}^3\mathbf{3}$ in the $(\lambda_3, \lambda_8)$ plane (@exr-lrep-root-ambient) and check that the highest
weight is $3\omega_1$. (c) Branch $\mathbf{10}$ under $\mathfrak{su}(2) \times \mathfrak{u}(1)$ with $\lambda_8$-charges,
and check that the charges add up to zero (@exr-lrep-branch-trace).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $\mathbf{3} \otimes \mathbf{3} = \mathbf{6} \oplus \bar{\mathbf{3}}$ (@exr-lrep-hw-6), and then $\mathbf{6} \otimes
\mathbf{3} = \mathbf{10} \oplus \mathbf{8}$, $\bar{\mathbf{3}} \otimes \mathbf{3} = \mathbf{8} \oplus \mathbf{1}$: $27 =
10 + 8 + 8 + 1$. (b) The weights are $w_a + w_b + w_c$, $a \leq b \leq c$, ten points of multiplicity one on a triangle
with corners $3w_u = (3, \sqrt3)$, $3w_d = (-3, \sqrt3)$ and $3w_s = (0, -2\sqrt3)$; the highest is $3w_u = 3\omega_1$.
(c) Grouping by the number of $s$ quarks, the charges are $\sqrt3$, $0$, $-\sqrt3$, $-2\sqrt3$ with $\lambda_3$-strings of
lengths $4, 3, 2, 1$: $\mathbf{10} \to \mathbf{4}_{\sqrt3} \oplus \mathbf{3}_0 \oplus \mathbf{2}_{-\sqrt3} \oplus
\mathbf{1}_{-2\sqrt3}$, the $\Delta$, $\Sigma^*$, $\Xi^*$ and $\Omega^-$ of the baryon decuplet. The charges sum to
$4\sqrt3 + 0 - 2\sqrt3 - 2\sqrt3 = 0$:

{{< sage exr-lrep-int-decuplet >}}
:::
::::
